#3558. The Martian Author Andy Weir Explains The One Thing He Would Change About The Story [Exclusive]

Looking back at the success of 2015's "The Martian," it's remarkable to realize just how influential this crowd-pleasing blockbuster really was. It helped launch author Andy Weir to the upper echelon of sci-fi writers, paving the way for even bigger box office hits like 2026's "Project Hail Mary." Alongside Christopher Nolan's "Interstellar" in 2014 and Alfonso Cuarón's "Gravity" the year before, Ridley Scott's adaptation also served as a bellwether for the mid-2010s "space race" in film. And, for those of a certain age, there's something genuinely nostalgic about the tone struck by both the source material and the movie — a last gasp of the sense of optimism and unity that defined the Obama-era U.S.

So, when I had the chance to speak with Weir over a Zoom interview, as he's promoting his newest original project as an executive producer on Audible's "Exoplanet" series (due later this month), I jumped at the chance to revisit the whirlwind experience of "The Martian." Has over a decade of hindsight given Weir a different perspective on his game-changing book, now that he's more established as a novelist? In response, the science-abiding author maintained he wouldn't change anything ... except for the natural disaster that sets the plot in motion in the first place on the surface of Mars:

"If I had it to do over again, there's a few minor changes I'd make. I'd probably make the initial problem not be a windstorm, because that windstorm was not physics-accurate. I'd probably have it be — well, I've since learned that there's lightning strikes on Mars, and that could be something. Lightning strikes something, it causes overload here, that causes an explosion there, and then [the other astronauts have] all got to bail, something like that."

When things just happen to fall into place perfectly, you count your blessings and don't look back. That's more or less the mindset Andy Weir has with "The Martian." Unlike his hands-on role with "Project Hail Mary," Weir notes in our conversation, he was much more of a passenger on this first adaptation of his work. As a result, he simply sat back and let director Ridley Scott and screenwriter Drew Goddard do their thing along with some of the best and most talented actors in the world.

Sure, the part of his brain obsessed with making things as realistic and scientifically-accurate as can be may have some corrections or two. In the book, everything goes haywire when astronaut Mark Watney is separated from his fellow crew during a hellish windstorm and is left behind on the surface of Mars, presumed dead. But while there are dust storms on the surface of Mars, Weir is correct to note that the atmosphere and gravity of the planet couldn't sustain one of this magnitude. "But other than that," he tells me, "I don't think I'd change anything."

He goes on to compare the success of "The Martian" to, well, I'll let Weir's quirky sense of humor speak for itself:

"It's like, have you ever been casually talking to a beautiful woman and then you realize she's interested in you, and you have no idea what you did right, but you don't want to jinx it? That's kind of what happened to me with 'The Martian.' I'm like, 'I don't know what I did right, but I'm sure as hell not going to change anything.' [laughs]"

For those interested in more sci-fi approved by Weir, "Exoplanet" hits Audible on November 5, 2026.

#3557. The Fitbit Edge Is Everything the Charge 6 Should Have Been

I’ve been using the new Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, and am happy to report that it’s quite good at its job. It shipped with more features than I expected (Google Maps directions were there from the jump) and corrects the missteps that Google made with the Fitbit Charge 6. After running the Fitbit Edge through its paces, here’s my breakdown of what works well, what doesn’t, and what I think of the device overall.

When I reviewed it in May 2025, I liked a lot about the Charge 6, but found it had a few serious flaws. Tightening the strap messed up its GPS readings (weird but true), and some of its features required a subscription (like the music controls that only worked with YouTube Music). Its promised side button wasn’t really a button, and didn’t even always work.

I’m happy to report that all of my biggest gripes have been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Or to put it another way: the Edge is what the Charge should have been in the first place.

Accuracy tests are always one of my top priorities in testing, but honestly I wasn’t expecting much from this device. A Fitbit can still be successful in my eyes even if its heart rate sensor is only “good enough.” Nobody should expect lab-level precision from a Fitbit.

But I was pleasantly surprised by just how capable the Edge is in this regard. It sometimes takes a few minutes to lock on to a heart rate signal (as most optical devices do), but after it does, it is spot-on—I think it might be in the running alongside the Apple Watch and high-end Garmins as one of the better heart rate wearables on the market. The Edge’s accuracy is notably better than the Fitbit Air's, even though they seem to share the same sensor hardware.

Location accuracy is also quite good, only deviating slightly from a Garmin I tested alongside the Edge. It may not be the best out there, but it’s miles ahead of what the Charge 6 was able to do.

The Fitbit Edge has real music controls, unlike the Charge 6. I can play something in Spotify or in Castro (my favorite podcast app) on my phone, and then control the audio from my wrist—and you no longer need to use YouTube Music or have a subscription to get this feature.

When the Fitbit Air and the Google Health app first launched, it was possible to pair both a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch to the same phone, but not two Fitbits. That has finally changed: I was able to connect the Edge to my phone without losing my connection to the Air. It also works to swap seamlessly between the two Fitbits. For example, one night the Edge was low on battery, so I slept with the Air on, and then swapped back in the morning once the Edge was charged. The app happily showed my sleep data from the Air and my activity data from the Edge without my having to do mess around in the app.

As a nice bonus, the charger for the Fitbit Edge is the same as for the Fitbit Air. (The chargers for the Pixel Watch and for the Fitbit Charge 6 are not compatible with the Edge.)

The Fitbit Edge is a similar size as the old Charge 6, but with noticeably more screen real estate. The strap fits pretty much the same way as a Pixel watch band—that is to say, normally, not with the strange hang-off-the-wrist stiffness of the Charge 6.

The Fitbit Edge also has a physical button—not a haptic nub like the Charge 6, but an actual, physical button. And it even works (to return you to the home screen) nearly every time I press it. The Charge 6’s nub was not as reliable.

Overall, I’m quite happy with the Fitbit Edge. It’s much better than the Charge 6, and adds accuracy and a screen to the things I already liked about the Fitbit Air. But there are a few things I don’t totally love.

One is that there is no NFC chipset, which means no option to use Google Pay. I don’t mind using my phone or card at checkouts (and I always carry my phone), so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I know a lot of folks love a wrist-based payment, and that’s missing from the Fitbit Edge. (Google reportedly said most Fitbit users didn’t actually use Google Pay, so they removed the functionality—presumably to fit in the other components while keeping the device small.)

The other downside is, I hate to say it, the Google Health app. It’s OK, but I still find myself arguing with the AI when it assigns me workouts I never asked for, and I have to agree with the redditors who are commiserating about the lack of a “yesterday” view. (On the bright side, Google recently added a feature that lets you turn off the AI insights, which helps a lot.)

Overall, the Fitbit Edge is a great fitness tracker. It measures heart rate and running/walking mileage accurately; it can control music in a sensible way; and it looks good, feels good to wear, and works smoothly. The price also tracks: It’s definitely worth the $20 premium over the Charge 6, and it’s not quite double the price of the Air, which I think is fair. For anyone who doesn’t want a smartwatch or a running watch and will be satisfied with just “a Fitbit,” this one is pretty much perfect.

#3556. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR looks awesome, but I’m not rushing to upgrade

After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet.

The new MacBook Pro is substantially lighter. That’s a major improvement, especially if you’re someone who carries around a 16-inch MacBook Pro. With this new PROLED XDR generation, the 14-inch model reduced in weight by 0.5 pounds, and the 16-inch model reduced by 0.7 pounds. That’s a great deal when you’re carrying it around in a backpack or similar. The new models are also marginally thinner.

For me, though, I find myself a bit surprised by the fact that nothing about the top case design changed. The keyboard, trackpad, speaker, and port layouts all look about the same, and the chassis didn’t change shape besides getting a bit thinner. For every MacBook Pro overhaul in the past, the top case has changed in a meaningful way. With this overhaul, it really feels like more of a display upgrade that’s also accompanied by a lighter chassis.

Was there anything wrong with the current MacBook Pro chassis? Not at all. However, you could also argue the same for most design shifts in Apple’s history. It would’ve been nice to have a slightly different look, beyond the display.

This is more of a personal point. That said, I already have an M4 Pro model, and given the fact that these new MacBook Pros are substantially more expensive ($400 more compared to the miniLED MacBook Pros, which are also $300 more than they were prior to the June price hikes), I’m not particularly excited to buy silicon that isn’t the latest and greatest. The M5 family kicked off last year, and we already know M7 is coming next year.

I fully understand why Apple opted to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but it sure does make this MacBook Pro feel ever so slightly more uninteresting.

Apple already alluded to the fact that they have more in the pipeline when it comes to macOS optimizations for touch, so maybe I’ll be wowed in the future. For now though, aside from being able to interact with the iOS simulator with proper touch, I don’t really see much of a need to have touch on my Mac.

It’s great that it’s there, and I’m certainly not disappointed that Apple added it – but I’m not yet convinced I truly need it.

None of this was to bash on the new MacBook Pro at all. In fact, I’ll most definitely be buying one in the future, most likely once it gains M7 Pro and M7 Max chips by this time next year. Hopefully touch feels more important by then. I certainly love the idea of having a glowing Apple logo again, just not quite yet – and it’s not like this product will be going anywhere if I don’t buy it during the first iteration.

I bought a ridiculously overpowered M1 Max with 64GB of memory back when they were first released, and I have zero incentive to upgrade to this day. This machine covers all my needs with ease still.

It’s also worth noting I haven’t yet seen the new display in person. It’s totally possible I’ll be blown away once I see it, but I still think I’ll be capable of waiting. Especially since my M4 Pro MacBook Pro already has a 1000 nit display, so I’m not missing out too terribly from the OLED model.

How do you feel about the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? Will you be buying one, or are you in a similar boat as I am? Let us know in the comments.

#3555. GTA 5’s Unsolvable Mystery Broke Fans for Over a Decade, and GTA 6 Should Do It Again

Mount Chiliad spawned thousands of theories

In Grand Theft Auto 5, one landmark was visible practically no matter where you were in San Andreas: Mount Chiliad. "Claimed by the Spanish in 1769, Mount Chiliad is the highest peak in San Andreas, sitting at a height of 2,744 meters," reads a sign at the nearby Silent Probe Mountain art installation. "Taken under Mexican control in 1821, it was then, and remains in American hands since 1847."

It's more than just a mountain, though. Once the player has achieved 100% story completion, standing atop the mountain at 3 a.m. during cloudy weather reveals a UFO, hovering in the night sky. It's marked with an F.I.B. logo, aka the Federal Investigation Bureau, implying that it was created by the government. However, there's also reason to believe that the mysterious aircraft is a hoax, because it doesn't react to bullets, and raindrops nearby become pixelated.

The running theory is that it's a hologram, as opposed to the two other functional UFOs in the game, which are physical objects. They're located high in the sky above both Fort Zancudo and the Silent Probe Mountain respectively, they can both be collided with, and they emit electromagnetic pulses that cause the player's vehicle to shut down if they get too close. There's reason to believe they're both also government-controlled: the former visually looks somewhat similar to a real-life B-2 Spirit stealth bomber and, when viewed using third-party software, has two human pilots inside. The latter also has F.I.B. printed on the side, much like the UFO above Mt. Chiliad.

Players knew there was at least one secret at the top of the mountain, thanks to graffiti on the back of the observation deck that reads "come back when your story is complete." GTA Online revealed that the mountain is also home to a nuclear launch facility. But some players are convinced that Mt. Chiliad holds one final mystery that is still unsolved to this day.

Inside the tramway station near the summit, a mural depicts an abstract interpretation of the mountain itself. At the top is an eye, while the exterior of the mountain has lightning bolts emanating from it. Inside the mountain is a maze of perpendicular connecting lines. Each one connects to one of eight squares. Five of them are small, marked with an X inside. The three larger ones at the bottom of the picture show, from left to right, a UFO, a cracked egg, and a person wearing a jetpack.

One week after GTA 5 was released, on Sept. 24, 2013, fans created the Chiliad Mystery subreddit. For the last 13 years, users there have been dedicated to uncovering the secrets believed to be held within. The community worked out that the X's correspond to petroglyphs hidden around the mountain, each of which depicts a weather status required for the Mt. Chiliad UFO to appear. There's also a theory that each X also represents the roman numeral for 10, and since there are five of them, it's representative of the 50 collectible spaceship (aka UFO) parts scattered across San Andreas.

In the GTA Online mission involving the nuclear facility, the player escapes by using a jetpack. Is that what the jetpack drawing on the mural is referring to? It’s one of the mural’s lingering riddles. It's certainly plausible, if a little underwhelming, because the common belief was that unraveling the mystery would result in a permanent jetpack vehicle, usable in GTA 5’s single-player mode, not exclusive to Online. However, some think the jetpack just refers to the UFO above Fort Zancudo, because in GTA: San Andreas, the jetpack is found at the military base.

Then there's the cracked egg. This has been the biggest source of confusion for the sleuths working on the mystery, and there are a number of theories. It could refer to the Epsilon cult, as they believe the world hatched from an egg. It could also tie in to the fountain by the Maze Bank Tower in Los Santos, as the two bear a close resemblance. Or there's the most common theory, which is that it is simply a hint to the underwater UFO found in Paleto Bay, on the northern coast of San Andreas.

So with all of that in mind, there's every chance that the mural is simply one giant hint to finding each of the UFOs in GTA 5. But believing that would also mean believing that the Chiliad mystery is solved, and there's no fun in that, because it would be a seriously disappointing outcome. And for the users on the subreddit, that isn't even a possibility.

There are hundreds of loose ends and theories players have discovered. Even in the last year, they’ve posted dozens of new ideas. Here's user Alexisuwuu23, who is convinced an in-game film, "Capolavoro," holds the secret because a billboard ad for it can be found at the location where streetlights form a question mark if looked at from the observatory, and it all ties into a disappearing ladder. "Intentional, obviously," reads one reply. "Gotta be a marker or something. The hunt continues."

In September, AntelopeIcy6558 posed a theory about the eight lights on top of the Maze Bank Tower helipad. "I believe that to solve the secret, you need to shoot these eight lights in a certain order," the post reads. "Why? I believe there are eight locations around Los Santos that we need to find. Each of these locations from some angle resembles a keyhole, which is one of the main symbols of this mystery."

There are other theories that think the mystery stretches beyond GTA 5, and also includes Red Dead Redemption 2. Cancelled DLCs and datamined files have revealed a vast array of potential clues, but since those projects were never officially released, they're unlikely to ever provide a definitive answer. Then there are those who predict GTA 6 will provide a resolution.

Twelve years ago, user talkol made a post titled "pretty solid proof that the game was released without a jetpack or flyable UFO," which outlined what is still the most damning evidence we've had: there is nothing hinting at either of those vehicles in the game's files. Of course, that didn't dissuade the masses, because posts like these have been non-stop for the last 13 years.

Last year, as reported on by IGN, YouTuber Gator Keys uploaded a video titled "This is The End of the Mount Chiliad Mystery." He kicks it off by stating what many realists would agree with: "I'm not claiming I'm the first person to come to this conclusion. I'm sure many other players did in 2013, but for some reason, the Mt. Chiliad mystery remains in 2025. So there needs to be a video that puts an end to it before GTA 6 releases."

Gator Keys goes into plenty of detail in the eight-minute-long video, but to sum it up, his explanation is that the mystery is nowhere near as deep as the community had believed. The answer is essentially that the government is all-seeing and all-powerful, as represented by the F.I.B. logos on the UFOs and the eye on top of the mural. It's simply a satirical take on real life, similar to the idea of the Illuminati.

Ultimately, the "true" answer for the Chiliad mystery is irrelevant. The mystery itself spawned a thousands-strong community, with everyone cooperating and theorizing. It's reminiscent of when that kid at school promised they'd found Mew underneath a truck in Pokémon Red and Blue. Easter eggs and gaming mysteries these days are usually solved within days, thanks to datamining and the sharing of information via the internet. GTA 5, on the other hand, whether intentionally or not, gave players something to talk about for 13 years.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

There's no doubt GTA 6 will spawn plenty more theories and Easter eggs, whether they're a continuation of the Chiliad mystery or something entirely new. It'll also likely be the biggest video game of all time, whether it includes a decade-long mystery or not. But the longevity of the Chiliad mystery makes one thing clear: Rockstar is the champion of this type of lore, and including something similar, where the game never truly feels complete without it being solved, will keep a huge portion of the community occupied for years to come.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there’s one thing I know about Rebecca Yarros and her Fourth Wing books, it’s that she’s not afraid to kill anyone. That was clear from the moment Violet and co. stepped onto the parapet, and it became painfully obvious after our dearly beloved Liam’s death in the first book. Now, as we wait for book four (and the book-to-screen adaptation that just found its Violet and Xaden), the author has revealed that she had plans to kill off more characters than she did in Onyx Storm, and they’ll have to go in the next installment. So, yeah, I’m worried, and I’m really anxious about one specific character.

Listen, I spiral over comments Yarros makes about what’s going to happen in her books even harder than I spiral over updates and fancasts for the Fourth Wing TV show. So, you can imagine the panic I was sent into when she said the following at Iron Flame Night (via domloves2read):

So, I know when I’m in the book, when I start the book, who is going to die. Now, when I wrote Onyx [Storm] I actually was going to kill off other people at the end. And the way I had to shift the plot, and the way I had to shift things so that it wouldn’t feel like other books and it would have its own separate ending, it left some people alive that should not be alive that I will have to take care of in this book.

Yarros went on to clarify that she didn’t tell the audience if said characters “were good or bad,” and she poked fun at them, saying they are prone to jumping to conclusions that often involve her “plotting Ridoc’s murder.” She also said she always knows who she’s going to kill in a battle before she writes it, and she plants seeds ahead of time so we feel connected to those characters.

So, with all that in mind, I’ve realized I’m actually super duper worried about one character who (at least for now) is alive.

I know, I know, I can’t believe I’m writing this either: I really think Rhiannon could die in book four, and maybe Yarros had plans to kill her in Onyx Storm. So, let’s walk through why.

I actually got to this conclusion through a weird process of elimination. I was mostly thinking about what characters are either dealing with loose ends or are such a vital part of the story that they can’t die. Think characters potentially involved in the brother mystery, like Bodhi and Garrick, or those involved with Violet’s memory loss, like Imogen. Along with that, characters like Aaric are so powerful that it feels like they have a greater purpose to serve.

Plus, with the death of Violet’s mom, I don’t think Brennan or Mira will go (yet). I also don't think Dain or Sloane will die, considering their seemingly budding relationship. Then, just from a vibes perspective, I don’t think Ridoc will die (yet). And Swayer has already been through too much with going through first year twice and losing his leg.

Through that process, considering whose death would hurt Violet the most and just thinking about what’s happened in the first three books, I landed on Rhiannon as the character who was maybe going to die in Onyx Storm.

Other than Xaden and her siblings, I think Rhi’s death would hit Violet the hardest since she’s her best friend.

Now, adding to all that, a brutal Fourth Wing parallel led me to this conclusion, too. Think about it, of all the people in Violet’s crew, Rhi is probably the best of the bunch. She’s a natural leader, she was born to be a rider, and she’s simply a very good person. You know who else was near-perfect and all those things? Liam. And he died toward the end of Fourth Wing.

Yarros specifically said she didn’t kill a character in Onyx Storm because she didn’t want it to feel like the end of other books. If Rhi had died, it could have felt a whole lot like what happened to Liam. It would hurt Violet in a very similar way, and it would be the death of another hero, a good one, in this story.

So, yes, going into book four, I’m very worried for Rhiannon. However, for now, I’m going to choose to be very happy that she’s still alive and will live to see another page (for now).

#3553. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

#3552. 50 Years Ago Today: John Carpenter Directed A Gritty Action Thriller That Became A Cult Classic

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Retired filmmaker John Carpenter is best known for his horror films. After all, we don't have the modern slasher film without "Halloween." But before Michael Myers returned to Haddonfield on Halloween night 1978, Carpenter tried his hand at an action-exploitation film: 1976's "Assault on Precinct 13," which opened in theaters 50 years ago today.

Carpenter was born in 1948, the perfect age to grow up on cowboy movies. He dreamed of going to Hollywood to make Westerns, not horror films. But, by the time he enrolled in University of South California film school in 1968, Westerns had already faded as Hollywood's biggest genre. Throughout his decades-long filmmaking career, Carpenter never directed a Western — but you can see that longing in "Assault on Precinct 13." The movie has a courageous lawman who has to hold his ground against the black hat gangs. The catch? The movie is set in contemporary Los Angeles, not the Wild West.

Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is overseeing the closure of the LAPD's Precinct 13. A prison bus, carrying convicted murderer Napoleon Wilson (Darwin Joston), also stops at the precinct for a respite. Before long, the building is under siege by bloodthirsty gang members. Bishop, Wilson, and surviving secretary Leigh (Laurie Zimmer) are in a literal fight for their lives as unlikely allies.

Made on a meager budget of $100,000, "Assault on Precinct 13" wasn't an instant mega-hit. Reviews weren't too enthusiastic either. Whitney Williams of Variety was ambivalent, writing backhanded praise like, "some exciting action in second half packs enough interest to keep this entry alive for the violence market." Ellen Edwards of The Miami Herald condemned the film for its "hideous, unmotivated violence." But "Assault on Precinct 13" found its audience. It even got a remake in 2005, starring Laurence Fishburne and Ethan Hawke.

One of John Carpenter's acknowledged influences for "Assault on Precinct 13" is one of the most beloved Westerns ever: Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," about a sheriff (John Wayne) and his deputies trying to keep a murderer with a rich brother and many hired guns locked up. But "Rio Bravo" is not a tense thriller; often called a hangout movie, it's leisurely paced with only bursts of gun violence.

In "Assault on Precinct 13," the threat is everywhere. There's not even a reason for the siege beyond violence for its own sake; there's nothing of value inside the precinct besides more lives to end. That leads into one of the other movies that inspired Carpenter: George Romero's 1968 "Night of the Living Dead," the first modern zombie movie. When asked if "Night of the Living Dead" inspired "Assault on Precinct 13," Carpenter said, half-seriously, "Everybody who made a low-budget film was inspired by ['Night of the Living Dead']."

The comparison rings even more true here. Both movies are about people trapped inside a small building, surrounded by a horde outside that wants to break in and kill them. Both films also cast a Black man as their hero: Stoker as Lt. Bishop in "Precinct 13" and Duane Jones as Ben in "Night of the Living Dead." That was a bigger deal in the 1960s and '70s than it is now, and one spot where Carpenter's exploitation movie is rather progressive. "Living Dead" ends on a famously cynical note, with Ben shot by white men who mistook him as a threat. In "Precinct 13," Bishop and Napoleon Wilson achieve mutual respect; at the end of the movie, they walk out of the basement together as equals.

After its U.S. theatrical release in 1976, "Assault on Precinct 13" played along the European festival circuit, including the Cannes Film Festival and the London Film Festival. (At the latter, it received "deafening applause" per a contemporary review by The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.) Seeing the movie at Cannes, George Romero paid forward the compliment of Carpenter modeling his movie after "Night of the Living Dead."

The most shocking scene in "Assault on Precinct 13" is when a little girl, Kathy (future reality TV star Kim Richards), is shot in the chest after buying an ice cream cone. It's a jaw-dropping scene, and the movie is clearly having perverse fun turning such a taboo of violence against children into a spectacle and sick joke.

Quoted in Jason Zinoman's "Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood, and Invented Modern Horror," Romero testified to this scene's impact: "John Carpenter at Cannes wiped us off the face of the earth with 'Precinct 13.' Right from the scene when the little girl gets blown away, I was blown away." (The same book reports that, to get an R instead of an X rating, Carpenter cut the girl's death from the rating review board then added it back in before the film went to theaters.)

This sort of gang violence is echoed in Carpenter's later "Escape From New York," which is all about a future where the gangs like those in "Precinct 13" have taken over the Big Apple. Like "Escape from New York" and many of his other movies, Carpenter also composed the score for "Precinct 13." The title sequence theme, a synthesized anthem of droning dread, is still the most perfect mood setter for an action thriller even 50 years later.

Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones about a month and a half ago. I can't imagine what it feels like to learn you've been cast as one of the most recognizable characters in the Harry Potter franchise, especially when you're following in the footsteps of the late Alan Rickman. That's exactly the position Paapa Essiedu found himself in when he landed the role of Severus Snape in HBO's upcoming book-to-screen series adaptation. While you'd expect some excitement after getting that phone call, the actor admitted his celebration lasted about as long as it takes to say "Expelliarmus" before reality came crashing down.

With the highly anticipated series arriving on the 2026 TV premiere schedule this Christmas, Essiedu recently spoke with People at the Time100 Next Gala about taking on the iconic Potions professor. The 36-year-old actor admitted he initially experienced "five to 10 seconds" of excitement when he found out he'd gotten the part. Then he remembered that accepting the job meant actually having to play Snape, and his reaction was wonderfully blunt:

It's like, wow, what an honor, what a privilege. And then there's a kind of crushing kind of reality of the reality of what is to come. 'Oh, fuck. I've got to do it now.'

I love how quickly that went from being honored to realizing he'd signed himself up for one heck of a challenge. Honestly, I get it. Rickman's portrayal of Snape remains one of the most beloved performances in the original eight-film franchise. His delivery, intimidating presence and ability to make even the simplest lines sound vaguely threatening helped turn the character into a fan favorite.

Those are some pretty big shoes to fill, and Essiedu knows it. He's already faced considerable backlash over his casting, including racist abuse and death threats from people upset about the decision. The actor previously addressed those reactions, explaining that he understood there would be criticism but remained committed to the role.

Still, despite the pressure surrounding the production, Essiedu seems genuinely excited about the experience. During the same interview, he credited the people working alongside him for making the enormous responsibility feel manageable:

It's a beautiful thing. And with something like this, it's also so much about the people that you're collaborating with, and I feel so much trust and endeavor in the people who I'm standing alongside on this journey. There's a lot of feelings, but they're all good.

That confidence extends to the show's young stars, too. Essiedu had particularly kind things to say about Dominic McLaughlin, Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton, who are taking over the roles of Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, respectively.

Essiedu acknowledged the tremendous responsibility the three child actors carry, especially considering how closely audiences associate the characters with Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson. He described his young co-stars as mature, hardworking performers and said he couldn't wait for audiences to see what they've accomplished.

I think that's worth remembering as we approach the premiere. Much of the conversation surrounding HBO's new Harry Potter adaptation has understandably focused on how the cast will compare to the original movies. But these actors also have the chance to explore the characters across an entire television series, potentially giving them room to develop aspects of the books that the films couldn't fit.

The eight-episode first season, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, premieres Dec. 25 on HBO and streams with an HBO Max subscription. John Lithgow will play Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer takes over as Minerva McGonagall, and Nick Frost steps into Hagrid's enormous boots.

As for Paapa Essiedu, I have to appreciate his willingness to admit that the thrill of getting the job wore off almost immediately. Hopefully, once audiences finally see him teaching Potions at Hogwarts, he'll get to enjoy a little more than 10 seconds of excitement.

#3549. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Pumpkin Lights’ adds a fun jack-o-lantern to your Mac’s menu bar

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Pumpkin Lights is a nifty little menu bar app for Mac that lets you quickly toggle between light mode and dark mode with a ray-traced jack-o-lantern that drops down from the top of your screen. It’s completely free, and very fun to utilize.

If you remember the Festivas menu bar app from Mac year, Pumpkin Lights is very similar in concept.

Pumpkin Lights brings a jack-o-lantern to your menu bar, just in time for halloween. It’s a nice decoration, and there’s plenty of different ways to customize it. You can “grow” many different pumpkin designs, as well as pick between four different color variants.

When you click on the pumpkin or pull on it, your Mac will toggle between light and dark mode – at least by default. Pumpkin Lights also has the option to open an app/website, keep your Mac awake, mute a sound, run a command, or run a shortcut of your choice.

The jack-o-lantern does have proper physics, so you can actually toss it around a bit and move it around in a novel way. You can customize the rope it hangs from, and much more. There’s also an option to have a hanging light bulb that serves a similar purpose.

Why Pumpkin Lights? Here’s what the developer has to say:

The idea came from something most of us do every day without thinking: switching between Light and Dark Mode. It’s always a toggle buried in Control Center or System Settings, and it never feels like anything. I wanted it to feel like touching a real object. So instead of a flat icon, the pumpkin and the bulb are real 3D models, ray-traced in real time, hanging on cords you can swing and spin. When the candle lights, its glow comes through the carved face. I spent most of my time on small details like how the cords move and how light falls on the pumpkin, because I wanted it to still feel delightful the hundredth time you use it, not just the first.

Pumpkin Lights is a completely free utility. You can download it from the developer’s website here, and it’s available for any Mac running macOS 14 Sonoma or later. You can also follow the developer on Twitter.

#3548. ‘Loser Core,’ ‘EBK,’ and Other Gen Z and Gen Alpha Slang You Might Need Help Decoding

If constantly being mogged by sigmas has you feeling like a fuhuhluhtoogan, and you have no idea what any of that means, you've come to the right place. This glossary aims to define and explain popular slang words and phrases of Generation Z (usually defined as people born between 1997 and 2012) and Generation A (anyone born between 2012 and now) so you'll know what the hell people are talking about.

A word of warning: If you aren't of those generations, and/or you need an online list to know what slang words mean, you should not say them aloud unless you're trying to be embarrassing.

Ballhog: A fashion trend among Gen Z and Gen A characterized by wearing vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique retro clothing.

Benny tripping: Intentionally overdosing on Benadryl to experience an (almost always unpleasant) "trip."

Crunged: The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

EBK: stands for "Extreme Baller Knowledge." It goes beyond the sports reference to apply to to anyone who has deep knowledge of a subject. It's usually used ironically.

GiGis: Good game. Pronounced like the name Gigi. The post game pleasantry "good game" has been a staple in sports since forever. Gamers adopted it and shortened it to "GG" in text. So GiGis is a way of saying "good game."

Glass skin: Describes skin that is so smooth, luminous, and clear, it seems to shine.

Loser core: A youth sub-culture/musical sub-genre categorized by listening to depressing, alternative-inspired music and dressing in drab, oversize clothing.

304: Hoe. (Type "304" on a calculator and turn it upside down.)

4+4: Ate. Four plus four is eight, or "ate." (See "ate.")

6-7 (or 67): This piece of Generation Alpha brainrot slang doesn't mean anything. It's just funny to some people to say "6-7," especially in answer to any question involving numbers. Ex: "Q: What time is it? A: six-seveeen."

6-7 weekend: A weekend in which Saturday falls on the 6th day of the month and Sunday on the 7th.

7x7=49: Often refers to a man who is attractive in a self-evident way. Based on the belief that the equation 7x7=49 makes intuitive sense in a way other equations do not.

80/20 rule: An axiom in online incel spaces, the 80/20 is the idea that 80% of women only date the "top" 20% of men.

Algo speak: Coded language used to bypass online content moderation. Examples: "regarded" used instead of "retarded" and "unalive" instead of "kill."

Alpha male: Taken from animal ethology, an alpha male is the dominant member of a group of males, or just a male who is in charge. (See "beta male" and "sigma male.")

Alpine divorce: An alpine divorce is when a man takes his wife or girlfriend on a hike, usually in the mountains, and then just leaves her there to fend for herself.

ASAP (or A$AP): When a rapper has ASAP or A$AP in front of their name, it indicates affiliation with the ASAP Mob, a New York hip-hop collective.

Ate/eat: Done very well, often regarding clothing. e.g.: "You ate that outfit." See also: "serving."

Aura: Someone who is mysterious and cool is said to "have aura."

Aura battle: Aura is coolness or charisma ("rizz" if you prefer). An "aura battle" is a public contest in which the person with the most aura, as determined by the crowd and/or comment section reaction, wins. (See "Aura")

Aura farming: Depending on the context, “aura farming” can refer to a person who does something cool without trying or someone who is trying too hard to appear cool.

Baby Boo syndrome: A joking reference to people who are very into the Baby Boo memes popular on TikTok.

Baddie: A bad/wild girl. Meant as a compliment.

Baka: Japanese word meaning “crazy" or “foolish.” Used mainly in the anime community.

Bed-rotting: Staying in bed all day. You may know it as “lazing around.” (See "Hurkle-durkle.")

Beez: Popularized in Nicki Minaj's 2012 track "Beez in the Trap," beez means something like "I am always." So "beez in the trap" means "I am always in the trap." (See "Trap.")

Beta male: A beta male, or just "beta," is a weaker, subservient male. (See "alpha male" and "sigma male.")

Boombayah: A euphemism for having sex. It’s used mostly online, often to defeat censorship algorithms.

Bop: A girl who sleeps around. Also: a great song.

Boy aquarium: TikTok slang that describes hockey games.

Boy kibble: The male response to "girl dinner," boy kibble is food boys eat. It usually consists of rice and ground beef, often served without spices or vegetables.

Boysober: Someone who has sworn off sex, relationships, and/or dating.

Brain-rot: A description of the overuse of stupid slang. See also: “Skibidi.” Also used to describe the effects of being overly online.

Brat: The contemporary meaning of "brat" is an adjective describing a person who is edgy, imperfect, and confident. It was coined by pop star Charli XCX who defined it as "that girl who is a little messy and likes to party and maybe says some dumb things sometimes. Who feels herself but maybe also has a breakdown."

Bruzz: Bros. Part of the -uzz family of slang words. See "Huzz" and "-uzz."

Bubba truck: A lifted or otherwise modified pick-up truck.

Catch a fade: To have a fight. (See "fade.")

Chad: An attractive man; an “alpha male.” See "Giga-Chad."

Chat: A reference to streamers addressing their chat windows aloud. Saying “chat” in real life is an ironic joke.

Cheesin': The slang word "cheesin'" refers to smiling, particularly a big, goofy smile. It comes from the common exhortation to "say cheese!" before a photo is taken. The word "cheesing," with a "g" at the end, often means the same thing, but it can also refer to the trend of throwing slices of cheese at cars and/or people.

Chopped: Ugly. Chopped is often applied to someone's face or outfit, but anything that isn't aesthetically pleasing could be called "chopped," as could anything that is generally not good, like an awkward situation.

Choppelganger: A portmanteau of "chopped" and "doppelgänger," a choppelganger is someone who looks like another person, but worse. (See "chopped.")

Chud: A physically unappealing person. Sometimes used for a man who holds right-wing views.

Clanker: A slur aimed at robots and AI agents pretending to be human.

Clock that: "I understand and agree." Not to be confused with older slang, where "clock" meant to see, or even older slang where "clock" meant "to hit or punch."

Corn: “Corn” is algo-speak that means “porn.” Used in online spaces where the word might cause your account to be flagged or banned.

Cortisol-coded: Describes something that's meant to be relaxing but is actually stressful, like watching a video of the 5 a.m. yoga routine of an influencer surrounded by $400 candles.

Coworker-core: A catch-all description for things that are unfunny or uninteresting in a way that appeals to older people.

Cracked: This slang term has two meanings: to have sex, as in "I got cracked last night," and to be really good at something, like "he’s cracked at Fortnite."

Crashout: To have an intense emotional outburst, usually accompanied by impulsive behavior. Crashing out is often due to being overwhelmed or overly frustrated.

D1 Crashout: An epic, elite level, extreme crashout. (See "crashout.)

Dah Bih Gah: "That bitch good," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dah Bih Tah: "That bitch tough," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dead: Past tense of having died laughing. If someone responds to a joke with "dead" or a skull emoji, they find it funny.

Deadass: Seriously. Used like, "I am deadass not lying."

Deriod: A combination of "dick" and "period," deriod refers to men seeming to experience the mood swings commonly associated with women's menstrual cycles.

Dih: Algo speak for “dick.” (See "Algo speak.")

Doi doi doi: This piece of brain-rot slang doesn't mean anything. It's correctly pronounced by putting your hand up to your mouth and saying "doi doi doi" in a way that sounds funny.

Doomer: A person who is overly negative and/or cynical.

Dwerking: A male-centric variation of twerking. A sexually suggestive dancing characterized by rapid, repeated hip thrusts and shaking of the dick. Other variants include "pwerking" and "bwerking" where the "p" and "b" stand for pussy and boobs.

Edgar: A variation of the Caesar haircut worn especially among Hispanic males. Also refers to the kind of person who wears the haircut.

Fambushing: A combination of "family" and "ambushing," fambushing refers to young people checking where their parents are on location-sharing apps so they can get free food—if you see mom at Chipotle, you ask for a burrito.

Fanum tax: The theft of food between friends. Named for streamer Fanum, known for “taxing” his friends by taking bites of their meals or stealing fries.

Fax, no printer: Telling the truth. Since "fax" and "facts" are pronounced the same, this is a colorful way of saying "facts, no cap."

Fent-fold: A description of the bent-over posture of people nodding on heavy drugs.

Fuhuhluhtoogan: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. Often paired with "Jittleyang."

Fujoshing: The verb form of the Japanese slang term "fujoshi," fujoshing describes women/girls enjoying media that depicts romantic relationships between men. This word is used almost exclusively in online fandom communities.

Gamer dent: The temporary indentation left on someone’s hair or skin after wearing headphones for too long.

Glaze: To overly praise someone, often insincerely, or with the hope of getting something in return.

Gleek: An older slang term that is gaining prominence lately, gleeking describes squirting saliva from under the tongue.

Glizzy: Hot dog. "Glizzy" was originally slang for Glock or gun, but came to mean hot dog based on the hot dog shape of a Glock's magazine.

Green fn: An interjection one might used when someone does something cool or impressive. Often used ironically.

Goonbait: (See "gooning") Goonbait is, essentially, media that exists to inspiring gooning.

Gooner: A man who goons. (See "gooning.")

Goonette: A woman who goons. (See "gooning.")

Gooning: Extended masturbation without orgasm done for the purpose of entering an altered state of consciousness. (See "gooner," "goonette.")

Gyatt or Gyat: Once an interjection used when seeing someone sexy, like “god-DAMN,” “gyatt” has come to mean “attractive booty.”

Heavy soda: Pop with extra syrup. Some gas station soda machines have settings that control the ratio of syrup to carbonated water. A heavy soda is a soda with the syrup level set very high.

Hewwo: An overly cute way of saying "hello." Usually used online, and often ironically.

HGS: Abbreviation for "home girls" used in comment sections.

Hiplet: Derogatory slang for a woman who has "hip dips," i.e. inward curves on their outer thighs just below the hip bone.

Hozier yell: Named for singer/songwriter Andrew Hozier, a "Hozier yell" refers to the sound one makes when experiencing a peak, climactic, and/or awe-inspiring moment.

HTN: This acronym comes from the online incel community, where fairly good-looking men are described as "high-tier normies" or "HTN." (See "normie.")

Hurkle-durkle: Based on an archaic Scottish word, “hurkle-durkle” means to lounge in bed after it is time to get up. See also: “bed-rotting."

Huzz: -uzz slang for "hoes." See "bruzz" and "-uzz."

"It's giving": Used to convey that something has a specific vibe. Example: "That dude texts you every 10 minutes; it's giving desperate."

"It's so over": The situation is hopeless. The opposite of "we're so back." See also: "Doomer."

IWEL: This comment-section acronym is short for "I wouldn't even lie." Sometimes written as "IWL."

Jelqing: The use of stretching or weights in an attempt to increase penis size.

Jittleyang: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. See also: "Fuhuhluhtoogan."

JOMO: A play on FOMO (fear of missing out) JOMO is an acronym that stands for “joy of missing out.”

"Learn Chinese": Sports slang directed at failing players. They are in danger of being sent to play in China, so they should "learn Chinese."

Loaded water: Water enhanced with something—a flavor boost, fruit juice, electrolytes, carbonation, and even vitamins or prebiotics. The idea is to increase hydration by making water more palatable.

Looksmaxxing: Maximizing one’s physical attractiveness through personal grooming, working out, and dressing stylishly. See also: “-maxxing.”

🪫 (low battery emoji): The low battery emoji means "I am experiencing emotional depletion, heartbreak, or a general feeling of 'I can't anymore.'"

Lowkenuinely: This mash-up of "low key" and "genuinely" expresses sincerity but in a way that says "let's not make a big deal about it."

Lucky Scoops: Lucky Scoops are a kind of TikTok or Instagram video where buyers purchase a scoop that represents a chance to win merchandise. These videos are very popular with children; critics feel like they are a form of gambling.

Mason (or Mason 6-7 kid): A "Mason 6-7 Kid" or "Mason" is a stereotypical male member of Generation Alpha. Mason kids are known for their love of baseball-inspired fashion (caps and shorts), their "ice cream" haircut, and for repeating brainrot slang like "6-7."

-maxxing: A suffix used with any word to indicate trying to improve. Seeing your friends could be called "friendmaxxing," working out could be called "gymmaxxing," making jokes could be called "jestermaxxing," etc.

Mewing: A facial exercise meant to strengthen the jawline.

Mirror sex: Using a mirror to watch yourself have sex.

Misery girl: A young woman with piercings, a penchant for the darkly dramatic, and highly stylized makeup that makes them appear to have a skinny, pointy nose and huge eyes and lips.

Mog: To be more attractive than someone, usually in an intentional or aggressive way. Example: "I was rizzing up this girl, but he walked in and totally mogged me."

"My 90 in a 30": A song played while driving that inspires speeding.

"My steak is too juicy": The phrase "my steak is too juicy" and other variants like "my lobster is too buttery," are online insults that suggest someone is complaining about something they should be grateful for.

Neurospicy: A different way of saying “neuro-divergent.”

Normie: A person who is considered normal or average. It's sometimes an insult suggesting someone is boring and witless. (see also, "mid.")

NPC: Non-player character. Originally describing video game characters, NPC is now used on the internet to mean people who don't think for themselves.

Opp: Short for "opposition." Someone who is out to get you. An enemy.

Performative male: An insult for young men whose tastes, hobbies, and lifestyle are seen as a performance aimed at obtaining societal approval, especially the approval of young women.

Pheromone maxxing: Trying to influence the behaviors of others through your stink. Supposedly, young men in the "looksmaxxing" community are skipping showers and not washing their clothing in an attempt to make young women like them more. (See "-maxxing").

Phonk: The word phonk can refer to one of two musical sub-genres. It originally referred to throwback '90s hip-hop categorized by slow-tempo "chopped and screwed" production and vintage Memphis rap vocals. It now more commonly describes the heavily distorted, up-tempo EDM used in brainrot videos.

Pink cocaine: Also known as "pink snow," pink cocaine is slang for a powdered drug mixture that usually contains some combination of ketamine, MDMA, meth, opioids, and other substances.

"Press F for respect:" In 2014 video game Call of Duty: Advanced Warfighter, the player attends a funeral and a prompt is given that reads "Press F to pay respects." Now, a singular "F" in a chat window indicates respect. It's usually ironic.

Quiet on the creek: A fishing-inspired way to say "keep it on the down low" or "be cool."

Rawdogging boredom: Rawdogging is "doing something with no safeguards or support," so "rawdogging boredom" is consciously doing nothing.

Regarded: “Regarded” is algo-speak for “retarded."

RegencyCore: A fashion and design aesthetic that springs from the popularity of the fantasy-regency era look of the Netflix show Bridgerton, RegencyCore combines the opulent style of the British Regency era of the early 1800s with fantasy elements like pastel colors and gold accents.

"Reheating your own nachos:" This slang phrase comes from cultural critics in online fandom communities. It refers to performers and/or artists whose new works are seen as trying to recapture what was good about their previous artistic output. It's not always negative; it's possible to successfully reheat your own nachos.

Rizz: As a noun, "rizz" means charisma. As a verb, "rizz" or "rizz up" means attracting someone with your charisma.

Scientology speedrun: Young people running into a Scientology building and acting foolish until they are ejected.

Scorigami: A slang term among football fans for when the final score of an NFL game has never happened before in the league's history. The most recent scorigami was on September 28, 2025, when the Green Bay Packers and Dallas Cowboys tied 40 to 40.

SDIYBT: An acronym for "start digging in your butt, twin," this brainrot phrase doesn't mean anything. Some people just think it's funny to say.

Sendy and “Let’s get sendy": Sendy is an adjective based on the older rock-climbing and extreme sports slang phrase "send it." A shortened version of "ascend it," "send it" is said right before one is about to do something challenging. "Sendy" describes a person who is prone to doing bold things. "Let's get sendy" means something like "Let's get wild." It's been adopted by brainrot fans, so it's often repeated with no meaning meant to be attached.

Serve: Wearing a particularly stylish outfit. See also: "ate."

Serve cunt: To act in a powerfully and unapologetically feminine way; to slay.

Sharking: Looking for people to hook up with.

Side quest: A side quest in a video game is a quest that is not necessary to complete the game's main objective. In slang, a side quest is anything you do in life just for the experience of doing it.

Sigma male: An internet-created male classification, a "sigma male" is as dominant as an alpha male, but is outside the male hierarchy, i.e.: a lone wolf. Originally used seriously, the concept was so widely derided it's now almost always used ironically. (See "Alpha male" and "Beta male.")

Skibidi: Named after “Skibidi Toilet,” a popular series of YouTube videos, “skibidi” itself has no specific meaning, beyond ridiculing the overuse of slang itself. See “brain-rot.”

Skrt: Onomatopoetic word for the sound of tires squealing upon acceleration.

Slopcore: This term describes the countless 100s of millions of cheesy-looking, unsettling, AI-generated images, videos, and songs that have hit the internet since AI was given to the masses a couple of years ago.

Slopper: Insult directed at people who use AI programs too much, people who takes conversations with LLMs too seriously, and people who have basically offloaded their thinking to an algorithm.

Snatched: Very attractive and/or flawlessly styled.

Spawn point: Mother. Based on the spot you start in a video game.

Surf Dracula: A hyper-specific phrase that describes "prestige" television series. The joke is that if there were an older TV show called "Surf Dracula," Dracula would be surfing in every episode, but modern shows would make the whole first season about how Dracula got his surfboard.

Sweat: A person who tries too hard, usually used in reference to video games. The adjective form is "sweaty."

SYBAU: An online acronym that stands for “shut your bitch ass up.”

That's AI: "I don't believe you" or "I doubt it," even when not connected to artificial intelligence.

TLPUR: This supposed acronym section has no meaning. The joke is to tell people it means something like "True Love Pills Until Rope" or "Too Late for Puberty."

Tradwife: Believer in traditional married gender roles.

Trap: Once used to refer to a house where drugs are sold, trap has come to describe both a form of music and any place where one works or hustles.

Treatler (and Treatlerite): "Treatler" and "Treatlerite" are online insults that combine "treat" and "Hitler" to refer to entitled users of services like Doordash or Uber Eats who regard luxury delivery services as a human right, and don't consider the hardships of the people who do the work that makes "private taxis for burritos" possible.

TS: TS originally was AAVE shorthand for "this shit," but it is often used to just mean "this."

Turnt: Excited or intoxicated, or excitedly intoxicated.

Tweaking: In older slang, "tweaking" referred to the nervous and erratic actions of someone on drugs, specifically, speed. Generations A and Z have expanded the definition to refer to any actions that are erratic, or even just mildly energetic, not necessarily related to drug use.

Tylenol baby: After President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a scientifically dubious link between the active ingredient in Tylenol and autism, kids have been calling each other "Tylenol babies."

Unc: Short for "uncle," used to describe slightly older people. Example: "The class of 2024 are unc-status to the class of 2028." See "yunc."

-uzz: -uzz slang words use "uzz" at the end of any word, so "bros" becomes "bruzz," "hoes" becomes "huzz," "granny" becomes "gruzz," etc.

"We're so back": Opposite of "it's so over."

Venus tummy: When a woman's belly is a little fat, but not too fat, she is said to have a Venus tummy. Named for ancient Greek statues of Venus and Aphrodite who were a little fleshy.

Viking rap: A musical sub-genre consisting of AI-generated Vikings rapping about longboats, raiding, and other Viking things.

Wojack: The name of a style of internet drawings used to quickly stereotype someone. See this post for a full explanation of the Wojak universe.

Yapping: Describes a presentational style often seen on online streams of talking a lot and/or quickly while not saying anything worthwhile.

You the birthday: A phrase that means "you're awesome" or "you're great" in the way a birthday is great: fun, exciting, extra, etc.

Young ho: "Young ho" is both a reclamation of the word "ho" and an expression of youth-based solidarity. Young women are posting videos of themselves defining what makes them "young hos," noting things like "Getting up at 7:50 to be at work at 8," and air-frying chicken nuggets.

Yunc: Yunc is a variation of "unc." In AAVE, a "yn" is a "young n-word." So "yunc" means something like "young uncle," or a person who may be young but has uncle vibes or unc status.

Zoomer Perm: A curly on top, short on the sides haircut popular among young people.

#3547. Marshals Season 2 Episode 5 Exposes A Major Problem With The Yellowstone Spin-Off

"Marshals" Season 2 Episode 4 ended on a deadly cliffhanger that left the fate of Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz unclear. Caught in an explosion, the pair were flung through the air just before the episode cut to black. What would become of Kayce and the character with whom he's clearly developing deep feelings? Well, nothing. The latest "Marshals" installment quickly establishes that they were both fine in what is the latest example of one of the show's most frustrating problems.

It's no secret that Grimes' procedural has struggled to live up to "Yellowstone" and its fellow spin-off "Dutton Ranch." There are many reasons why. For one, "Marshals" Season 1 had no idea what it was about, with the show jumping from premise to premise in an attempt to find its footing and ultimately never succeeding. But there are several other issues with this show, and one of them is its proclivity for building things up only to disappoint viewers in the most unnecessary ways.

Consider the Season 2 premiere. "Marshals" Season 1 ended by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton taken captive by investor turned rancher Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey). Tate was supposedly being shuttled to Texas, where it seemed we might get the first official crossover between "Dutton Ranch" and "Marshals." But in the Season 2 premiere we learned that Tate was having a grand old time fishing on a Wyoming ranch. By the end of the episode, Tom Weaver had been apprehended and Tate was back to barely featuring in the series. Now, we've had yet another cliffhanger undermined and it's starting to get ridiculous.

"Marshals" Season 1 seemed to introduce a love triangle between Kayce Dutton, Andrea Cruz, and Dolly Weaver (Ellyn Jameson). Now that Dolly's out of the picture, however (she died in that disappointing "Marshals" Season 2 premiere), Andrea and Kayce are free to embrace their attraction.

Season 2, Episode 4, "Blast Radius," saw the pair growing closer than ever. Turns out this duo have been executing warrants as an extra-curricular activity to distract them from their sleepless nights. But it's clear there's also a slow-burn romance developing between the two. As such, when they were seemingly blown sky high in the episode's closing moments it looked as though the writers were about to leverage this burgeoning love affair for some dramatic tension. There was no way Kayce was going to die, but perhaps his new love interest's life would be left hanging in the balance?

Nope, they're both fine. Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" opens in the immediate aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding his bomb in range of Kayce and Andrea. We see the former lying unconscious on the floor, before he wakes up and crawls over to Andrea, who's also coming to. Meanwhile, their fellow Marshals do a sweep of the barn, determine Rudy's gone for good, and after that everything's back to normal. It's a frustrating opening as it calls to mind all the previous "Marshals" cliffhanger moments that have similarly come to nothing.

"Marshals" is a CBS procedural in the vein of "SEAL Team" — the show from which its showrunner Spencer Hudnut hails. As such, we know there's a case-of-the-week format, and we know that a network show isn't necessarily beholden to the production values of, say, an HBO drama. But is there any rule that states the show has to be made with the dimmest possible audience members in mind?

"Marshals" keeps reiterating the plot of each episode in the simplest terms possible, with the latest example coming in "Secret Weapon." After the team finds tire tracks near the barn where Rudy Carpenter died, it becomes clear that someone other than Carpenter is transporting missing bombs elsewhere. Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) then announces, "Someone's driving this bomb around right now and we got no idea what the target is." Is this like the Netflix thing where they assume people are on their phones and aren't paying close enough attention?

These frequent consequence-free cliffhangers are another aspect of "Marshals" that gives the sense of a show doing an impression of a better show. It's like the writers know cliffhangers can be compelling, but don't want to cause any actual distress to an audience they evidently assume is made up of phone-addicted simpletons barely following the plot. So, we get these half-baked moments of tension, after which nothing changes. Remember when "Marshals" Season 1 introduced a powerful Dutton family rival who'd apparently been at odds with Kayce's family for generations, only for that same rival to be arrested several episodes later, never to be heard from again? It's the same thing. A threat arises, then it's neutralized. I get that "Marshals" isn't "Yellowstone." But does that mean it has to be bad?

#3546. 25 Years Later, Aragorn's Best Lord of the Rings Quote Still Defines the Entire Trilogy

No other character is doing it quite like Aragorn

Peter Jackson’s adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings trilogy remains one of cinema’s most poignant and beautiful works. For better or worse, the trilogy also helped shape the visual style we now associate with fantasy. No matter how much time has passed, The Lord of the Rings has left a lasting mark on the genre.

However, The Lord of the Rings also proved extraordinary in other ways. For one thing, every character, major or minor, has at least one fantastic quote that adds tremendous depth. Gandalf might have some of the best lines in the franchise, but Aragorn — the cloaked ranger who stole all our hearts the moment he first appeared — also has plenty of quotable zingers delivered perfectly by Viggo Mortensen.

But what is Aragorn’s best quote? That’s a tough one to pick, especially with amazing lines like “For Frodo” and “I do not fear death.” Still, we think we’ve picked Aragorn’s most memorable line, and it perfectly captures the heart of The Lord of the Rings trilogy.

Aragorn is one of Middle-earth’s most honorable characters. Though he has spent much of his life in the background, hoping for something simpler, he will do whatever it takes to do the right thing when push comes to shove. That doesn’t make him a bastion of goodness — he has selfish moments, too — but overall, Aragorn is defined by his loyalty to those around him.

This loyalty is on full display when Frodo approaches Aragorn at Amon Hen during The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. After seeing a vision of destruction and war, and only shortly after surviving Boromir's attack to seize the One Ring, Frodo is convinced he must head to the fires of Mordor alone. When Frodo tells Aragorn his plan, Aragorn isn’t pleased, but accepts his decision, knowing the Ring is too tempting and can turn people against one another, as it did with Boromir.

Yet before Frodo leaves, Aragorn displays just how noble and reliable he is with this heartfelt quote:

“I would have gone with you to the end, into the very fires of Mordor.”

After losing so many allies, and with the Fellowship breaking apart so soon, Aragorn’s words show that the ranger deeply believes in Frodo’s mission—even if he won’t be there to see it done.

It’s established early in The Fellowship of the Ring that Frodo’s journey will ask those in the Fellowship to endure innumerable hardships, pain, and sacrifice. Even so, what a person must sacrifice — whether it be their sanity or even their life — only becomes apparent as the group continues its journey.

By the time the movie ends, the Fellowship has split up. It would be all too easy for Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli to rescue Pippin and Merry, then simply wait to see whether Frodo and Sam can evade Sauron’s forces and cast the Ring into the fires of Mordor.

However, Aragorn and the rest of the Fellowship have faith in Frodo, so they would never abandon their mission. When Frodo offers him the Ring, Aragorn feels its temptation, but realizes he can best serve Frodo by letting him go. He acts not out of fear, but from the inner belief that, though he will part ways with Frodo, the hobbit is strong enough to carry on.

Aragorn’s faith in Frodo sustains the Fellowship through doubt and seemingly hopeless odds. At Helm's Deep, despite Legolas's warning that victory is unlikely, Aragorn remains committed to his allies, as he did at Amon Hen when he risked his life to help Frodo escape. Though loved ones depend on him, he believes the risk is worthwhile if Frodo can defeat Sauron and save Middle-earth.

Though Aragorn’s best quote may not feel as badass as the lines he delivers in the heat of battle, it captures the Fellowship’s steadfast belief in Frodo — and remains one of the most definitive lines in The Lord of the Rings.
