#3524. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is Still Perfect on Switch 2 | Review

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

Somewhere among all its gods and ghosts, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time draws its true power from its human center: a familiar story about growing up and returning home after a long absence.

As the time-afflicted Link comes to learn in the seminal Nintendo 64 classic, a lot can change in seven years. Shifting political struggles leave a neighborhood in total disrepair. That one local eccentric he came to love is nowhere to be seen. There’s a Starbucks — or an archery range, I mean — in town now. Seriously? But underneath the jarring changes that taunt your memory, you know that the place that you love is still there. You can feel its heart beat when you plant yourself in the shade of that tall tree you played around as a kid.

It’s what makes the concept of an Ocarina of Time remake so challenging, but impossible to resist. How fitting — fated even, written in stars and ancient code — to bring generations of adventurers back to the sprawling field where they first learned to run. Like your hometown, a game as foundational as this is perhaps meant to be revisited throughout a lifetime rather than locked away in your long-term memory.

Nintendo doesn’t squander the opportunity for a meaningful homecoming in its lovingly crafted Switch 2 remake. The timeless classic is still a joy to reappraise in its dazzling new form, even if some of its modern developments might send protective fans marching to town hall. Yes, there’s a Starbucks where that quaint café used to be now, but Ocarina of Time’s soul still shines bright enough to guide you home.

One part faithful remake and one part modern retelling, the new version of Ocarina of Time is bound to take old players off guard in its opening moments. The story is unchanged: After getting paired with a fairy, Navi, for the first time, a young Link gets swept into a kingdom-trotting quest to save Hyrule from the nefarious Ganondorf. The sequence of events is unchanged from the original, but the presentation is very different. The Switch 2 remake leans into the fairy tale nature of the original game with storybook narration that clearly lays out the “legend” being told. It’s a smart bit of narrative framing, emphasizing that Ocarina of Time is a story meant to be passed down and retold like a fable.

What’s less successful, at least initially, is fully-voiced new dialogue that replaces the comparatively sparse text boxes of the original game, which featured no voice acting outside of a few stray grunts. An opening conversation between Navi and the Deku Tree, Hyrule’s guardian spirit, loses its moody texture in a brightly-lit cutscene where a squeaky-voiced Navi lays out all the exposition you need to know. It’s a common struggle that Nintendo faces anytime it tries to give its games a cinematic treatment; the more you scale a game like Star Fox 64 up, the more it starts to look like an Illumination-flavored animated kids movie. It’s no wonder that Nintendo saw enough of itself in the Minions studio to entrust it with Mario.

That change in energy takes some getting used to, as an introductory jaunt through Kokiri Forest teases a remake that has been overly polished to a modern sheen. That opening is more tutorial-heavy now, for instance — and that’s saying a lot considering that Navi is gaming’s original hand-holder. It’s not enough for a Kokiri child to tell you how to use your sword anymore; you now need to perform each action multiple times in a practice session before you’re trusted to explore your first dungeon. Those small changes have a way of stacking up early on, creating a shaky first impression as you learn all the ways an old favorite has changed.

But part of growing up is learning to accept, and even embrace, change. That’s where the remake’s controversial visual overhaul makes a statement. When the game was first revealed with a short teaser, it was met with some immediate disgust from players who feared that Nintendo was trading in its cartoon charm for flat Unreal Engine realism. That snap judgment is destined to age like Lon Lon Milk, because the remake is both highly stylized and stunning in motion. That’s apparent right off the bat when strolling through the dreamy Kokiri Forest, with streaks of light poking through the thick roof of greenery that protects the town. It’s a dreamy and nostalgic sight that sets the right tone for the rest of the adventure, one that has the emotional resonance of dusting off an old picture book you read as a kid.

What’s miraculous is how Nintendo is able to retain the grandeur of the world without scaling its locales up beyond recognition. Hyrule is compact by modern game standards, split into only a few tightly designed areas, but it still feels sweeping here. The open air of Hyrule Field is still breathtaking to take in, emphasized with more detailed grass instead of needless space-filling activities. Lake Hylia is just a round body of water, but the glistening light reflecting off of it makes it feel like a cool, serene getaway. Even Kakariko Village’s graveyard benefits from minor changes, with once low-poly headstones now detailed with embellishments that invite you to pull them to reveal the secrets buried underneath them. The only area that really loses some of its former aura is Hyrule Castle Town, as the pivot to smooth 3D camera controls does away with eerie fixed camera angles that were once so important to selling the village’s eventual decay.

If there’s an issue to take with the visual design, it’s that it can be inconsistent. While the detailed environments look spectacular, they aren’t exactly a match for the smooth character design. Link looks like a porcelain doll in hand-stitched clothing, which is a thematically appropriate choice that once again gets at an old childhood toy feel. It’s just a shame that the world doesn’t have a dollhouse look of its own to suit that style. Maybe that’s what has left fans so split as they see Princess Zelda’s glassy eyes or a hookshot that looks like a clay miniature contrasted against a more natural world.

Throughout Ocarina of Time, anything that felt off at first glance grew on me over time, especially once Link himself grew up in the story’s iconic turning point. The natural swap from a hokey animated cartoon to a Grimm’s fairy tale locks every artistic choice into place. The directed cutscenes become a highlight once Link is having tender musical duets with the mysterious Sheik. The reimagined visuals pay off once you get to see monsters like Redeads and Like Likes in their horrifying new forms, emphasizing Ocarina of Time’s roots as a true horror game. Freshly reorchestrated music makes everything feel more operatic without rewriting melodies that now feel as standard to musical canon as “Ode To Joy” — at least if you grew up humming “Zelda’s Lullaby.”

As jarring as the remake’s clean sheen can feel next to the meaningfully grungy Hyrule of olde, the changes don’t get in the way of what makes Ocarina of Time special. And how special it still is 27 years later!

While much has changed from an aesthetic standpoint, Nintendo is very careful not to adjust much about the adventure outside of handy quality of life tweaks. The addition of a dedicated jump button is an inoffensive touch, and Nintendo makes good use of modern controller layouts to make item swapping more seamless (even if Breath of the Wild’s dreaded horizontal item menu returns here), but the core of the game remains wisely unchanged. You still trek between locations across two ages, clearing elemental-themed dungeons full of monsters and puzzles, and obtaining items that gradually open up the world. It’s a structure that inspired an entire genre of adventure games in 1998, but the Switch 2 remake reaffirms that no game has ever nailed that formula as well as Ocarina of Time.

Upon revisiting the story for the first time in two decades, I came to appreciate so much about a game I thought I had mastered years ago. What immediately stands out about Ocarina of Time next to modern games — even modern Zelda games — is how not a moment feels wasted. Every interaction with a jolly Goron feels meaningful, hand-placed there for a reason. Every side-quest, minigame, or hidden grotto feels bespoke, like it was sculpted to contain one memorable secret. A gaggle of singing frogs perched next to a river, a pair of scarecrows baking in the sun, a diving tank in a mad scientist's house. No two activities feel like the result of designers copying and pasting assets throughout the world just to fill a game with more hour-eating busy work. It stands in proud contrast to modern adventure games that do so much less with so much more.

There was never a dull moment in my 20-hour playthrough, even when I was backtracking across Hyrule Field or up Death Mountain. That’s made possible in part thanks to Ocarina of Time’s fantastic dungeon design. Each one is a perfectly crafted puzzle box that builds unique enemies and challenges around the dungeon’s theme and key items. Navigating twisted hallways in the Forest Temple with your newly-discovered arrows or cutting your way out of an oversized fish belly is always a surprising delight that feels unlike anything you’ve done before. The remake keeps all of those iconic dungeon designs intact, only making some welcome tweaks to the dreaded Water Temple to make it easier to navigate at a glance. I have to wonder if the remake partially exists as a way to wean players off of Breath of the Wild’s open-world freedom, and reignite a desire for something crafted with more precise intent.

What I appreciate most of all is Nintendo’s restraint. It remains confident in the original game’s design, understanding that Hyrule Field doesn’t need to be an immersive playground full of new secrets to evoke an emotional response from new players. There’s a version of this remake in an alternate timeline that goes full Halo: Campaign Evolved, overhauling entire systems to bring an old game in line with its modern peers at the expense of the original game’s ethos. Nintendo largely rejects that, and that choice always pays off.

What a relief it can be to play something like the Ocarina of Time remake and find that the magic is still there.

Look to the remake’s swordplay for a shining example of that. Nintendo could’ve easily followed modern trends and buffed up Link’s move set by giving him a parry, a time-slowing dodge, or more sword-slashing combos to use against spongy enemies with bigger health bars. Instead, the remake sticks to the fundamentals of slashing and dodging to retain the Punch-Out!! style dynamics of Stalfos duels. Rather than aiming for artificial complexity, the remake puts its focus on giving every motion more feedback. When you land a successful slash on an enemy, you’re rewarded with a fireworks flash of particles and a grand slice sound to give your strike power. Even taking out a simple Deku Baba feels like a heroic act. It’s the best that combat has felt in a Zelda game since Wind Waker, and it’s accomplished by reinforcing the foundation instead of pulling up the floorboards.

That’s the strength of the remake at large. Like a good fable passed down through oral tradition, the heart of the tale remains intact; all that’s really changed is the embellishments. Little changes to room layouts in dungeons or exaggerated duels are akin to a storyteller putting their own flourishes on a story to make the fiery Volvagia sound like an even fiercer foe. It’s hard to lose the spirit of Ocarina of Time in that game of creative telephone because every word of it is unforgettable.

The Ocarina of Time remake’s technical excellence has nothing to do with why the adventure is actually special, of course. Revisiting Ocarina of Time feels a bit like plunging the Master Sword back into its pedestal in the Temple of Time; I’m young Link again, back in the peaceful shade of Kokiri Forest where I grew up. Part of that is because the original Ocarina of Time is so closely tied to my hometown; the first video game review I ever read was written by my late friend Andrew for our 4th grade newspaper. To me, Hyrule is a small town in Massachusetts, and I have always felt a fierce loyalty to it because of that.

There’s a sensitivity that comes with that, one that I’m sure many players feel when a meaningful piece of media from their childhood gets reappraised. Over the last two decades, I’ve watched the cultural consensus on Ocarina of Time shift from hailing it as an untouchable classic to a dated N64 game that downright sucks to play. I’ve always felt a protective instinct kick in every time a new player dips into it for the first time and starts complaining about this or that. You weren’t there! You couldn’t understand!

The reality is that I know it’s a defense mechanism. I’ve spent decades now scared to replay Ocarina of Time for fear that I won’t like what I find. Maybe I’ll find that it’s changed too much — or, worse, maybe I’ll find that I have. It’s not dissimilar to how I used to feel about coming back to my hometown after college; there is a discomfort in returning to something that once felt magical only to discover it’s small and mundane in the context of a wider world. Maybe that’s why video game remakes often elicit such strong reactions from players who lament their very existence or gasp at every minor change. It’s easier to protect the past by locking it up in our memories.

So what a relief it can be to play something like the Ocarina of Time remake and find that the magic is still there. Any fear I had that its design would feel antiquated or that a glossy visual overhaul would pave over its plucky spirit disappeared the first time I whistled out the jaunty notes of “Saria’s Song,” like a kid discovering how to make music for the first time by tooting out “Hot Cross Buns” on their dinky recorder. The world of Hyrule felt every bit as big and beautiful as I remembered, so full of discoveries for anyone curious enough to take a wrong turn in the Lost Woods.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

I’ve spent the better part of my life hearing people repeat the claim that Ocarina of Time is the greatest game of all time. At some point, it starts to lose all meaning, like saying The Beatles are the best band of all time based solely on an accepted cultural consensus. But the Switch 2 remake reminds us why Ocarina of Time earned that accolade in the first place. Set aside any nostalgia and you’ll still be met with a big-hearted fable set in a lively fantasy world filled with characters who are as familiar as close friends. Link’s journey to adulthood and back again remains a meaningful odyssey about finding the courage to save the soul of the place that lives in your heart — a love that transcends time itself. Every word in my friend’s 4th grade assessment of that epic adventure he connected with as a kid still applies here, and that’s a testament to what could have been a soul-crushing double dip.

That’s the intangible thing that I look for in a remake, something personal that’s hard to articulate in a technical breakdown. Forget the jump button or the smooth framerate: Does The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time still feel like home? Yes, it does, even with a few changes that trigger a “back in my day” reaction. I’m no longer afraid of returning to Hyrule Field and watching the sun set again. I’ve only grown to appreciate the peace and quiet more with age.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released Nov. 5 on Nintendo Switch 2. The game was reviewed on Nintendo Switch 2 using a prerelease download code provided by Nintendo. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

It could be argued that the breakout star of You Can See Everything is Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans. He plays a big part in the documentary, which is the surprise hit of the 2026 movie schedule. The A24 release, co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, has a lot of WTF moments, and quite a few come from Evans. One of those moments comes when he admits that he’s been posting on X as Holmes from her account.

This week, Evans took to his own X account to do an AMA (Ask Me Anything), and one of the most-asked questions was about all the sniffling Evans was doing in the second half of the movie. He poked holes in one theory that fans brought up and insisted that he has been dealing with allergies since the movie Texas, where Holmes is serving her sentence in a Federal prison for her fraud convictions.

Evans answered a lot of questions over a couple of hours, and one question that came up multiple times in the AMA asked why he was sniffing so often. X user asked, and Evans responded that it was kids and allergies:

Solo parenting 2 toddlers, you are sick approx 75% of days. Allergies in Austin, TX are no joke. I take Claritin daily. Much less sniffling.

This was followed by another user asking if it was cocaine, and Evans was clear that it wasn’t, answering the user with “Never been a fan.” At another point, someone else asked the same question, and he had a similar response (along with a William Huang joke):

1) I love William Huang 2) I moved to Texas. The cedar here is no joke.

Evans also got into other things about You Can See Everything, including admitting that he does not regret making the movie, though he never answered a question as to why he and Holmes chose Fielder to direct the project. That’s a question even Fielder himself hasn’t been able to answer.

Evans also explained why, as he reveals in the movie, he has power of attorney over Holmes’ affairs. He was clear that it had nothing to do with posting from her X account (which he also insists Holmes is completely fine with), but rather to handle things on the outside while Holmes is serving her time. That is one of the things that actually makes sense to me.

It’s an interesting AMA, and I’d love to see Evans do it again. I’d really like to know more about what he thinks about the documentary, and if there is anything that was left out that frustrates him. He admits that a lot of footage was left on the cutting room floor, of course. In the meantime, I’ll continue tracking anything and everything about You Can See Everything, including all the reactions, its Oscar chances, and everything else.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

#3519. 5 Best Movies Like The Love Hypothesis

There was never any doubt that Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" would become a big hit for Prime Video. Streaming platforms have struck gold by taking romance books and turning them into comforting crowd-pleasers for the small screen. Sometimes this results in films as vapid as "My Fault: London," but often it results in charming movies that take allow us to indulge romantic fantasies via two hot people falling in love.

That's exactly what we got when "The Love Hypothesis" transformed from "Star Wars" fan fiction, of all things, into a novel and then a streaming movie. Ali Hazelwood's book about a biology PhD student who pretends to date her professor, only for the two to fall deeply in love became a hit, and was promptly given a film adaptation in which Reinhart plays the student, Olive Smith, while British actor Tom Bateman plays the ornery professor, Dr. Adam Carlsen.

There were two main tropes to both the book and the film: mismatched lovers who cross a boundary to be together, and the good old fake relationship that becomes very real. Of course, this is far from the first time these tropes have been used in romance movies, which is why it's actually quite easy to recommend films just like "The Love Hypothesis." While there are plenty of golden-age romance movies that used these plot devices (1941's "Come Live with Me" saw James Stewart and Hedy Lamarr fake a marriage only to fall head over heels), we're betting that fans of Reinhart's movie will want more modern examples. With that in mind, here's a list of the best movies like "The Love Hypothesis."

"My Oxford Year" may have a controversial ending but it's got everything you could want from a modern-day streaming flick based on a book. Melodrama and fairytale romance combine in this Netflix movie, which stars Sofia Carson (who's fast becoming the streamer's go-to romantic drama leading lady) as American exchange student Anna De La Vega. Before descending into a life of corporate drudgery, Anna decides to study Victorian poetry at the University of Oxford for a year. Wouldn't you know it, once there she meets an unreasonably charming and handsome English DPhil student and tutor named Jamie Davenport (Corey Mylchreest).

"My Oxford Year" shares much in common with "The Love Hypothesis." Not only are both based on books (though the former actually began as a screenplay before it was adapted into a novel), they both feature a student/teacher relationship that gets off to a rough start only to flourish into a modern-day fairytale. Both also feature strapping English leading men (though Bateman plays an American in "The Love Hypothesis") who start out as jerks only to reveal a tender side as things progress.

It is worth noting that there's a tragic element to "My Oxford Year," so if you're looking for something that wraps up as neatly as "The Love Hypothesis," this might not be the ideal watch. But otherwise fans of Lily Reinhart's movie should fall madly in love with Carson's alternative.

These streaming movies are all well and good but there has to be at least one undisputed classic on this list. There's no better example of the fake relationship trope than this 1990 romantic comedy in which we got to see prime-era Richard Gere and Julia Roberts fall for one another. The movie did what "The Love Hypothesis" and its fellow streaming-age rom-coms did decades before Netflix was even a thing, bringing together impossibly beautiful stars via a fake relationship that blossoms into the real thing.

If you don't know the plot of what might just be Julia Roberts' best movie, I'm not sure what to tell ya. He's a corporate raider, she's a sex worker he asks for directions. So begins a love affair that sees Gere's Edward Lewis paying Roberts' Vivian Ward to spend a week with him and act as his girlfriend. Needless to say, this confected relationship becomes a real one. Ward melts Lewis' cold corporate heart and Lewis draws out the real Ward from behind a wall of dissociation built up over her time spent as a sex worker.

If you're somehow yet to see the film, and are worried the tale of a millionaire corporate raider falling for a sex worker might not have the wholesome charm of "The Love Hypothesis," don't worry. There's a reason Roger Ebert called the film "the sweetest and most openhearted love fable since 'The Princess Bride.'" "Pretty Woman" is as romantic a comedy as they come. But beyond that, it somehow manages to feel grounded thanks to its multi dimensional characters, without compromising the fairytale romance aspect.

Sofia Carson will soon have a monopoly on streaming romance movies. Her 2025 romantic drama "The Life List" dominated Netflix just prior to the similarly successful release of "My Oxford Year." But before either of these movies, Carson made her Netflix romance debut with the 2022 film "Purple Hearts." Guess what — the whole thing was based on a book, Tess Wakefield's 2017 novel of the same name.

In "Purple Hearts" we get a modern day version of James Stewart's "Come Live with Me." This Carson-led love story sees the former Disney Channel star play diabetic waitress and musician Cassie Salazar, who's working herself ragged just to afford insulin. Her salvation arrives in the form of hunky Marine Luke Morrow (Nicholas Galitzine), who agrees to marry Cassie so she can gain health coverage and he can benefit from a pay bump. You can see where this is going.

Much like with "The Love Hypothesis," this is a story about a couple who agree to act as though they're together only to develop real feelings along the way. There's plenty of BookTok-style melodrama on display here, too, which should please anyone who enjoyed the tension of the third act fall-out in "The Love Hypothesis."

It's the film that made Glen Powell a star and proved Sydney Sweeney could make popular stuff outside of "Euphoria." If your favorite thing about "The Love Hypothesis" was watching two attractive people make out, then "Anyone But You" should be right up your alley. In fact, "Anyone But You" is arguably the apotheosis of the modern day two-hot-actors-fall-in-love rom-com. But there's a stronger connection between this film and "The Love Hypothesis."

Lily Reinhart's Olive Smith and Tom Bateman's Dr. Adam Carlsen agreed to fake a relationship for mutually beneficial reasons, and the same happens with Sweeney's Beatrice Messina and Powell's Ben. The duo pretend to be a couple so that Bea's parents will stop trying to repair her relationship with her ex, and Ben can make his own ex jealous. We all knew where it was going from the very beginning but that didn't make it any less enjoyable to watch.

Unlike with "The Love Hypothesis," the guy in this romantic comedy isn't a complete jerk. Full of himself, maybe, but not an anti-social hermit like Bateman's "Dr. Evil." Still, he and Sweeney's law student don't exactly get along, especially after their first meeting ended on awkward terms. That, alongside the fake relationship trope, gives Powell and Sweeney's couple a similar dynamic to that of Olive and Adam in "The Love Hypothesis." So if you somehow missed the unlikely box office smash that was "Anyone But You" back in 2024, now's the time to remedy that.

In 2018, "To All the Boys I've Loved Before" became the new gold standard for teen rom-coms. It also happens to be a nice little companion to "The Love Hypothesis." Based on a book? Check. Fake relationship trope? Check. Academic setting? Sort of check. Rather than college, this tale of teen love, adapted from Jenny Han's YA novel, plays out in high school, where Lara Jean Covey (Lana Condor) writes secret letters to her crushes. Of course, she never intends for any of them to read her missives, but guess what — that's exactly what happens.

Lara Jean's biggest crush is Josh Sanderson (Israel Broussard), and when she sees him approaching with his letter in hand, she kisses another one of the letter recipients, Peter Kavinsky (Noah Centineo) in an attempt to throw Josh off. Soon, Peter and Lara Jean are fake dating. This allows the former to distract from the embarrassment of Josh receiving a letter, and the latter to make his ex-girlfriend Gen (Emilija Baranac) jealous. But you know how this goes. Real romance develops, melodrama ensues, feelings get hurt.

"To All the Boys I've Loved Before" is, however, more than your standard BookTook phenomenon turned Netflix romance movie. The film is surprisingly well shot, retains a heartfelt sensibility throughout, and isn't afraid to embrace its classic fake relationship rom-com influences. It's a touching little high school melodrama that's well worth a watch for anyone who even remotely enjoyed "The Love Hypothesis."

#3515. AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into the App Store

Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store.

An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

I feel like this going to be a never ending cat and mouse game. Much like Apple has always had with jailbreaks.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

#3512. TV Legend Ed Asner Appeared In This Classic '60s John Wayne Western

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In 1966, John Wayne visited Vietnam and began formulating one of his biggest on-screen blunders, "The Green Berets." Before he could get around to making the one John Wayne film that Roger Ebert called "cruel and dishonest," however, he had another couple Westerns to get through. "El Dorado" was the first. It premiered in the United States in June 1967, exactly one year after Wayne made the rounds in IndoChina. At the time, the Duke was becoming increasingly irrelevant as the Western genre began its shift into the revisionist age. Nonetheless, "El Dorado," which saw Wayne reunited with his frequent directorial collaborator Howard Hawks, became a success. It also remains the only film to feature Wayne and Ed Asner, who at the time was just three years away from debuting in his best-known role as Lou Grant on "The Mary Tyler Moore Show."

Asner began acting in the mid-1950s. He made his TV debut in 1957 on "Studio One" and his film debut in 1962, appearing alongside Elvis Presley in "Kid Galahad." Oddly enough, he didn't appear in a Western film until 1966 when he joined Wayne in "El Dorado," which considering any working actor of the 1960s was bound to wind up in a Western at some point is surprising.

Asner did, however, appear in some classic Western TV shows, guesting on "Outlaws" in 1962 and "The Virginian" the following year. He also appeared in two episodes of "Gunsmoke" and in 1965 joined Robert Horton for a single installment of "A Man Called Shenandoah." When he set foot on the "El Dorado" set, then, while he hadn't yet appeared in a big screen Western, he was well acquainted with Hollywood's vision of the Old West. Now all he had to do was face down John Wayne.

"El Dorado" is directed and produced by Howard Hawks. His frequent collaborator Leigh Brackett wrote the script, which she considered to be her finest work. In Todd McCarthy's "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," Brackett is quoted as having said, "I wrote the best script I have ever written and Howard liked it, the studio liked it, Wayne liked it, and I was delighted." Unfortunately for her, Hawks wanted to play things a little safer by essentially remaking "Rio Bravo," the 1959 John Wayne-led Western that launched an unofficial trilogy.

"Rio Bravo" was the result of Hawks and Wayne's hatred for "High Noon," which featured a sheriff too scared to confront the antagonists alone. Hawks and Wayne's retort featured a more muscular hero who had no problem facing evil solo. It proved so successful and seemingly suited Hawks' sensibility so well he essentially remade it twice, once with "El Dorado" and again with 1970's "Rio Lobo" — both of which starred the Duke. The former was a more lighthearted movie, however, with James Caan as John Wayne's sidekick providing much of the comic relief due to his poor aim.

Otherwise, "El Dorado" starred Robert Mitchum, the film noir legend who was also no stranger to the Western, as the alcoholic sheriff of the titular town, J.P. Harrah. His old pal, gunfighter Cole Thornton (Wayne), arrives in El Dorado after being been hired by local tycoon Bart Jason (Ed Asner) to drive the poor MacDonald family off their land so he can claim it for himself. After talking to Harrah, however, Thornton refuses Jason's offer, and things don't exactly go smoothly.

Ed Asner — who passed away in 2021 at the age of 91 — played the villain of "El Dorado." It must have been intimidating for the early-career Asner, then in his mid-30s, to have to square up to John Wayne. "I found myself going into uncharted territory," he told Jake's Takes in 2021. "I regarded myself as a big liberal. I hadn't been proved yet as a liberal, but a big liberal, and here I was going against one of the biggest reactionaries of the times. I didn't know how I'd be treated." According to Asner he was "roasted on the first day" but "passed the roast test" and ultimately found the Duke to be "a nice reasonable fellow."

It probably helped that "El Dorado" was a success. Roger Ebert called it "the most entertaining Western to turn up this year" and according to "Howard Hawks: The Grey Fox of Hollywood," the film did "outstanding business" following its 1966 debut in Japan. It then went on to generate "rentals of $6 million on box office receipts of $12 million," which ultimately made it the 12th biggest picture of 1967. Not bad for Asner's first big screen Western.

Ironically, considering his initial collaboration with Wayne was so amiable, the very series that made Asner a star, "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," came to represent a form of TV entertainment that heralded the end of the TV Western as a result of the "rural purge." Not that Wayne himself was affected, but the more urban-focused TV slate of the 1970s was one major signifier that the world was moving on from the days when Wayne and his fellow Western heroes proudly rode the plains.

#3511. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3508. I'm Not A Star Trek Fan – Here's What I Learned After Watching Patrick Stewart's Best TNG Episodes

I love my job and promise I'm qualified to do it, but sometimes, I have to admit that I, as the kids or Taylor Swift might say, don't "know ball." After admitting that I'd never seen "Jurassic Park" or ever sat down and watched "The Mummy," I wrote about the experience of watching these gems for the first time right here at /Film, and across the board, I'm always excited to learn about some new corner of the pop culture world for the first time.

Then my editor asked me to watch "Star Trek."

I need to be exceedingly clear: I don't have any actual beef with the Star Trek universe, but I am a spiteful and deeply stubborn person who has been asked — begged, at times — to watch this show by some of its more passionate fans who have flitted in and out of my life. There came a point where I felt like proving some sort of inane point by not watching this show, even though my refusal to do so affects nobody and nothing anywhere in the world. Then, Sir Patrick Stewart died, and my lead editor asked if he could give me a list of five particularly fun Picard episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and I could write about them. I said yes, because despite my well-documented spite, I'd like to pay my respects to Stewart's legacy. (A note! "Best of Both Worlds," "Family," and "Chain of Command" were only excluded from this list because they're multi-part episodes.)

Some important context! I've never watched this show before. I don't really know who most of the characters are, nor do I know what's going on at most given moments. So what do I think of these handpicked Picard episodes of "Star Trek: TNG?" Let's see.

I started with "The Measure of a Man," a relatively somber Season 2 episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that involves a legal, ethical, and moral dispute over whether the ship's android guy Data (Brent Spiner) is a sentient being or the property of Starfleet, to be dismantled and studied. The whole thing progresses into a miniature legal drama where Captain Philippa Louvois (Amanda McBroom) has to oversee Data's case and make a declaration one way or another. (Also, I love that this show goes out of its way to remind us, regularly, that Patrick Stewart's Captain Jean-Luc Picard is way hot. Louvois is practically panting at him during most of their scenes.)

"The Measure of a Man" is a relatively somber treatise on what it means to possess a soul, artificial intelligence, and what can and should be sacrificed in the quest for more knowledge, but I really can't stress this enough: it's also the first Star Trek anything I've ever watched. With that in mind, I admittedly didn't follow every single plot beat but instead paid close attention to Stewart's performance, which is, obviously, outstanding. The way he approaches a world where the guy next to him is in full body paint as if it's a Shakespearean drama is incredibly rad, but it also lends some gravity to the entire situation. (Get it? "Gravity." The show's about space! Nevermind.)

As news spread of Stewart's passing, it became quite clear to me that he was a massively important actor for so many people thanks to the Star Trek franchise, and this episode was a perfect first introduction that helped me understand why. How could you not side with the guy arguing to save his friend?

"The Drumhead," the second Patrick Stewart episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" that I turned on, is a tiny courtroom drama focused on an explosion on the Starship Enterprise that may or may not have been outright sabotage. After the arrival of retired rear admiral Norah Satie (Jean Simmons), the crew tries to officially get to the bottom of it, as Worf (Michael Dorn), a Klingon dude that I referred to as "the guy in a Chewbacca mask" to tick off one of my Trekkie coworkers for fun, reveals that his hilariously named fellow Klingon J'Dan (Henry Woronicz), is betraying them; it turns out he is, but he didn't cause the explosion.

Satie turns on Picard, angry that he's vehemently defending his own crew — even though the explosion wasn't sabotage at all, as it turns out. The reason that "The Drumhead" ended up on this list is, indisputably, because of Picard's masterful monologue defending himself; Stewart, of course, performs it beautifully and with the solemnity of a soliloquy delivered by Hamlet or Macbeth. (The scene with him and the Klingon whose name is definitely Worf and not Not-Chewbacca is also quite nice.) Again, there's a steadiness to Stewart's performance that's obviously what drew in "Star Trek" fans for decades. Even as you know that Picard is falsely accused, Stewart's real concern and frustration in the moment is palpable, and his moral center remains clear even as he deals with political scapegoating and fear-mongering. That's not just a prescient message for our current times; it's a message that has remained relevant in the decades since Stewart turned in this performance in "The Drumhead," and it's easy to see why Picard is so important to so many.

In this episode, which my editor insists is a must-watch because it shows off Captain Jean-Luc Picard's sillier side — and Patrick Stewart's by extension — Picard is bullied into going on vacation by his colleagues because he won't stop working and just go already. (As a freelance writer, I find this sadly and disturbingly relatable.) Picard finally agrees to go to a planet called Risa when he finds out that Deanna's (Marina Sirtis) mother is coming to visit — I asked around, and apparently, she's a real pain in the butt — and when he gets there, a woman he ultimately learns is named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick) kisses him to try to get away from an enemy. (They do it later, probably crazy style. I don't know what the sexual norms are in the Star Trek universe and am only sort of afraid to ask.)

After that, Vash and Picard have a whole subplot involving some sort of MacGuffin called the Tox Uthat — and a brief borderline kidnapping by that aforementioned Ferengi character Sovak (Max Grodénchik) — and by the end of the episode, Picard goes ahead and destroys the Uthat with the Enterprise's help because I guess it's very dangerous or whatever. I don't know about all that. What I do know is that "Captain's Holiday" is an episode of "TNG" that reminds you that Picard is a hot captain who f***s. In that sense, it's incredibly effective, and I am sorry for how much I objectified Sir Stewart throughout this episode. (No, I'm not.) In all seriousness, though, Stewart took the challenge of this silly, relatively fluffy episode and performed it with the utmost sincerity and wit.

I was given next to no information about "The Inner Light" and the assigned episode that follows (more on that in a second, obviously), and that definitely improved my viewing experience ... because not only do these feel like relatively standalone episodes, they're also both incredible showcases for Patrick Stewart as a performer. After getting hit by some sort of energy beam in a probe on the Enterprise, Jean-Luc Picard wakes up in another universe as a guy named Kamin, who lives with his wife Eline (Margot Rose) on a planet called Kataan. Picard then spends several decades there hanging out with his wife and his friends, raising children, and noticing, all the while, that the sun's radiation will eventually cause widespread drought, something he hopes to prevent despite the government repeatedly telling him that they don't have the technology to prevent it.

Spoilers for this pretty old episode, but when I learned that the whole thing was a series of memories implanted in a probe to show others what life on Kataan was like before it was lost to time, I was pretty shaken! (Also, the fact that 40-odd years only take 25 minutes for Picard is nuts.) All in all, this was the most emotionally resonant episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" I watched in this bunch. As I watched Stewart's Kamin try, over the course of years, to save the planet he calls home and protect his loved ones in the process — despite that mission ultimately being doomed — I ended up weirdly hoping that Picard wouldn't return to the ship, only because Kamin seemed so happy and comfortable with his loved ones. Picard was a cultural father figure, and this episode explains why pretty perfectly.

A sort of "Sliding Doors," "A Christmas Carol" episode completed by journey into the Star Trek universe — and yes, I'm talking about "Tapestry." (No, I did not know who John de Lancie's Q was going into this, and I still don't! Sorry!) After Jean-Luc Picard is wounded on a mission — an understatement, considering it's a large sucking chest wound — he's taken something that may or may not be the afterlife where he meets up with Q and is able to revisit a crucial moment in his life, seeing what would happen if he didn't get wounded in a bar fight and receive an artificial heart in the aftermath.

After changing his past and sleeping with his fellow cadet Marta Batanides (J. C. Brandy) — I love that all of these episodes drive the point home that Picard is super popular with the ladies — Picard decides to not fight the alien who stabs him in the heart, only to learn that, without taking that massive risk and nearly dying, he doesn't become the captain of the Enterprise ... but becomes a loser junior officer that nobody really respects. I genuinely did not see the "Picard goes back and gets stabbed" conclusion coming here, but it ends up making a weird amount of sense that he needs to push himself to end up on the correct life path. Once again, Stewart delivers a deeply considered and serious performance as a man grappling with a fork in the road that he actually has the power to change (or not), but this is probably the most complicated look at Picard in this bunch, and Stewart sells that conflict in him throughout every single second. Stewart was one of our finest actors, bar none. Episodes like "Tapestry" prove that handily.

"Star Trek: The Next Generation" is streaming on Paramount+.

#3506. 20 Years Later, Bong Joon-Ho Looks Back at His Sci-Fi Thriller Masterpiece: 'It Was a Very Tough Process'

The Oscar-winning director looks back at his breakout monster movie, The Host — and teases his next project

Two decades ago, in a 2006 interview with a Korean newspaper, Bong Joon-ho made a surprising statement about his then-new horror movie, The Host. The director, who would go on to make Parasite, Snowpiercer, and Mickey 17, revealed that the mutated monster from The Host was based on an actual creature he'd spotted in Seoul’s Han River, 19 years earlier.

"I don't know exactly what it was," Bong said at the time. "What is clear is that it was a living creature, and it wasn't human. Its size was probably similar to a monster from a movie."

I came across this bizarre detail while doing research on The Host for an interview with Bong himself. (The film turns 20 this year and is celebrating with a 4K remaster and a return to theaters.) So when I get on a Zoom call with the director, it's one of the first things I ask about.

"Attending high school comes with a lot of pressure," Bong tells Polygon. "So that's maybe what led to that kind of a delusion."

OK, mystery solved. Bong Joon-ho didn't actually see a mutated river monster when he was in high school, but he did imagine one under the pressure of college-placement exams. (His youthful obsession with another famous monster might have contributed, too, but we'll get to that in a minute.)

Read on as Bong answers six of our most pressing questions about The Host, while also teasing his upcoming animated feature, Ally, which shares a surprising connection with the 20-year-old monster movie.

Ahead of the interview, I received a digital copy of the remaster and watched a few of my favorite scenes. This new version of The Host looks amazing, especially the CGI used to create the film's iconic monster. I wondered if perhaps Bong and his team had done some touch-ups on the creature, especially since the original film had a famously small budget. But according to the director, no specific changes were made to the film.

"Our overall goal in the restoration was to recreate that feeling of watching a 35-millimeter print, the highest quality print on the first day of release," Bong says. "Of course, it was a digital restoration, but that was our goal to use the digital restoration to create that film look of watching the film on a high quality print for the first time. There wasn't anything that we changed digitally."

Again, the answer is no, but Bong's full response reveals even more about the early inspirations for what would eventually become The Host.

"Attending a Korean high school comes with a lot of pressure," he says. “It's a very tough environment. So I must have been in a pretty fragile mental state back then, where I was having some sort of delusion."

That said, Bong points to two other factors that might explain why he thought he saw a monster back then — and how we wound up with a movie like The Host in the first place.

"What was not a delusion were two facts," he says. "The first fact is that the place that I was living in at the time, our apartment was near the Han River, and I would see the river every day. And the second fact is that I was very fond of the Loch Ness monster. I would try to seek out articles and photographs of the Loch Ness monster. And so those two things combined in my mind, the fact that I was seeing the Han River every day and I imagined what if a monster like the Loch Ness monster appeared in this river that is right in front of me."

While plenty of Bong's movies have horror elements (Parasite has some moments of terrifying tension), he's never truly returned to the genre since making The Host. According to the director, that may change soon.

"It's not a monster movie, but there are horror thriller ideas that I'm developing at the moment," he says. "My iPad is always filled with movie ideas, and there are five right now that are becoming more specific. And out of the five, two of them could be classified as horror."

He also notes that while his next movie, Ally, definitely is not a horror film, the upcoming animated feature does have one thing in common with The Host.

"I'm in the middle of the post-production of my new animation movie," Bong says. "It has many creatures, and one of the creatures really looks like a monster, but a very funny monster. He's quite the character."

The inciting incident in The Host involves an American doctor ordering his Korean subordinate to pour a large amount of formaldehyde into a drain that dumps into the Han River, which leads to the creation of the mutated monster. This scene draws on a real incident that directly inspired Bong's movie.

"The scene of the formaldehyde being dumped is based on an actual event, the McFarland Incident, that happened in 2000 in Korea," he says. "At the time, there were a lot of environmental groups that were protesting in Korea. That actually felt like the beginning of a horror film to me."

The other direct inspiration for The Host's premise is pure fiction.

"Maybe you remember a movie called Alligator — a very interesting American monster movie from the 1980s," Bong says. "That movie has a similar beginning. There's a chemical experiment and they release a baby alligator into the sewers. That alligator later becomes this huge monster. That's a film that I was really fond of at the time."

"Those two ideas combined and that led to the political satire and everything else that's shown in The Host."

In previous interviews, Bong has pointed to his love for the Godzilla movies as a direct inspiration for The Host, but when I bring this up now, he deflects, pointing instead to two other fan-favorite monster movies.

"I liked the Godzilla films when I was younger. I would see them on TV. And I was also fascinated by the characters that appeared with Godzilla, like Mothra. But Godzilla didn't directly influence The Host," Bong says. "The monsters are very different in size. I wanted a monster that wasn't destroying buildings, but was more realistic and could be found in real life — a monster that could possibly hide between buses."

"At the time of making The Host, I was probably more influenced by Ridley Scott's Alien and John Carpenter's The Thing. So I was actually drawn to monsters that are smaller in size."

The Host centers on the Park family, led by the lazy and buffoonish Gang-du (Song Kang-ho), who are struggling to get by even before the monster steals Gang-du's daughter and disappears. At the climax, the Parks reunite and face off against the beast in a thrilling sequence that ends in a hard-earned victory and an emotional family reunion.

The ending more than holds up 20 years later, especially with this stunning remaster, but looking back now, the primary emotion Bong recalls from shooting that scene is embarrassment.

"The problem was, it was at a real location, the riverbank," Bong says. “It was not a soundstage, like the Alien movies. A lot of people were there watching the very famous Korean stars doing something on the riverbank. But unfortunately, there was no monster on set, of course. So we were doing very strange things in the air. We were pretending that there was something there. Song Kang-ho was already a huge superstar in Korea at the time, and he was screaming and doing these crazy things and people were watching and wondering like, 'What the hell is he doing?'"

Shooting that moment, we just felt embarrassed.

"Shooting that moment, we just felt embarrassed. We were just hoping they would watch the film later with actual VFX. But that's the predominant emotion I remember from shooting that scene: embarrassment."

When storyboarding the scene, Bong also had to be extremely sparing in his use of the monster due to the film's limited budget.

"It was a very tough process because we had a super limited budget for VFX," he says. "If you actually rewatch it again and count the number of times the monster is actually shown in its entirety, it's actually not many shots. I could only use seven shots of the monster in this sequence."

"Without the monster in the frame, I had to make the audience feel the existence and the scariness of the monster. I had to maintain the terror throughout the scene. I had to think about how am I gonna do that without actually showing the creature? And in the end, I believe that led me to be more creative."

The Host returns to theaters on Nov. 20, 2026. Tickets are available now.

#3505. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3504. Jake Gyllenhaal's 124-Minute Sci-Fi Disaster Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

In 2004, "The Day After Tomorrow" clumsily delivered a message about climate change via a movie in which Dennis Quaid and Jake Gyllenhaal try to save the world from a new ice age. The questionable part of the film was the science, which as NASA Goddard Space Flight Center meteorologist J. Marshall Shepherd told USA Today, warranted "a D minus or an F." Otherwise, "The Day After Tomorrow" was a grand old time at the movies, and now it seems modern audiences are having a similarly wonderful time with the end of the world over on Netflix.

The sci-fi disaster film was co-written, co-produced, and directed by Roland Emmerich, who prior to this had taken a break from big-budget sci-fi fare to make "The Patriot" with Mel Gibson. "The Day After Tomorrow" saw him return to familiar territory, with a film based on on Art Bell and Whitley Strieber's 1999 book "The Coming Global Superstorm."

Dennis Quaid stars as Paleoclimatologist Jack Hall, who's dismayed to find that global warming has finally brought about a new ice age that's preceded by extreme weather events which batter major cities around the world. His son Sam Hall (Gyllenhaal) happens to be in New York just as the big freeze sets in, prompting Jack to set off on a rescue mission.

The movie isn't the most critically acclaimed thing Emmerich has ever done. But it did gross $552.6 million on a $125 million budget and remains an impressive showcase of early 2000s CGI and arguably the best natural disaster movie of the era. If it's been a while, or you're yet to catch "The Day After Tomorrow," why not join in the celebration over on Netflix?

"The Day After Tomorrow" hit Netflix on November 1, 2026 and immediately took over the streamer's charts like an unstoppable climactic event. Streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol shows the movie debuted at number one on the Netflix Top 10 movie charts on November 2, 2026 in the United States. What's more it maintains that position at the time of writing and it will be interesting to see just how long Jake Gyllenhaal's disaster flick can hang on to the top spot.

Otherwise, there are plenty of other disaster movies streaming on Netflix, just in case you don't necessarily fancy the early 2000s stylings of Roland Emmerich and co.

#3503. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.
