#3502. Taika Waititi’s Delusional ‘Klara and the Sun’ Instagram Post Exemplifies the Dangers of a Growing Divide Between Critics and Artists in the Digital Age

I’ve seen enough: Taika Waititi is no longer riffing on a level that is frickin’ sublime. A quick update for those of you who don’t get your news from DiscussingFilm and/or obsessively listen to “Who? Weekly” in order to keep tabs on Rita Ora: On Saturday afternoon, writer-director Taika Waititi opened Instagram and posted — to his grid! — a less than equanimous reaction to the reviews of his new motion picture “Klara and the Sun,” which was in the process of making less money per screen during its second weekend than the average movie theater employee. It wasn’t the most embarrassing self-own of the pre-midterms weekend (that honor belongs to Michigan congresswoman Hayley Stevens, who committed political suicide on live TV with Anderson Cooper), but I’d argue that Waititi’s faux pas has more to say about how the reality distortion field of today’s media landscape has made it all too easy for highly visible people to misperceive the world around them in a crisis. Related Stories The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound

“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years,” the director wrote under an image celebrating the 53-point mismatch between the film’s audience and critics scores on Rotten Tomatoes. “But I do listen to the people, so this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit 😂 🤷🏽‍♂️.’ Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.🗑️😢🫶🏽.”

When I saw that his post had been modified, I assumed that Waititi had deleted the part where he wrote “and another thing: I’m not mad. Please don’t put in the newspaper that I got mad.” In truth, he had simply tweaked the bit where it said that “sad lost souls” like me had settled as critics. Good note! Much as fallen angels plummet from the heavens before landing in the depths of Hell to anguish for all eternity, critics don’t settle for a life of press screenings so much as we pathetically free fall into it, plummeting from the sacred highs of making “Thor: Love & Thunder” to the wretched lows of watching it. It’s that natural eye for editing that explains why “Next Goal Wins” felt like it had been cut with a soccer cleat.

Of course, I don’t take any of this too personally. (Don’t you dare fucking put in the newspaper that I got mad.) For one thing, I was actually quite tolerant of “Thor: Love & Thunder,” if only because I believe that casting Christian Bale as a guy named “Gorr the God Butcher” in and of itself makes that movie better than most of what Marvel was pumping out at the time. For another thing, I haven’t even seen “Klara and the Sun” — not because I was busy when it screened here, or because I live in one of the many countries where its release has been canceled on account of the movie’s supposed awfulness and verifiable lack of public interest, but rather because I adore the Kazuo Ishiguro novel on which it’s based, and I was convinced that hiring the director of “Jojo Rabbit” to adapt such a poignant tale of loss and brokenness would be like hiring Peter Farrelly to remake “The Remains of the Day.” Except worse, because I’ve always felt like the Merchant Ivory version of that book could have used a few gratuitous jokes about Anthony Hopkins’ swollen balls.

The truth is that the perceived quality of Waititi’s film is irrelevant to what I found interesting about his Instagram post, in much the same way as its quality is seemingly irrelevant to everything else as well. And in much the same way as the perceived quality of Waititi’s other films is irrelevant to the hissy fit he decided to throw about this one. Are “the same people who also hated ‘Jojo Rabbit’” in the room with us? Because that Oscar-winning movie is sitting at 81 percent on Rotten Tomatoes (Certified Fresh™!). OK sure, I hated it, but, as we’ve previously established, I am quite literally not “the same people” who hated “Klara and the Sun.”

On the other hand, I would very much consider myself to be among the large cohort of critics who adored Waititi’s earlier features like “Hunt for the Wilderpeople,” “What We Do in the Shadows,” and “Eagle vs. Shark.” I suppose I could look up the aggregator metrics for those movies as well, but there isn’t any need — that most of the people reading this article have even heard of such modest Kiwi treasures is testament enough to the groundswell of critical support they received around the world. Perhaps, if he’d read a review in the last 15 years, Waititi might have been able to put that together for himself.

But that’s OK. As a public-facing person whose work offers considerably more fodder for mockery than praise (both by virtue of its nature, and also by that of the je ne sais quoi I bring to the job), I would never sincerely begrudge an artist for not wanting to read their own press. Especially now. Perhaps it used to be possible for celebrities to engage with such things in good faith (it was certainly easier in the days when pans were only found in newspapers, and personal attacks limited to their gossip columns), but the internet is a machine designed to make you hate yourself even more than you hate everyone else, and even our finest “anti-hate satires” have proven incapable of solving the problem.

For some folks, especially those with much greater profiles than my own, the only viable way to navigate the digital world without being fully consumed by self-loathing is to decide that all of the people who snipe at you from the sidelines aren’t really people at all. They’re more like ubiquitous wraiths — eyes looking at you from behind a painting, shadows that your subconscious might warp into an ominous shape, visions in the bog that almost lured Frodo to his death in “The Two Towers.” To let any of it in is to let all of it in, and there’s no amount of fame, money, or adulation that can fully inoculate sensitive people against the poison that seeps into their skin every time they pick up their phone (take it from me, someone who doesn’t have any of those things).

And so critics have gone from being a healthy part of the artistic ecosystem to something that artists feel like they need to be immunized against. Which isn’t to suggest that the animus between artists and critics is anything new. On the contrary, it’s as time-honored a cinematic tradition as popcorn at the movies or, say, the old trope of talented indie filmmakers who completely lose the plot once they become too successful.

If anything, that animus used to be a lot more personal, if only because it was expected that artists would know critics by name. Vincent Gallo famously called Roger Ebert a “fat pig with the physique of a slave trader” after Ebert panned “The Brown Bunny” at Cannes. Uwe Boll offered to box his biggest haters after he got sick of being a critical punching bag, and he beat the absolute shit out of all five of the people who took him up on it. Pauline Kael got so far under Clint Eastwood’s skin that he paid a psychiatrist to figure out what her problem was (the shrink naturally concluded that Kael just wanted to fuck Eastwood), while her review of “Ryan’s Daughter” caused David Lean such a crisis of confidence that he almost retired from directing altogether. And he made “Lawrence of Arabia”! (Which Kael also hated).

I’m not so bold as to presume that I — or any of my contemporaries — have a pen worthy of Kael’s poison or place in the public sphere, but the contrast is telling all the same. Instead of headline-making beefs that stand the test of time, today’s critics might be the subject of a petulant DM or a horde-summoning quote tweet. A prominent action director used to get drunk and send me crude messages about my wife via Instagram, but I think he’s sober now. Ron Perlman once called me a “cunt” on social media because I shat on some Christmas movie he made about furries, but I’d be shocked if he remembered that. Or really if he remembered “Pottersville” at all. I had a funny back-and-forth with a good-natured David Ayer after I trashed his Netflix debacle “Bright”; his promise to put my review on his fridge suggested a much less formal riff on Ridley Scott’s decision to frame Kael’s “Blade Runner” pan and hang it in his office. These days, film critics typically only get put on blast by name, at scale, when they make a major sociopolitical misstep of some kind, such as by arguing that a cartoon about red pandas somehow limits its scope by spotlighting Toronto’s immigrant community, or by fixating on the sexual possibilities that could be explored as a form of Mrs. Incredible’s superpowers. (Pixar movies are just irresistible rakes for critics to step on, I guess).

Today’s filmmakers and stars are certainly still aware of their alleged shooters (bracing for another “Dune” situation, Timothée Chalamet asked me to be kind to “Marty Supreme,” though I’m generally a fan, and he had nothing to fear in that case), but most publicly shared pushback is aimed at “the critics” writ large, if only so we can be reduced to cynical strawmen who exist in contrast to “the fans.” The marketing campaign for “Gotti” argued that critics “put out the hit” on the New York mob classic, and then asked people who they trusted more: themselves or “a troll behind a keyboard.” Ignoring the fact that this troll was behind his keyboard in a fucking tuxedo because that movie premiered as an unofficial selection at Cannes, the poptimistic notion that “real people love things” has become a go-to gameplan for an era where reality is easier to warp than it is to reckon with. In an ironic example of life imitating art, “Digger” recently adopted a similar approach.

I suspect that the systemic diminishment of arts criticism is both a cause and a symptom of this ever-worsening phenomenon. There was a time in this country when arts criticism was valued as a worthwhile pursuit unto itself, as opposed to a wonky and unreliable component of the promotional apparatus. The likes of Gore Vidal, James Baldwin, and Norman Mailer were regular fixtures on late night TV and panel shows; they were as famous as any of the people they wrote about, and when artists pushed back against their critics, it was seen as a debate between equals.

Because of that standing, the brightest minds of their generation were able to thrive as public intellectuals, and even invited to leverage their success into lucrative Hollywood careers of their own (as Vidal and Mailer both did before the resulting feud between them led to Mailer headbutting Vidal in the green room of “The Dick Cavett Show”). Today, the Vidals, Baldwins, and Mailers of the world would never belittle themselves by reviewing “Klara and the Sun” for $150, only for their work to be subsumed into a content aggregator that reduced it to a number in a larger set of numbers. In lieu of meaningful financial and intellectual compensation, any thinkers of such caliber today might understandably find arts criticism unworthy of their time and/or just share it to their Letterboxd for free.

That brings us to the reason why Waititi’s post was so excruciatingly tone-deaf, even though he’s hardly the first director to try the “Am I so out of touch? No, it’s the children who are wrong!” defense. The hierarchy of power in the discourse universe has grown as wildly lop-sided as the hierarchy of power in every other arena of public life. Even the most high-profile of critics are barely scraping by, while anyone successful enough to make news with a “the critics put out the hit” post is likely to be a millionaire several times over.

You’d have to be completely disconnected from reality not to recognize how gauche and myopic it is to call journalists of any kind “obsolete” for speaking truth to power and/or product, but I suppose that’s a side effect of spending 15 years in an ecosystem designed to protect itself at all costs. It’s an ecosystem supported by influencer screenings, celebrity interview podcasts, and so many other quality-laundering tactics that it feels like a desperate and radical act when a star like Tom Cruise dares to sit down with a real magazine writer. Only in an ecosystem like that could someone sharp and humane enough to direct “Boy” and the funny parts of “Thor: Ragnarok” become convinced that everyone who hated “Klara and the Sun” did so out of resentment for their own shortcomings. Only in an ecosystem like that could someone that sharp make a movie like “Klara and the Sun” at all. (Which is not to specifically denigrate the actual “Klara and the Sun,” which again I have not seen.)

Of course, it’s not Waititi’s fault that he’s a product of his time, and in light of Aaron Sorkin’s considerably more sensible and self-effacing response to the reviews for “The Social Reckoning,” it’s worth considering whether his relative grace has something to do with the fact that he first came to success during an earlier iteration of Hollywood, where perspective was easier to come by. Whatever the case, we’re all trying our best to protect ourselves in the face of a world where imitated humanity is of limitless value, and actual humanity is an Achilles’ heel — a world in which one of the great modern authors might be moved to write a fairy tale-like story that questions the distance that has grown between people as a result of our efforts to create external vessels for our souls.

Reading Waititi’s tactless Instagram post back for what I pray is the last time, I’m reminded of a resonant line from Ishiguro’s novel, a line that unsurprisingly failed to make it into Waititi’s adaptation: “What was becoming clear to me was the extent to which humans, in their wish to escape loneliness, made maneuvers that were very complex and hard to fathom.” Perhaps, in some abstract way, Waititi’s Instagram post captured the essence of “Klara and the Sun” better than his film ever could.

#3501. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3500. Skydance Inherited Massive Flops From Warner Bros. Deal - And Things Could Get Worse

There's a new mega-studio in Hollywood, and it's got a lot to prove. The Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger was recently made official, with the new company named Skydance. This $111 billion deal has been met with intense scrutiny, in no small part because Skydance is now saddled with billions of dollars in debt. So, to make all this look even remotely tenable for the foreseeable future, that means Warner Bros. has to deliver at the box office.

Unfortunately, the new owners at Skydance inherited a string of massive flops ... and it may get worse before it gets better.

Indeed, a report from Page Six has examined Warner Bros.' ex-film bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy's "free spending" ways. Recall that Warner Bros. set a huge box office record in 2025, with six movies in a row earning at least $40 million on opening weekend. But this year has not been kind to the studio, with this report stating that Warner Bros.' 2026 slate will lose around $800 million. Can it really be that bad? Yes, it can.

Here's a full breakdown of Warner Bros.' 2026 at the box office, movie by movie:

"Wuthering Heights" — $80 million budget/$241 million worldwide

"The Bride!" — $90 million budget/$24 million worldwide

"They Will Kill You" — $10 million budget/$19 million worldwide

"Lee Cronin's The Mummy" — $22 million budget/$90 million worldwide

"Mortal Kombat II" — $80 million budget/$129 million worldwide

"Supergirl" — $170 million budget/$126 million worldwide

"Evil Dead Burn" — $20 million budget/$72 million worldwide

"The End of Oak Street" — $90 million budget/$121 million worldwide

"Practical Magic 2" — $75 million budget/$106 million worldwide

"Digger" — $180 million budget/$49 million worldwide

"Clayface" — $44 million budget/$84 million worldwide (still in theaters)

I previously broke down how movie box office actually works. Basically, without getting too far into the weeds, theaters keep around half of all money from ticket sales, and budget figures don't include marketing expenses. Taking that into account, we can see that only "Wuthering Heights," "Lee Cronin's The Mummy," "Evil Dead Rise," and "Clayface" will go down as hits for Warner Bros. this year, when all's said and done. And some of those are rather modest successes at best.

The rest of the slate is either filled with big disappointments or crushing flops. Tom Cruise's "Digger" will lose a lot of money at the box office, potentially as much as $250 million. That's just the tip of the iceberg, too. "The Bride!" also lost a fortune, while "Supergirl" flopped in a rather terrible fashion. Movies that were expected to be blockbuster hits instead became shipwrecks, with the debris washing up on the rocks. It's been bad.

The validity of that $800 million figure is somewhat irrelevant. It's crystal clear that WB's 2026 slate, overall, is going to lose a lot of money. Even if movies like "They Will Kill You" eventually made money on VOD/streaming, Skydance needs big hits. What it's gotten is a string of disastrous flops.

Even "One Battle After Another" was still a box office bomb ($213 million worldwide/$170 million budget) despite winning Best Picture at the Oscars. This Page Six report estimates it lost around $75 million. The Oscar helps, but probably not quite that much. Hence, Skydance needs Warner Bros. to deliver at the box office more than ever, and the hope is that 2027 will deliver green pastures. But that's far from a sure thing at this juncture.

On paper, there are some surefire bets on Warner Bros.' upcoming slate in 2027. 2024's "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, so it stands to reason that its sequel, "Godzilla x Kong: Supernova," will be a hit as well. But Warner Bros. will have to split that revenue with Legendary, so that's a somewhat qualified winner.

There's also the studio's much-anticipated return to Middle Earth. Even though Peter Jackson isn't directing "The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum," it has a lot of appeal and revives a multi-billion-dollar global franchise. Optimistically, that should pan out pretty well, too, though how well remains to be seen. On top of that, there's the "Minecraft Movie" sequel, James Gunn's "Superman" follow-up "Man of Tomorrow," and "The Conjuring: First Communion," the latter of which ought to deliver. Remember, only six horror movie franchises have made over $1 billion at the box office, and The Conjuring Universe is one of them.

Outside of that? It gets far more murky. Director J.J. Abrams' "The Great Beyond" was pushed back to 2027, presumably because WB wanted an IMAX release. It's expensive and far from a sure thing. Even riskier is the new Nancy Meyers rom-com tentatively titled "Paris Paramount," which reportedly cost a dizzying $120 million. As for Sam Esmail's $60 million "Panic Carefully" and the CGI/live-action hybrid movie "Animal Friends?" They're big question marks.

For seemingly every sure thing on WB's 2027 slate, then, there's a real risk. Skydance film bosses Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg have a lot of decisions to make. For now, though, It's be less about the movies they want to make and more about how they're going to handle all the dicey prospects they've inherited.

#3499. The Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Is the Best-Reviewed Game of the Year by Far

Critics hail the return of the 'greatest game ever'

Nintendo has been deluged with rave reviews for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, its Switch 2 remake of the classic 1998 adventure.

Defined by reverence for the original and admiration for Nintendo's careful redrafting of it, Ocarina of Time's reviews are the strongest any game has received so far in 2026 — and by some distance, too. It currently has a rating of 96 on the review aggregation site Metacritic, and 95 on OpenCritic.

That's a little short of the near-perfect 99 enjoyed by the Nintendo 64 original on Metacritic, but two points ahead of the 94 awarded to Ocarina of Time 3D, the game's last significant re-release, from 2011.

Most critics have a few quibbles, noting inconsistencies in the art style, or some updates that are less welcome than others. But the consensus is that the remake has made the aging masterpiece much easier to enjoy while chiming resonantly with its themes of change and the passage of time.

"Nintendo’s modern Zelda team have turned one of the best games of the 1990s into one of the best games of the 2020s, and made time-travellers out of us all," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote in her five-star review. Like many (but not all) reviewers, MacDonald, a passionate fan of the original, found herself won over by the game's divisive art style, which she called "not so much realistic as hyperreal," and the new cutscenes which "brought out the latent epic drama in a previously sparse tale."

"Despite all of this new sheen, Ocarina of Time retains its understated melancholy," MacDonald wrote. "There is an essential tragedy to this tale about a boy hero whose childhood is stolen by an evil king. It is a dark fairytale that begins with a nightmare and the death of a forest god, sometimes scary and, like all children’s tales that stand the test of time, totally unpatronising."

In another five-star review, Eurogamer's Christian Donlan admits he "kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards," but was struck by enjoyable and revived it felt. Donlan found that the game had gained in visual majesty in some areas and lost its distinctiveness in others: "You could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment," he wrote. "It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore." But he had nothing but praise for "quietly transformative" gameplay tweaks that mean the game "now races along at an astonishing clip."

Above all, Donlan found that playing this remake of a thirty-year-old game which is itself about the passage of time only increased its power. "Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent?" he asked. "It's impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

From a purely technical perspective, Digital Foundry's William Judd judged the Ocarina of Time remake to be "of incredible quality, delivering a surprisingly dark, atmospheric experience that fully leverages Switch 2 hardware while still honouring the timeless structure of the original masterpiece." Performance is transformative, too. "While the N64 original operated at a conservative 20fps, the Switch 2 remake targets and holds a fluid 60," Judd wrote. "Frame delivery remains exceptionally consistent across both docked and handheld modes, providing an effortlessly smooth experience. This dramatic leap in fluidity greatly improves action sequences, platforming timing, and general exploration throughout Hyrule."

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

Polygon's Giovanni Colantonio said that the remake only underlines the greatness of the original game, and the way its age works in its favor. "What immediately stands out about Ocarina of Time next to modern games — even modern Zelda games — is how not a moment feels wasted," he wrote. "Every side-quest, minigame, or hidden grotto feels bespoke, like it was sculpted to contain one memorable secret. [...] No two activities feel like the result of designers copying and pasting assets throughout the world just to fill a game with more hour-eating busy work. It stands in proud contrast to modern adventure games that do so much less with so much more."

Colantonio concluded: "I’ve spent the better part of my life hearing people repeat the claim that Ocarina of Time is the greatest game of all time. At some point, it starts to lose all meaning, like saying The Beatles are the best band of all time based solely on an accepted cultural consensus. But the Switch 2 remake reminds us why Ocarina of Time earned that accolade in the first place."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is released exclusively for Switch 2 on Nov. 5.

#3498. How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google

Do you rely on IndieWire‘s film and TV coverage? If so, please consider taking a moment to ensure you never miss an important story via Google‘s new Preferred Sources feature.

Choosing IndieWire as a preferred source ensures that Google will prioritize IndieWire stories in all of your queries, including traditional searches, Discover, and AI Overviews. Whether you’re searching for movie release dates, TV recommendations, or the latest breaking news, you’ll have access to IndieWire’s reporting and analysis.

If you want to add IndieWire as one of your preferred sources, you can either click this link, click the “Add Us As a Preferred Google Source” button at the top of this article, or manually adjust your preferences by following the instructions below.

First, head to Google.com and search for any entertainment topic. A movie, a TV show, or a film festival will all work perfectly.

Head to the “Top Stories” section of your results that links to news websites. In the top right corner, you’ll see a starred icon that says “Customize.” Click it.

Clicking the customize button will open a new search bar that asks you to type in your preferred sources. That’s where you can add IndieWire.

Once you’ve selected IndieWire as a preferred source, simply click the “Reload Results” button in the bottom right corner, and you’ll be all set!

#3497. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir's Sci-Fi Recommendations For Capturing His 'Vibe' [Exclusive]

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're an aspiring science fiction novelist, you would do well to take the advice of author Andy Weir, who's red hot in publication and Hollywood thanks to the runaway successes of "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary." That the former was self-published before getting turned into a bestseller and a blockbuster film directed by Ridley Scott — one that starred Matt Damon and earned seven Academy Award nominations, including a nod for Best Picture — is the dream of every up-and-coming writer.

So, genre authors have good reason to hang on Weir's every word, especially when it comes to capturing his profitable vibe. And while I'm a firm believer in finding your own vibe, there's a time-honored tradition in this industry of proving you can write comfortably within established formulae. With Weir, it's about straddling the line between hard science and uplifting, humanistic engagement with a vast universe that needn't be as harsh as we've been led to think. We can always, as Damon's character in "The Martian" says, "science the s*** out of" our various predicaments. I think that's naively hopeful in an age where the United States government is vehemently anti-science (unless it lines the pockets of AI-shilling tech billionaires), but Weir's got that storytelling magic that makes you want to believe we're not too far gone.

Weir is but one man, though, so if you're wondering where you can find his vibe in other work, he shared some suggestions with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, starting with his go-to recommendation:

"Well, if you consider an Andy Weir vibe to be just hard science fiction, with accurate science in there, then you got to go for [James S.A. Corey's] 'The Expanse.' That's really, really good hard sci-fi. That's really solid."

"The Expanse," for those not familiar, deals with a relatively realistic colonization of our solar system that does not initially involve interstellar travel. There's literally a lot of space to fill, but it's subject to the kinds of territorial disputes that have sparked wars on Earth. Ultimately, the narrative expands, bringing in aliens and the like, but, in its television incarnation, Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby (who brilliantly adapted P.D. James' "The Children of Men" in 2006) approach the scenario with intellectual rigor.

Andy Weir also voiced enthusiasm for Blake Crouch's "Dark Matter," a frantically paced sci-fi novel that's been successfully adapted into an Apple TV series via the author himself. The small screen version of Crouch's parallel universe thriller stars Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly, and it finds the former's character struggling to skip back to his reality (where his family is being appropriated by an alternate universe version of himself).

Finally, Weir is a proponent of Ben Bova's "The Grand Tour" novels, most notably the fourth entry in the book series titled "Mars." As Weir explained:

"That's a fairly hard sci-fi approach to a mission to Mars. It's about the first mission to Mars. It's got some pretty interesting twists in there that turn out to be ... at first, they look a little bit woo-woo, aliens, oh no. Then you find out the twist reveal of what's going wrong, and the thing is absolutely scientific and completely sensible and you're like, 'Ah, nice one.'"

Again, I'd advise you to find your own vibe, but if you want to catch the eye of publishers or studio execs, maybe check these works out and find your way forward the Weir way.

#3496. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3495. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3494. DC Studios Officially Casts Mason Thames As Robin — Will He Play Him In Live-Action?

We might not know when the DC Universe will unveil its version of Batman, but we just got news that the franchise has cast its Robin. Well, at least we know who'll be voicing one of the Robins in the upcoming "Dynamic Duo" movie. In an interview with Collider, DC Studios co-head Peter Safran confirmed that Mason Thames has been cast as the voice of Dick Grayson in the upcoming film.

Thames is best known for starring in "The Black Phone" and its sequel, as well as playing Hiccup Horrendous Haddock III in the live-action "How to Train Your Dragon" movie. But it seems he's been gunning for a DC role. "We always talk about wanting volunteers and not recruits to be part of the DCU, to be part of DC Studios," said Safran, "and Mason always wanted to be Dick Grayson. He just did."

According to the producer, Thames came in to read for Grayson and "auditioned the s*** out of it." "He's a wonderful young actor," he continued. "But boy, did he want this. He was just obsessed. When he came over to the DC offices, he came over with his dad at the time, and we've got tons of great archives and stuff in there, and wanted to take a picture of everything and with everything. He's a fan."

That certainly bodes well for a committed performance from the 19-year-old, who most recently appeared alongside Dave Franco and O'Shea Jackson Jr. in the most startling comedy of 2026, "Idiots." The question is, will Thames actually play Dick Grayson in live-action? According to past comments from Safran's DC Studios co-head James Gunn, that's exactly what will happen. But there's no confirmation as of yet.

"Dynamic Duo" is an animated film that's being developed by DC Studios in collaboration with Swaybox Studios. The latter's unique animation style combines puppetry and CGI to create a stop-motion-like effect that will be used to tell Jason Todd and Dick Grayson's origin stories. Mason Thames' casting as the latter had previously been rumored, with scooper Jeff Sneider reporting it in September 2026. But now it's official, meaning Thames will join Logan Kim, who's playing Jason Todd, in "Dynamic Duo" — much to the dismay of "Titans" star Curran Walters, who reacted to the news of the Jason Todd recasting with disappointment.

The movie is set for a September 22, 2028 release, with Arthur Mintz, who co-founded Swaybox with Theresa Andersson in 2013, directing. For now, further details about the film are scarce, but Lee Pace and Steve Buscemi have reportedly been cast as members of the Red Hood Gang.

As it stands, we at least know who will be voicing two of the most significant versions of Robin in the DC Universe. The question is, will Thames and Kim portray their characters in live-action? They certainly should, given James Gunn's prior comments.

When he and Peter Safran became co-heads of DC Studios in 2022, they promised this latest on-screen superhero franchise would not simply be more of the same. Gunn touted a shared universe without a house style and confirmed that DC Universe actors would portray their character across film, TV, animation, and even video games, streamlining the franchise in a way that sounded as though it could be bad news for animation voice actors. But it remains to be seen whether he will stick to that claim moving forward, especially since much has changed since 2022.

James Gunn has repeated his claim about actors portraying their DC Universe characters across mediums on several occasions. In 2023, he told DC.com "Television, movies and games all intertwine within the same universe. We're going to cast actors that are going to be able to play the characters in this, as well as in other things, some of which we've already cast." Thus far, Frank Grillo has played Rick Flag Sr. on the big screen in "Superman," on TV in "Peacemaker," and voiced the character for animation in "Creature Commandos." As such, it would make sense for Logan Kim and Mason Thames to follow a similar path.

But as we've seen in recent years, nothing is set in stone. Leaving aside the Warner Bros. Discovery/Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026, James Gunn and Peter Safran announced a slate of movies back in 2022, some of which have now been scrapped. Gunn confirmed that DC had cancelled the planned "The Authority" movie, for instance, and he has spoken openly about how plans for the DC Universe otherwise shifted following Warner Bros.' initial announcement. All of which raises the question of whether he's sticking to his plan for actor continuity across mediums.

It would certainly make a lot of sense given his previous explanations. In 2023, Gunn spoke to The Hollywood Reporter about how Aaron Pierre would be playing Green Lantern John Stewart in both the HBO series "Lanterns" and on the big screen in the upcoming "Man of Tomorrow." "We don't want the series to feel in any way like step-children or lesser-than," he told the outlet. "[The show is] just another way to tell a story." Time will tell if the same holds for Kim and Thames.

#3493. D&D World of Warcraft Designer Learned From the Game’s Most Controversial Edition

“The goal here is to recreate D&D in Azeroth, not to recreate the MMO experience.”

The Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion allows Dungeon Masters to run games in the world of Azeroth where players battle bosses in dungeons inspired by the MMORPG. But lead designer James Wyatt never wanted those adventures to feel too much like the video game.

“There have been times in D&D's history when it has leaned a little bit closer to the MMO experience, with short rests being shorter and spells being a little bit more like buttons,” Wyatt told Polygon in a virtual interview. “That’s not the direction we wanted to go. What this book is about is the world, and how to make that world the setting of your D&D game.”

D&D 4th Edition was released in 2008, four years after the launch of WoW, and it entirely reworked the 3.5 Edition ruleset by turning both weapon attacks and spells into a set of powers that could be used at will, once per encounter, or daily. The shift, combined with language that divided classes into roles like Defender, Striker, and Leader, led many players to criticize the new rules as being too much like WoW.

“I think there's an anxiety among the fandom about losing what they love to the new wave of entertainment,” Wyatt said. “I think 4th Edition followed WoW’s lead in a direction that wasn’t great for the tabletop game.”

D&D: WoW provides rules for translating all of WoW’s classes and builds into D&D, but Wyatt focused more on getting the feel right than upping the complexity to be more in line with a WoW character’s ability rotations and cooldowns. His team considered creating mechanics for managing enemy aggro, but decided to just stick with the already present rules for a Battle Master Fighter’s Goading Attack and the Protection Fighting Style feat. Sometimes more transformative work was needed, like replacing many Paladin class features to turn them into Death Knights.

“It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution,” Wyatt said. “It’s a lot like the alternate class features in Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, except that they are packaged together. Paladins got all this light and healing stuff, and that doesn’t really fit the Death Knight flavor, so let’s change that to death and necrotic damage and darkness stuff.”

Wyatt’s biggest challenge was evoking the feel of a WoW Shaman in D&D. He eventually settled on a redesign of Barbarian that swaps out Primal Knowledge for the ability to create totems that can help allies and hinder enemies. Wyatt is currently playing the class himself and took the feat Magic Initiate (Druid) to further mimic the WoW class that blends melee fighting and primal magic.

“When I enter my rage, I describe the orbs of elemental energy circling around my body and I’m hurling ice and fire and lightning at foes, and it feels very shamany,” he said. “I even took Ritual Caster, so I’m going to get in tune with the elements and do shamany stuff when I’m out of combat. There’s a lot of possibilities for how you conceptualize the character within that framework.”

While D&D’s World of Warcraft spells are designed to evoke abilities from the video game, Wyatt expects many of them will make their way into D&D games that don’t take place in Azeroth. DMs will still want to use their discretion with some of the more unusual options like Arcane Pulse, a cantrip designed for Nightborne Elves that slows enemies in a burst instead of scaling in damage like most cantrips.

“The spells are balanced against other spells in the Player’s Handbook, so they should work just fine if you pick them up in other places,” Wyatt said. “There are a couple that might feel a little weird in other characters’ hands, but they will still be balanced and work.”

While he was working on the new sourcebook, Wyatt wrote himself a list of design guidelines that wound up in the book’s section on Adventures in Azeroth. They serve to remind DMs that they shouldn’t try to make their games feel like an MMO. Dungeons might take multiple sessions to clear rather than being fought through in a few hours. Characters are going to want to find creative ways to interact with the world and NPCs rather than just following preset paths and killing everything they encounter.

“In D&D, most of the time, monsters stay dead when you kill them, and you can’t expect characters to run Icecrown Citadel over and over again to get the loot that they want, with everything just resetting to the way it was before,” Wyatt said. “Their actions need to make a difference, and the spotlight really needs to be on them. It’s not massively multiplayer. It’s minimally multiplayer.”

#3492. To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

After I watched Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in the weeks leading up to its world premiere as the opening night film at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, I had a long list of things to talk to the filmmaker about.

Curb cuts — those graded concrete ramps at the edge of sidewalk corners that allow anyone and anything with wheels to glide gently onto the street below — aren’t really the sort of thing most people think about. But if you need them, if you’re in a wheelchair or pushing a stroller or dragging a heavy suitcase, they’re tough not to think about. It’s hard to jump off a curb if you can’t, well, jump. At best, you need help. At worst, you just can’t do it. Related Stories The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound

Starring British actress Ruth Madeley as the iconic activist Judith Heumann, “Being Heumann” wastes no time putting our star in the middle of a busy New York City street, with not a curb cut to be seen. She doesn’t really have a choice. A wheelchair user for most of her life (Heumann contracted polio as a toddler), Heumann grew into the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement,” and the film finds her at an important crossroads.

First, she needs to be able to navigate the world around her, which was simply not built for her. No curb cuts.

But things are changing. When the film begins, the first U.S. federal civil rights protection for people with disabilities, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, has been signed, but no one is putting it into actual action. Heumann set out to change that. The film jumps ahead four years, following Heumann as she leads hundreds of fellow activists and disabled people into a massive protest, including a historic sit-in in the San Francisco Federal Building that lasted a month.

It’s real history, but it’s also rousing and funny and entertaining. And deeply human.

It is, of course, very similar to Heder’s previous film, “CODA,” which followed a deaf family and their one hearing child as they navigated a world not built for them. The film premiered at the 2021 Sundance Film Festival, where it proved to be a huge crowdpleaser (no easy feat, as that edition of the festival was held entirely online). A year later, it won Best Picture, changing Heder’s life forever.

After her big Oscar win, Heder had some immediate needs to meet. “I had worn these high heels for so many hours the night of the Oscars that my toes went numb, and it took maybe two months to come back to life and have feeling in my toes again,” she told IndieWire with a laugh. “But there was a moment of recovery, not just from the energy that it took to go through an awards campaign, to do a Q&A every night, to fly all over the world with the movie, but also the adrenaline leaving your body, which was a very intense feeling.”

Choosing what project she’d take on next was also top of mind for Heder, who admitted that it took awhile for her to get back into the process of actually creating after spending more than a year sharing “CODA” with the world. That was intense, too.

“It’s shocking moment as a filmmaker, because suddenly there’s a bunch of eyes on you that were never there before,” she said. “‘What are you going to do next?’ and ‘How are you going to follow that up?’ It took some time for me to tap back into why I tell stories and what moves me. I developed a lot of projects. I had maybe five different movies that I was developing or writing or overseeing a writer on and didn’t really know which one would come together first.”

And then there was “Being Heumann,” which Heder has been working on in earnest for about five years. She first met Heumann at Sundance in 2021, when Nicole Newnham and James LeBrecht’s documentary “Crip Camp” premiered, in which the irrepressible Heumann appeared as a young woman. (Heder also co- wrote the script alongside Rebekah Taussig, based on Heumann’s autobiography.)

“It was before ‘CODA’ had come out, it was before I had taken the whole Oscar ride,” Heder said. “I had been drawn to this story because it was a great story, long before I was thinking about what’s the right move in the industry or how do you follow up a film that goes on to do [win Best Picture]. It was just very close to my heart.”

There was also Judy Heumann. Heder said she knew from her very first meeting with Heumann that she wanted to make a film about her. She hadn’t even been aware of Heumann until she saw the documentary, and then? She couldn’t take her eyes off her.

“There’s a scene where she’s yelling about lasagna in the cafeteria at summer camp, and I was like, ‘Who is this woman?’ She looked like she was conducting a senate hearing, but she’s talking about what they’re going to have for dinner,” Heder said. “I was very intrigued by her as a character, but I felt like there was a deadly version of this story, which would’ve been a traditional biopic.”

Heder had been working with Heumann for nearly two years before Heumann died in March 2023. Heder said she had a “a very strong feeling that Judy died having chosen me to make this movie and tell the story, and so there was a sense of responsibility to her and her legacy.”

There was also, by her own telling, “a little bit of fear of, if I follow up ‘CODA’ with another film that’s about disability, are people going to put me in that box? But after ‘CODA,’ I had a rare moment of power in the industry where a lot of people wanted to make what I wanted to make. There was a moment where I could have used that capital to go make a Marvel movie and get a big paycheck and move out of my small home in Eagle Rock or use the capital to try to tell the hardest story I could imagine trying to tell and probably a film that not a lot of people would’ve financed or gotten behind.”

She went with the latter. “I knew it was going to be an all-disabled cast with a lot of new actors and without movie star names, and it was a period piece and it was more expensive than your average indie movie,” Heder said. “So it felt like if there was ever a moment that I could push it through to tell this story, that was the moment I was in.”

And while it was not an automatic yes from Apple, which also distributed “CODA,” Heder said, “They believed in the movie for sure, and they believe in me as a filmmaker. But, on paper, this movie is a challenging film.” Those challenges went beyond the already-daunting needs around casting.

“Yes, on one hand, it’s a story about a disability rights activist in the 1970s,” Heder said. “It was important to me that the film not feel like ‘eat your spinach’ or that it was not there to educate people on something important that they should know about. What I pitched to Apple is ‘I want to make “Dog Day Afternoon” with disabled people. I want to make a story that has a lot of momentum and humor.’ These people were building sex tents in the hallway, they were smoking pot, and the Black Panthers showed up! That’s a movie that I think will be fun to watch and joyful and entertaining. They understood not just that I was trying to tell the story, but the way I was trying to tell it.”

While Heder eschewed any “eat your spinach” angles, she’s still very passionate about sharing the incredible impact of Heumann’s work in the disabled community. “Most disabled people at the time didn’t even really understand that they could demand to be a part of society or demand equal rights,” Heder said. “There was a feeling of, ‘Well, your body is broken, so you don’t deserve to leave your house,’ and I think a lot of people had internalized that, and Judy awakened that understanding in a lot of people.”

Judy Heumann’s story also awakened a different understanding in Heder herself. The film doesn’t canonize Heumann, instead showing her as dedicated leader who is also prickly, brash, and set in her ways. Heder didn’t just want to tell a story about a leader, but what it actually takes to be a leader and continue growing in that role.

“There are so many tropes around disability, so the idea of meeting this young person who feels invisible and finds her voice and becomes an activist and comes into her power was the more expected story,” the filmmaker said. “But meeting someone who is at the height of their power, who has this radical empathy where she’s fighting for people to be seen and heard, and yet has a really hard time seeing and hearing and including other people, was a much more interesting character arc. On one hand, Judy is fighting for this group of people to be seen as human. But being a human on a very basic, connective level? Saying thank you to the people who are helping you, being kind, putting the people first? That was also a journey Judy had to go on.”

There’s a moment in the third act of the film when Judy is unable to physically be at the San Francisco sit-in. She not only has to trust that the more soft-spoken Kitty Cone (Madeline Delp), who has become her closest confidant, can keep the sit-in going in her absence, but she must also say that to her. You can see how hard that is for her, but how revelatory, too.

“I do think, as a director — and not to say ‘woman director,’ because I hate constantly qualifying director with my gender — there was a feeling when I started out as a young woman that I had to always have the answers, always seem in control and I knew what I was doing because if I expressed any self-doubt or any waffling, it would be perceived as ‘she doesn’t know what she’s doing,’” Heder said. “It took me a long time to get comfortable enough with my skillset, with my ability to be on a set, and go, ‘I actually don’t know. I actually don’t know where we should put the camera right now. What do you think?’”

Casting that kind of powerful person to portray Judy was charged on many levels. There was no question that Heder would find a disabled actress, but how do you cast someone to be Judith Heumann, so naturally without peer? Heder had worked with the real Judy for years. She knew all the important people in her life.

“There was an intimacy that you almost never have with your lead character,” Heder said. “Yes, Judy was a wheelchair user, but that was one element of her identity. It was also about Judy’s blunt sense of humor, Judy’s directness, Judy’s drive, Judy’s sense of humor, and all of those qualities were things that I was looking for. It was trying to find someone that physically resembled her, who also could embody her energy, which was very specific.”

She likes to joke that her casting directors, Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell, had to take on the “casting Olympics, because every character was a unicorn.” “I was like, ‘Hey, go find me a 19-year-old Black blind man who can sing, who has this relentless optimism and just embodies Dennis Billups,’” Heder said with a laugh. (They did, with first-time actor Charlie Rush-Reese, a gem in a sea of them.)

She found Madeley in a slightly different way. “I was working with a deck designer to put images together when I was trying to get the movie greenlit at Apple, and he was British, and he said, ‘This character really reminds me of this actress, Ruth Madeley. Do you know her work?,’” she said. “I didn’t know her, but she was in this film called ‘Then Barbara Met Alan,’ and I watched the film and I could see exactly what he was talking about. She has an earthy, wry humor, and she exudes intelligence and has this big well of emotion and vulnerability.”

Still, Heder said with a laugh, she didn’t make it easy on Madeley. “Ruth had done so much work before I ever met her, but I put her through the ringer. I auditioned her many times,” Heder said. “I saw many, many actors for that role, and she truly won that part. I knew it was going to be an incredibly difficult film to make, and I felt I really had a partner with her. Even aside from performance, which is the most important thing, having a true collaborator in your lead actor is invaluable as a director.”

Heder’s film is filled with incredible star turns by a number of new (and, in some cases, brand-new) performers. Among their ranks is, however, one very recognizable name: Mark Ruffalo, cast here as Joseph Califano, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. He’s the guy who needs to sign the meaningful regulations that would put 504 into actual action. And, for most of the film’s running time, he refuses to do it. He’s the bad guy of the story, sort of, and to have an outspoken activist like Ruffalo in that role adds real dimension to the part.

“Mark is someone who has been unafraid in his life to be principled and stand by those principles, whatever the cost,” Heder said. “And Califano was someone who really considered himself a good guy and had, throughout his career, protected the Selma March, pushed forth the Great Society Program, had stood with the students at Kent State, and really felt like ‘I’m on the right side of history.’”

When the film begins, he has just started to work for President Jimmy Carter, and the pressure is on. The president gave Califano a strict mandate: cut the federal budget by $3 billion. He was less than three months into his job when the sit-ins began. The moment he signed the 504 regulations, he’d have 60 days to enact the necessary changes to meet its requirements. And they would cost $3 billion.

“The more I read about Califano, the more I felt like you could tell this story from his perspective, you could absolutely understand that he was between a rock and a hard place, but that’s when people’s principles are actually tested,” Heder said. “In my first meeting with Mark, he was talking about fear, and there are a lot of politicians now who are living in a state of fear, whether it’s their reelection, whether it’s losing money that backs their campaign or offending lobbyists or constituents.”

She added, “The reality is, the movie is not speaking to a mustache-twirling villain who is out to make life hard for disabled people, it’s speaking to the good guys who are stuck in inaction because it feels too hard or too scary. That’s very timely for me, because we all have something to protect that you risk by going out on a limb and announcing what you believe in. There’s a lot of fear right now, and we see it real time, and so there are actual repercussions to speaking up and standing by your morals.”

Inaction isn’t Heder’s bag. In making a film like “Being Heumann,” which is literally about the fight for accessibility, there was no question she had to build a production that was comfortable, creative, and open for all. That didn’t scare her. Why should it? It’s attainable.

“With ‘CODA,’ we were trying to make a set accessible to a deaf cast, which was one very specific thing, and so it was about communication and ‘where do we put interpreters?’ and ‘how do I call action and how do I call cut?,'” she said. “But it was all working toward meeting a very specific set of needs on this movie because it was cross-disability. Someone who is paraplegic has very different needs than someone who is an ambulatory wheelchair user versus someone who lives in chronic pain. It was about making a set that is accessible to a deaf cast at the same time that you’re making that set accessible to a blind actor. And we didn’t know what we didn’t know.”

Heder and her crew had to figure out how to navigate everything from ramps to scripts. How do you do a table read with a blind actor? How do you do ADR when they can’t see their own mouth moving? How many braille scripts do you need? Will audio earpieces help? How many interpreters need to be there for the deaf performers?

“At every stage of the process, we were coming up against these hurdles that were unexpected, even though we had built an accessibility team and we had really done our best to do intake forms for every actor to understand what their needs were on set,” Heder said. “A lot of our cast had never been in a movie before, or some of them were non-actors and so didn’t even know to ask, didn’t even know what they would need to ask, because it’s very different to say, ‘Yes, I’m fine in a vintage wheelchair, but are you fine in a vintage wheelchair for 12 hours?’ Because that’s what a movie set is. There was a lot of real time adjusting that had to happen and problem-solving in the moment. It never stopped.”

Heder is clear, however: this was worth it. “I never want people to take from this at all that it is too hard to work with a disabled actor, I think it’s about knowing what you need,” she said. “Once we figured out what people needed, it really did flow and run as any other set would. It was just a learning curve figuring out what those accommodations were. Judy impulsively led a hundred disabled people into this federal building, many of whom went in without their attendants or their caregivers and then had to figure out how to survive in this building over this 30 days. They all had to find their superpower in their own disability.”

The challenges they faced (and overcame) also helped align them with what Judy Heumann and the rest of the protestors felt during the sit-in. “When I interviewed Dennis Billups, who is blind, he said he was standing lost outside the protest, and he offered to push a wheelchair user if they would guide him into the building,” Heder said. “There was all of this interdependence that started to happen in the protest that was about survival, and that happened in real life on our set, where our cast started jumping in to fill each other’s needs in a way that is very hard to describe and was incredibly profound.”

I mentioned how touching it is to see the way that Heder shows that on the screen, that everyone is useful and that everyone has something that they can do, when she added a compelling corollary. “Not only is everyone useful, but everyone needs help,” Heder said. “Everyone needs help. It’s not just the disabled cast that needed help. There were moments where my non-disabled cast needed help, and there were moments where people on the crew needed help.”

She continued, “It’s like the same way when I was a new mom and I was pushing a stroller around the city, ‘thank God for curb cuts,’ or getting off the subway in New York City and having to lug a stroller up the stairs, ‘thank God for the elevator.’ We all have these moments where you understand that accessibility helps everybody. We built ramps onto our set from every direction, and the grips were like, ‘Thank you. We are lugging thousands of pounds of equipment, and this is the first set I’ve been on where there are ramps everywhere you look, and we can wheel that stuff up.'”

It’s the exact lesson we see in the film, and one that people still need to be reminded of: we can make the world a better place for everyone, but we have to work together.

“I remember there being a big scandal or pushback when there were directors who came out and said, ‘I don’t allow chairs on my set,’ and what you are saying through that,” Heder said. “I understand the intention, which is ‘I want people committed and energized and not kicking back and not participating.’ However, you are also saying that you are not inviting anybody onto your set that cannot stand for 12 hours. … When you refuse to provide any accommodations, you are shutting off an avenue to so much talent and creativity.”

Heder added, “That was the thing I really felt more than anything on this. It was profound to me that what Judy did with these protestors, how this group of people physically changed our world. It’s things that we all take for granted, now that there are curb cuts or Zoom or FaceTime or even texting. All of these moments of innovation came out of inclusiveness that are now accepted as our reality.”

“Being Heumann” will premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

#3491. Jurassic Park's Lost Animated Series Pitch Has Finally Surfaced In Video Form

It's been over 30 years since "Jurassic Park" changed movies forever, with Steven Spielberg's 1993 adaptation of Michael Crichton's sci-fi thriller novel delivering not only a perfect film, but a production that brought a systemic change to how Hollywood made movies. It also marked the last time a dinosaur franchise would become a bonafide hit, as Hollywood continues to try and fail to make audiences care about dinosaurs unless the title includes the word "Jurassic." (David Robert Mitchell's "The End of Oak Street" is the latest example of audiences largely avoiding non-"Jurassic" dino movies.)

Given how incredibly successful the "Jurassic Park" franchise has been, it's no wonder it's expanded to include spin-offs, including video games, cartoons, and more. But what is surprising is just how slow this franchise has been to grow. After all, the first film came out in 1993, at a time when practically every big movie somehow got turned into a cartoon, regardless of whether the original was for kids or not.

"Jurassic Park" did almost get an animated series back then, but it never made it to production. Still, we've heard about this show on and off over the years, and now, we finally have the very first bit of footage, reportedly titled "Escape From Jurassic Park." The trailer surfaced on Twitter/X, and it quickly spread. Watch for yourself right below.

After all of these years, it has finally been found!

Fans of Jurassic Park, I humbly present to you, the animated Pitch Trailers for the canceled Jurassic Park Animated Show!

More info coming soon! pic.twitter.com/UGT5lOvvd5

— Jurassic Library (@JurassicLibrary) October 31, 2026

The trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated film, thought lost forever, doesn't show much, but it does perfectly capture the look and tone of the Spielberg classic and mixes it with that recognizable '90s Amblin animated look we saw in "Animaniacs" and other shows of the time.

There's not a whole lot of information about the lost "Jurassic Park" animated series. We do have old pitch decks and story treatments that give an idea of what the series could have been about, as well as old concept art from cartoon veterans Will Meugniot and artist William Stout, who were meant to spearhead the show.

Perhaps most importantly, the "Jurassic Park" TV series was meant to be a direct sequel to the first film, with the first season reportedly focusing on BioSyn creating its own rival dinosaur theme park, leading to — you guessed it — another dino outbreak.

According to William Stout, this "was not going to be a kiddy show (although kids of all ages, including myself, could enjoy it)," he said in his blog back in 2014. "They wanted the show to be a mature prime time series with top writers and state-of-the-art television animation augmented with quite a bit of CG animation."

That much is clear from the leaked trailer for the "Jurassic Park" animated series. Though it still features kids, a big sense of adventure and wonder, and a visual style reminiscent of Don Bluth, the trailer also makes it clear this is a show about man-eating dinosaurs, and seems to hint at an appropriate amount of violence.

We also know from reports about the series bible and its proposed episodes that the "Jurassic Park" cartoon would have been serialized, with each episode building up to the next and the first season ending with the rival park opening. That's a quite approach surprising for 1993, when serialization was virtually unheard of in animation.

Though the series never made it to production, we eventually did get a "Jurassic Park" cartoon (seen in the photo above), and it remains the best sequel to that original movie.
