#3489. Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

You too, Netflix? Netflix’s whole thing has been that its algorithm was designed in such a way that it knows what you’ll want to watch, that even small shows with no hype or stars like “Baby Reindeer,” “Adolescence,” “Squid Game,” “Ginny and Georgia,” or even “Stranger Things” once upon a time can turn into massive, organic hits. They call it the “Netflix Effect” for a reason.

But even Netflix has had trouble keeping people consistently engaged and in getting them to find that next show or film. Last month it overhauled its creative leads to meet that challenge, so it is turning to where so many other companies have turned to shake things up: AI. Related Stories To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

Netflix today launched AI Discover, which is a new tab on the streamer’s TV app where you can ask an AI assistant to help you narrow down a selection based on what you say you’re in the mood to watch. Fortunately Netflix didn’t do the Meta thing and come up with some cuddly meeple to be your virtual assistant.

The tool is built around themes, in which you select from a range of themes, each of which is previewed via a clip from a show or movie. You can say I want to watch “Something Light” or “Scare Me” or ask for something for families, something that’s popular, or something quick, to name a few options. The AI will give you recommendations, it will allow you to refine your selections further and you can continue doom scrolling, and you can finally “Tune Your Recommendations” to either keep a recommendation or tell the AI to not recommend it again.

What this is not is an AI chat bot. You don’t even type anything into it (TV remotes are sometimes hard for that), just pick from some pre-selected options until you get what you want. The AI also though won’t be available on kids profiles, for now it’s not available on mobile, just TVs, and the data collected won’t be used to inform future content decisions for what Netflix produces.

While this could be seen as just a fancy new search function with an AI label, Netflix clarifies that this is new tech they’ve been building with a predictive intelligence model that responds in real time and continues learning based on your preferences. It’s a function on top of the existing search that’s a bit more refined.

For now, AI Discover is only available for a handful of U.S. members who are using it in English and on supported TVs, but it’ll open wider in the coming weeks. The AI Discover function is indicated with a red gem icon and a “New” label on the top of your screen.

#3488. Will Ebenezer Be The Box Office Hit Johnny Depp's Hollywood Comeback Needs?

Johnny Depp is attempting to mount a Hollywood comeback. After years of being embroiled in controversy and starring in films you probably haven't heard of (like the colonial drama "Waiting for the Barbarians"), he's back in his first major studio movie in a long time. "Ebenezer" is a new take on Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol," with Depp playing Scrooge. The question is, can this be the box office hit that Depp needs?

Directed by Ti West ("X," "The Inkeepers"), "Ebenezer" is expected to pull in between $17 and $24 million domestically when it hits theaters next weekend, per Box Office Theory. Against a reported $38 million production budget, that would be a solid start for the Paramount release, especially since this one should be able to hang around through the holiday season. That is, assuming audiences like what West and Depp have cooked up. If it's eviscerated by critics and audiences alike? That's another conversation.

Competition shouldn't be a big issue, at least not right away. "Godzilla Minus Zero" could make box office history for the franchise topping the charts this weekend, but it shouldn't get in the way come its second frame. "The Cat in the Hat" is unlikely to be a major, direct threat, either. Rather, the biggest competition will come when "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" arrives on November 20.

The "Ebenezer" trailer positions Depp's "Christmas Carol" re-telling as being closer to a horror movie. Now, horror has been extremely hot at the box office lately, so that makes sense. Paramount is also selling the film with the tagline, "The name you know, the story you don't," and it has a star-studded supporting cast that includes Rupert Grint ("Harry Potter"), Andrea Riseborough ("Mandy"), Daisy Ridley ("Star Wars"), Trammell Tillman ("Severence"), and Ian McKellen ("X-Men").

There are obvious risks here. As mentioned, if "Ebenezer" is met with a bad response, all of these numbers could be meaningless, as word of mouth could wreck its ability to have legs. Still, it's likely to enjoy big returns on VOD and streaming, if for no other reason than curiosity from viewers.

The other issue is Johnny Depp himself. Depp dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise after a court case verdict tied to tabloid The Sun in 2018. That, coupled with his highly-publicized courtroom battle with his ex-wife Amber Heard over allegations of abuse, derailed his career. Even before that, though, it wasn't going as well as it once had been.

Depp proved his best days were already behind him with the big box office bomb that was "Mortdecai" in 2015. He hasn't starred in a meaningful hit since 2018. Yes, the "Pirates of the Caribbean" movies made billions of dollars, but that was a long time ago. Do audiences still care about Depp? That's the big question Paramount seeks to answer. It's betting the answer is "yes."

Beyond that, Ti West has never directed a high-profile movie of this size. He helmed the "X" films rather successfully, with "MaXXXine" sending off the trilogy on a box office high note, but we're still talking about a movie that made $22 million in total. This is a big step up for West, and in light of the Depp of it all, there's a lot of pressure. Was the director able to tune out the noise and deliver a crowd-pleaser? We'll know soon enough.

"Ebenzer" hits theaters on November 13, 2026.

#3486. Fortnite's Latest Reward Is So Good, It's Creating a Black Market

Players are in a frenzy over the Pirate Shop token

Fortnite launched its treasure hunting season this Sunday, which includes a One Piece collaboration that was one of the most anticipated collaborations of all time. No one expected a new item to steal the show, overshadowing the One Piece skins players had been requesting for years. Fans have been obsessing over the Pirate Shop access token, a recently introduced item that makes the whole Item Shop free for a fortnight. Thankfully, they might be able to end their search earlier than expected, as Treasure Hours are scheduled to begin soon.

This mini-season is all about treasure hunting. To go with the theme, there's a chance that players will find treasure in each chest. The most sought-after treasure is the Pirate Shop token, which gives players the opportunity to claim everything in the Item Shop for 14 days. It can be activated once before Dec. 15, 2026, and then again before Dec. 15, 2027. There are various types of treasure, ranging from gizmos to rare skins. Of course, most players are after the token, which is worth hundreds of dollars in V-Bucks.

The Pirate Shop token has taken over the lives of a majority of the Fortnite community. Gamers are spending hours of their free time in Battle Royale matches, looting as many chests as they can in hopes of finding this token. The exact chances of finding the token are unknown. Dataminer Blortzen's calculations indicate it's likely to drop about 1 in 2,000 chests. However, community estimates point towards one token in every 700,000 chests — a scary discrepancy for treasure hunters. While rare, its reward is so unbelievable that thousands of players have flocked to Fortnite to try their luck. It's been dubbed "Fortnite's response to GTA 6," a game that is sure to draw millions of players away from other titles.

This frenzy is why some have already found a way to profit from it. AFK tools are being sold to farm chests while players stand idle. Accounts with the Pirate Shop access token are available for sale on eBay for thousands of dollars. If a teammate is lucky enough to receive a treasure, everyone gets the same reward, so players are even buying carrying services, allowing them to camp out during a match while someone else opens chests for them. Using software or services to automate the game and trading or selling accounts goes against Epic Games' terms of service and can lead to permanent bans.

Treasure Hours start on Oct. 8, and they will be live every Sunday until the end of the season. While it has not been specified whether these events will increase treasure drop rates, it's entirely possible. Epic Games' official blog post on this season says Treasure Hours will provide "boosted drops."

Fortnite senior director, Chris Yu, has also confirmed Power Hours begin this Sunday. Treasure Hour times remain unknown, but effects are expected to be revealed once the limited-time event hours are announced. If treasure drop rates are in fact boosted, this will be the optimal time to grind it out with some squad mates and open as many chests as humanly possible.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3484. Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

The official Cannes synopsis for “Club Kid” is almost suspiciously vague: “A washed-up party promoter is forced to turn his life around when an unexpected visitor arrives.” Hmm…

Technically, that’s true. But it’s also the kind of carefully evasive logline you can only use if you’re an artist as charismatic and cunning as Jordan Firstman. A writer, actor, singer, comedian, and now debut feature filmmaker, Firstman has spent years making audiences feel like they know everything about him without fully surrendering the parts of himself that might actually hurt. Related Stories Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch To Follow Her Best Picture Win, Siân Heder Opted to Make ‘the Hardest Story She Could Imagine’

“People have trouble metabolizing me for a lot of different reasons, ” Firstman told IndieWire, ahead of his dazzling feature film’s world premiere at the Cannes Film Festival on May 15. “I think I remind them of someone they know, but also someone they don’t know. Or someone who deserves things, but also someone they went to high school with who’s just an annoying gay guy. Perception is weird.”

For years, Firstman’s public persona has existed somewhere between chaotic queer oracle and self-aware caricature — whether through his hilariously unhinged Instagram comedy, his writing and acting work on shows like “Search Party,” “The Other Two,” and “I Love LA,” or his caustic self-portrayal in Sebastián Silva’s “Rotting in the Sun,” which debuted at Sundance in 2023.

“I wanted the thing I did after that to be a bit softer and more like a version of me that I knew, but other people didn’t,” Firstman said. “There was a lot on me in that movie in terms of persona and people thinking about me in a certain type of way.” (Suffice to say, Firstman spends much of “Rotting in the Sun” cartoonishly chasing attention and ketamine on the beach.)

The “Club Kid” filmmaker also wrote the viral Laura Dern tribute that was performed by the Gay Men’s Chorus of Los Angeles at the 2020 Spirit Awards (“Top five moments of my life,” Firstman joked), which helped carve out space for his unique voice in Hollywood. Sliding effortlessly from incisive observer to chaotic flirt to exhausting narcissist, Firstman is never not in on the joke. But it took until now for him to finally explore what happens when that cyclical sense of self-parody stops working as armor and starts feeling like a weight.

“I didn’t want to win anyone over anymore,” Firstman said of his mentality heading into this project. “All I could do was tell the story I wanted to tell in the way that I wanted to tell it.”

A funny and melancholy look at one man’s deep feelings of isolation, appropriately set against the fast-changing experience of modern queer nightlife, “Club Kid” stars Firstman as Peter, a gay New York party fixture whose chemically accelerated existence is interrupted by the sudden arrival of a child he never knew he had. That setup could easily lend itself to a broader (read: straighter) comedy, but Firstman’s soulful consideration of finding both family and purpose hits a much more sensitive frequency than that.

Not nearly as interested in punishing Peter for his messiness as it is in helping explain why he built his life this way in the first place, “Club Kid” draws a lot of its tension from the inherent conflict between the pursuit of shallow visibility and the fundamental need for more meaningful types of intimacy. The damage and acceptance that kind of internal contradiction can bring to a person over an extended period runs through every frame of Firstman’s film, and the result feels less like a conventional dramedy than a decade-long discovery unfolding in real time.

With a slick, feel-good opening scene that smartly orients the entire experience, “Club Kid” charts Peter’s evolution from the mid-2010s into the spiritually scorched present with merciless specificity.

“I remember that era was the start of Europe coming to America gay-wise,” Firstman said. “Dark rooms were not really a thing before that. It was Molly, and maybe some coke, and that was kind of it.” Then came COVID. “I said this famously in the pandemic, but it’s like, you take sex away from gay people for a month, and they’ll make up for it for the next five years.”

According to Firstman, as the substances changed in many American clubs, so did the emotional atmosphere surrounding some parts of LGBTQ culture. “In 2020 and 2021, K got really big. Then G started in 2022. Then, the last couple years, the Mephedrone, the 3MMC, and 4MMC,” he explained. “You look around, and you see zombies where it should be a community. And sometimes that still feels like your community? It just changed.”

The brilliance of “Club Kid” lies in Firstman’s refusal to flatten those realities into an easy morality. His film understands the air of danger, loneliness, and instability often inherent in queer spaces — while warmly demonstrating why countless people keep returning to them anyway. No one in Firstman’s script is reduced to a victim or cautionary tale, least of all Firstman. And in the end, even his harshest skeptics will struggle to shake the affection they’ll feel for a character who has spent years finding and losing himself under the same strobe lights.

“Even when you strip back the surface layer of the drugs and the afters going on all weekend, beneath it is a bunch of queer people who are funny and sensitive and broken in some ways and artistic and just fully whole,” Firstman said. “That’s what I wanted to show.”

The heart of “Club Kid” is in Peter’s relationship with his son, played by newcomer Reggie Absolom, whom Firstman discovered after watching hundreds of audition tapes out of London. “I remember seeing the thumbnail and being like, ‘Please be able to act, please be able to act, because that’s him,’” Firstman said. “Then I met him, and we went for ice cream and talked about music. I sent all the kids the playlist I wrote the movie to. Reggie loved Massive Attack.”

At several points throughout our conversation, Firstman became emotional discussing his kid scene partner and their film’s larger themes of innocence, queer identity, and the cruel impermanence of self-perception. One moment in particular, in which Reggie bonded with the movie’s ensemble cast of queer and trans performers, overwhelmed him.

“For the rest of his life now he’s going to love trans people because he got to see how funny and creative [they are], and listen to music with them and joke around with them,” Firstman said, trailing off emotionally. “I think that’s the beauty of this story.”

That softness feels revelatory coming from an artist who has so often weaponized irony and overstimulation as an entertainment strategy. Moments earlier, Firstman had been casually breaking down the social consequences of post-pandemic partying and joking about his “level of hotness.” Then, he was crying and discussing chosen family.

“Everything shows on me,” Firstman laughed, describing the quality as a “gift and a curse.” “Maybe people have complicated feelings toward me because I can’t really hide anything.”

What makes “Club Kid” as hysterical as it is devastating? Its writer/director’s keen understanding that exposure and vulnerability are not the same thing. Peter has spent years being looked at — desired, consumed, partied with, projected onto — without ever fully learning how to let himself be seen. The arrival of his son has the power to change that, and viewers, too.

“A lot of queer people lose their innocence young and then go straight into this world that can be debaucherous,” Firstman said. “They don’t get a chance to go back to that. Then they don’t have kids. I think for a lot of people, kids bring out their inner child in ways they never expected.”

Speaking with IndieWire, the filmmaker repeatedly returned to the idea that queer adulthood can feel like an endless negotiation between freedom and self-destruction. But even at its saddest, “Club Kid” remains startlingly sweet. Firstman has an almost anthropological understanding of the contemporary queer social scene in New York, and his movie is packed with the kind of hyper-specific observations that can only come from somebody who has spent years studying how humor functions as both a tool for connection and an often unwieldy defense mechanism.

“I’ve softened a lot in the process of making it,” Firstman said. “I think I’ve struggled so much with my queerness, not in a traditional way, but more in the actual community and having so many mixed feelings about it. Because it isn’t simple. It’s very rich and full. And I think all this [with ‘Club Kid’] happened at the right time and when I could handle it in my life.”

For all its scenes of spiraling, “Club Kid” is ultimately about the terrifying decision to let yourself be loved without performing for acceptance first. The fact that Firstman can communicate a concept so psychologically naked suggests the arrival of a major new auteur unafraid to move forward on his own terms. “Club Kid” is the most honest Firstman appearance to date.

“Club Kid” premieres at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival in the Un Certain Regard section.

#3482. 6 Reasons South Park Season 29's Rotten Tomatoes Audience Score Is So Low

Since 1997, South Park has been on the cutting edge of comedy thanks to series creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Always raunchy, shocking, and unafraid to make the audience cringe, South Park recently entered its 29th season, a feat for any TV show, but this year the reviews aren't as positive as fans might have hoped. Though it's often the dedicated audience members who boost ratings for series like South Park, this time viewers aren't being shy about their disappointment with season 29.

South Park season 29 premiered on September 16th, 2026, on Comedy Central, marking the return of beloved characters after the South Park season 28 finale. As usual, South Park is making fun of everything and everyone, taking on popular internet trends, political leaders, and massive media franchises without fear. However, there's something about season 29 that isn't reaching fans the way Parker and Stone typically do, as seen in the audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

South Park's low Rotten Tomatoes audience score of 54% is a tough break for the popular satirical series. Unfortunately, it doesn't come as much of a shock after the audience ratings for seasons 28 and 27, which have seen some decline in viewers' reception. However, if there's one thing that South Park thrives on, it's controversy. Season 29 isn't over yet, and it's possible that the series could surprise fans, even though reviews indicate it hasn't connected with them yet.

When it was announced that South Park season 29 would rebrand to be titled South America, it was a funny choice. The title skewers President Trump's attempts to change the names of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America. This would be a great gag for a one-off episode, but using this as the show's title for the entire season isn't working as well as South Park might have hoped.

The change has ended up feeling confusing and out of place, highlighting the fact that South Park isn't very sure of its own identity anymore. It's far from the first time that South Park has criticized Trump and the current U.S. administration, and it certainly won't be the last. It's admirable that Parker and Stone are always ready to take on the most powerful institutions in the country, including their own parent company, but the change to South America feels more like a confusing subplot than anything else.

Any fan of South Park knows that Kenny is no stranger to getting killed and being brought back to life many times over. Each time Kenny dies, it's in a new, unique way. Usually, it doesn't take too long for Kenny to reappear and take his place within the ensemble. This season, Kenny dies in episode 1, "South American Biker Gangs," and he hasn't been back since. It seems that Kenny's death this season will be more permanent.

Additionally, Kenny's death has sparked a very different reaction from the characters than usual. Almost no one has acknowledged his death or mentioned him since the season premiere. It feels like he's really gone this time, and there's a hole left in his absence. Though South Park did come up with a solution to the Kenny problem, using Randy's transformation as a replacement, it doesn't scratch the same itch as having Kenny in the mix.

With e-bikes, a Sephora that looks like Backrooms, and even commentary on the beef shortage, South Park could be going too far and tiring its audience out. South Park has always made its name on sharp, relevant political and social commentary, never afraid to target all movements and ideologies, which is part of why the series has such wide appeal. However, as the series ages and attempts to keep up with the ever-changing internet trends, it's hard for the referential humor to stay as fresh as it once was.

A jaw-dropping mix of grotesque visuals and blunt political satire forces viewers to confront reality in South Park's latest shocking episode.

The turnaround of the present news cycle and internet trends that South Park mines for jokes is so fast-paced that it's nearly impossible for any TV series to feel contemporary. As soon as South Park has referenced something, it's nearly on its way out of the zeitgeist. For the series' younger viewers, it's easy to feel as though South Park is pandering to their interests and trends without fully understanding them. Conversely, older viewers might feel out of the loop and confused about what South Park is talking about.

Randy takes on a central role in season 29, episode 3, "You Like That On Your Face," making Randy a main character in season 29. While plenty of audiences have been fans of Randy and his role as a foil to many of the show's most outlandish characters, it comes as a surprise that he's getting so much screen time this season. Thanks to the events of episode 3, Randy looks and acts like a child in the wake of using too much anti-aging cream, another topical skewering of looksmaxxing.

In some ways, this makes up for Kenny's absence following his death, which still hasn't been reversed, letting the "young" Randy slip into a childish adolescent role. Randy's prominence in the show isn't new, as South Park has been leaning on his character for a few seasons now. However, it remains to be seen if viewers will accept the childlike version of Randy as part of the texture of the series, since it marks such a significant change in his character.

South Park has used both serialized and episodic storytelling throughout the seasons, but it's been a long time since Parker and Stone went back to overarching season-long plots. With only six episodes planned for season 29, this is a shorter foray into serialization, but it's a risky move for the series. After the mixed reviews that have come pouring in all season, it won't be easy for South Park to craft a season finale that's satisfying.

Keeping Kenny dead is part of the controversial choice of a season-long arc, and it's fair to say audiences are missing him. As Randy remains in child form and the characters have to tackle new beef and data-center-related disasters, multiple plot threads are piling up, and it isn't clear how South Park will come back from so many storylines that haven't received rave reviews.

The future of South Park isn't exactly uncertain, as Parker and Stone are signed on to produce 50 episodes for Paramount through 2030. However, the series has been running since 1997, and almost thirty years later, the audience reception indicates that the beloved satire might be running out of steam. Though the creators have never been too concerned with pleasing fans and doing what's popular, this season is making audiences question if the series can hold on much longer.

There are a few episodes left in season 29, so things might not be too bleak for South Park​​​​​​, as the series could always turn things around before the season finale. However, it feels as though every episode rehashes an arc or punchline that viewers have witnessed many times before on the series. If South Park is going to defend its reputation for being on the cutting edge of comedy, the show has to step things up soon.

South Park airs new episodes biweekly on Wednesday nights at 10 PM E.T. on Comedy Central, available to stream on Paramount+ on Thursdays.

#3481. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3480. Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

One of 2026’s distinct pleasures (for lack of a better word) has been getting to know Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ life partner and power of attorney holder who becomes the primary focus of “You Can See Everything.” Evans and Holmes have two kids together and are working to launch a new blood testing startup in the vein of Theranos. While Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film begins as a relatively straightforward documentary about Holmes and Evans’ life in San Diego during the last month before she reported to federal prison, it spirals into a larger investigation into Evans’ influence on Holmes and the nature of their partnership. Related Stories Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

It’s a three-hour movie, but you’re not alone if you left with unanswered questions about the couple. Fortunately, Evans himself is still active as ever on X — both his own account, and the one he runs for Holmes. And on Monday, November 2, Evans spent some time answering questions from fans… everything was on the table other than his caveat that every question “needs to be legally permissible.”

Solo parenting 2 toddlers you are sick approx 75% of days. Allergies in Austin TX are no joke.I take Claritin daily. Much less sniffling.

Evans claimed that it was a marriage proposal, and implied that he ended up getting there in time.

She was getting engaged. Married now, has a baby, glad I went. Family over everything

Evans pushed back on the idea that he wanted to do full frontal nudity in the documentary, dismissing that suggestion from a fan as a “false narrative.” He also linked to a PEOPLE story that claims he was “violated” by the scene and wrote “trust the sources.”

Evans also did not limit himself to questions about the film. Other AMA questions focused on his cultural tastes, and Evans used the platform to express his love for Chappell Roan, Kendrick Lamar, Charlie Kirk, and Taylor Swift (he said he bought Holmes’ engagement ring at the Reputation tour merch booth).

Fielder and Oppenheimer’s film makes it clear that nobody can really see everything in a documentary, but Evans appears committed to proving that you can post everything if you try hard enough.

#3479. Game Of Thrones: Rose Of The South Officially Announced

Game of Thrones has no shortage of beloved characters across George R.R. Martin's sprawling fantasy universe, but arguably one of the top fan-favorites among them is the lovely Margaery Tyrell. She became a standout thanks to Natalie Dormer's incredible performance in HBO's adaptation, though longtime book readers already had their eyes on her and House Tyrell as true power players in the Seven Kingdoms.

Where the Starks built their reputation on honor and the Lannisters wielded their wealth like a weapon, the Tyrells understood the value of appearance, influence, cunning, and knowing exactly when to make their move. Margaery embodied that approach, winning over the people of King's Landing while navigating some of Westeros' most dangerous royal alliances.

Alongside her formidable grandmother, Olenna, she helped give House Tyrell one of the best family dynamics in the entire series. Although the show's version of the family met a devastating end, the golden rose of Highgarden remains one of the franchise's most recognizable symbols. Now, House Tyrell is returning in a major way with the announcement of Game of Thrones: Rose of the South.

House Tyrell is officially back in the spotlight with the announcement of a brand-new release called Rose of the South. The new gear set for Conquest is part of November's Highgarden Harvest Festival, a month-long celebration dedicated to one of Westeros' most influential families, running from November 3 through November 27.

The Rose of the South gear set is one of the featured rewards for the event, offering a variety of combat bonuses for players looking to strengthen their armies. Its primary focus is on ranged units, with increased Ranged Health and Ranged Attack, alongside specialized bonuses against enemy ranged and infantry troops. Other notable perks include increased March Speed against players, improved maximum march size, and additional ranged attack and defense bonuses during Seat of Power battles.

While the gear set is arguably the biggest attraction for House Tyrell enthusiasts, it's far from the only new addition coming to Game of Thrones: Conquest this November.

The larger Highgarden Harvest Festival celebrates the lavish lifestyle of House Tyrell, with an emphasis on festivities, your standard political intrigue and backstabbing, and of course, romance. The event also introduces Mace Tyrell, Lord of Highgarden, as a brand-new playable Hero, bringing Margaery's father into the spotlight. Classified as a Heroic Master of Ships, Mace specializes in infantry combat, with bonuses to infantry attack, health, and march size.

Interestingly, Mace isn't the only new character joining the game, as Hotpie is also arriving as a Mythic Grand Maester Hero under the hilariously appropriate title of The Gravy Knight. He offers several cavalry-focused bonuses, making him another potentially valuable addition to players' collections.

The Highgarden Harvest Festival also features a busy schedule of limited-time activities, including Prepare the Banquet, Pruning the Garden, Maintaining Poise, and Culprit Revealed. Players can also collect Braavosi Loan trophies and exchange them for rewards during designated events.

Another notable addition is the Terror of the Tundra Dragon Gear set, beginning with a new Saddle that improves Dragon Ranged Health against players. With House Tyrell taking center stage throughout November, Game of Thrones: Conquest is giving fans another opportunity to celebrate the golden rose of Highgarden, even if Margaery herself isn't the focus of this particular update.

#3478. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3477. ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama

“The Intertwining” director Akira Yamamoto was mentored by Kiyoshi Kurosawa, and it shows. Yamamoto is one of many Japanese filmmakers to study under the legendary director of “Cure” and “Tokyo Sonata,” who was a professor at Tokyo University of the Arts from 2005 to 2023. And although he’s not Kurosawa’s most famous pupil — that would be “All of a Sudden”‘s Ryusuke Hamaguchi, whose style is also an influence here — he has clearly taken many lessons on composition and timing from his former teacher. To this end, Yamamoto’s latest feature takes a politically charged family drama and laces it with restrained, but palpable psychological tension, creating a film whose quietest moments are also its most uneasy ones. Related Stories Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was Jordan Firstman Opens Up with ‘Club Kid,’ His Hilarious, Tender, and Must-See Feature Filmmaking Debut

Yamamoto’s primary tactic for creating this tension is the long take. Shots in this film frequently linger just a few seconds longer than they’re “supposed” to, reflecting the pauses in dialogue scenes where characters choose their words before they speak. Many filmmakers who utilize this tactic like to punctuate these moments with bursts of sudden violence, but aside from the elderly woman collapsing on a city bus who serves as a catalyst for the film’s plot — filmed in a very Kurosawa-esque long shot, by the way — Yamamoto contains himself here, too.

The struggle in “The Intertwining” is all psychological, as the two women who respond to the medical emergency — both medical students, as it turns out — begin to realize that they have a lot in common. Ji-hyun (Jiyoung) is a fifth-year Korean exchange student, although she’s frequently mistaken for Japanese — as Nakano (Karata Erika) notes with surprise when they formally introduce themselves afterwards. They exchange numbers and hang out a few times, eventually figuring out that not only are their parents both in the hospitality business, but they were born at the same clinic around the same time.

Ji-hyun’s parents briefly lived in Tokyo before going back to their home country, discouraged by the discrimination against Koreans that’s still pervasive in Japan today. This becomes extremely important later on as Nakano, who’s never felt at home in her family, decides to test her DNA against those of her parents and brother after learning about DNA sequencing in class. Nakano is both shocked and relieved to discover that the parents she grew up with are not her biological mother and father, and her new friend Ji-hyun supports her as she tries to process these feelings. Then a nurse at the clinic gives Nakano an envelope containing the names of her real parents.

As it turns out, it’s not a coincidence at all that Ji-hyun and Nakano’s parents both sought treatment at the same fertility clinic. Ji-hyun and Nakano were both the product of IVF, and their embryos were implanted in their respective mothers on the same day. Except the doctor made a mistake, meaning that Nakano is actually Korean, and Ji-hyun — who’s also faced prejudice for her ethnicity while living in Japan — is actually Japanese. The scene where the clinic’s current head tries to explain what went wrong more than 20 years ago contains another of the movie’s rare outbursts, as Nakano’s father angrily confronts the doctor for “putting a Korean embryo into [his] wife.” In his mind, this is the worst betrayal of them all, and the way he prioritizes his family’s honor over his daughter’s happiness is one of the reasons why Nakano feels no guilt about leaving him behind.

Ji-hyun, on the other hand, loves her family very much. She does not want to become Japanese, and the political undertones of their respective identity crises are one of the film’s most crackling unspoken undercurrents. Ji-hyun pities Nakano, but maintains boundaries between them even after the two go to South Korea to visit Ji-hyun’s warm and supportive family at their picturesque restaurant by the sea. By this point, the bubble of unspoken words between these two women is straining with tension. But Yamamoto is too subtle, and too savvy, of a director to let it burst.

Instead, we’re left with some challenging questions about identity, and what makes a person who they truly are. Although it’s the central conflict, the mix-up at the clinic is not the only outrageous coincidence in this movie, and “The Intertwining” could have been even stronger with a slightly tighter narrative focus. Still, it’s a testament to Yamamoto’s filmmaking that these feel less like plot contrivances and more like the invisible reverberations of fate.

“The Intertwining” does require patience and active engagement, both of which are made possible by committed, but controlled performances from Jiyoung and Karata, who also starred in Hamaguchi’s “Asako I & II.” One could easily imagine the premise of this movie as the stuff of Sirkian melodrama. But Yamamoto asks his leads to internalize these big emotions rather than externalize them through his filmmaking, and the controlled intensity shown by all three key players is key to what makes “The Intertwining” work.

“The Intertwining” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3476. The 6 Most Perfect Sitcoms of the Last 25 Years, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Sitcoms sneak into your life in a way no other genre can manage. You do not merely remember what happened. You remember being among them. You remember the conference room, the terrible apartment, the break room, the campaign office, the stupid little corner where two characters always end up arguing.

That is the standard I care about for this list of 6 most perfect sitcoms of the past 25 years. Not most important” not “most influential,” not which one generated the cleanest critical consensus. I mean the shows where the cast chemistry becomes muscle memory, the jokes survive repetition, and even a five-second reaction shot can make you laugh because you already know everything that person is trying not to say.

Abbott Elementary follows a group of teachers working at an underfunded Philadelphia public school, with relentlessly optimistic Janine Teagues (Quinta Brunson) convinced that almost every institutional problem can be solved if somebody cares hard enough. Around her are veteran teachers Barbara (Sheryl Lee Ralph) and Melissa (Lisa Ann Walter), awkward Jacob (Chris Perfetti), increasingly competent Gregory (Tyler James Williams), and principal Ava (Janelle James), a woman whose relationship with professional responsibility remains wonderfully theoretical.

Brunson created the show, and her smartest instinct was making the school feel loved rather than merely dysfunctional. The broken facilities and absurd bureaucracy generate jokes, but the teachers are never treated like fools for caring about their students. I especially love watching Gregory slowly become somebody who belongs there, because Tyler James Williams can turn one tiny glance at Janine into an entire argument with himself. And then there is Ava, who should be unbearable on paper and somehow becomes essential. Abbott Elementary worked because everybody is ridiculous in a slightly different direction, yet when something genuinely matters, you understand exactly why these people keep showing up the next morning.

Four vampires share a house on Staten Island and spend much of eternity behaving like roommates who have somehow survived centuries without developing basic competence. What We Do in the Shadows centers on Nandor (Kayvan Novak), Nadja (Natasia Demetriou), Laszlo (Matt Berry), Colin Robinson (Mark Proksch), and Guillermo (Harvey Guillén), Nandor’s painfully devoted familiar, whose dream of becoming a vampire becomes considerably more complicated once we learn what he is actually capable of.

I adore how seriously the show takes completely stupid problems. A supernatural council can become office politics. Ancient blood feuds collapse into petty grudges. Laszlo can spend decades impersonating a bartender named Jackie Daytona and somehow make that feel emotionally complete. Jemaine Clement developed the series from the film he made with Taika Waititi, but the television version eventually creates its own magnificent rhythm. Guillermo is the secret weapon for me. He begins as the exhausted human cleaning up everybody else’s bodies and gradually becomes one of the most dangerous people in the house. The vampires barely notice. That gap between who these people think they are and who they actually are is comedy gold.

Selina Meyer (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) begins Veep as Vice President of the United States, a position she rapidly discovers has far less power than she expected and considerably more opportunities for humiliation. The show follows Selina and her catastrophically self-interested staff through elections, scandals, alliances, betrayals, and repeated demonstrations that practically nobody in politics is behaving for the reasons they claim.

The insults get quoted most, understandably, because some of them sound chemically engineered to destroy another human being. But I think the real genius is how Armando Iannucci built an entire political ecosystem where competence occasionally appears and is immediately punished. Selina wants power with such naked desperation that every brief moment of success makes her worse. Gary’s (Tony Hale) devotion becomes increasingly tragic. Jonah (Timothy Simons) keeps failing upward like a virus with congressional ambitions. And Louis-Dreyfus performs humiliation better than almost anybody alive. She can lose an election, destroy a friendship, receive terrible news, and still somehow make the funniest thing in the room the way Selina adjusts her face before somebody walks in.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

The Office (original one) turns the Scranton branch of a paper company into a documentary subject, trapping salesman Jim Halpert (John Krasinski), receptionist Pam Beesly (Jenna Fischer), terrifyingly committed Dwight Schrute (Rainn Wilson), and everybody else under the management of Michael Scott (Steve Carell), who desperately wants to be considered both an extraordinary boss and everyone's closest friend.

Greg Daniels developed the American version, but the thing that eventually separated it completely from its British inspiration was affection and its vlog-like camera-work. Michael can be selfish, inappropriate, exhausting, and spectacularly bad at reading a room. Then you see him quietly show up to Pam’s art exhibition when almost nobody else does, and suddenly the character expands. That is what the show keeps doing. Dwight stops being merely the weird guy. Jim’s effortless coolness occasionally becomes avoidance. Pam discovers that wanting another life and building one are different things. Even after you know every prank and every awkward meeting, those relationships still work. I can hear the first few notes of the theme and immediately feel like I know where I am.

Liz Lemon (Tina Fey) is trying to run a live sketch-comedy show while managing unstable performers, idiotic network decisions, and Jack Donaghy (Alec Baldwin), an NBC executive whose frightening corporate competence somehow makes him one of the most dependable people in her life. 30 Rock barely gives you time to recover from one joke before three more have already happened in the background.

Fey created a sitcom that seems actively offended by empty space. A throwaway sign can contain a joke. A character can mispronounce something once and the mistake can return two seasons later. Tracy Jordan (Tracy Morgan) is capable of saying something so irrational that the sentence becomes funnier every time you remember it. Yet Liz and Jack are why I keep coming back. Their relationship never needs to become romantic to matter enormously. He thinks she wastes her potential. She thinks he has allowed capitalism to replace several normal human organs. They are both occasionally correct. Beneath all the lunacy, 30 Rock understands the strange intimacy of finding one person at work who actually knows how your brain malfunctions.

Fleabag follows an unnamed London woman (Phoebe Waller-Bridge) stumbling through grief, sex, family resentment, friendship, and an extraordinary talent for turning emotional disaster into a joke before anybody can ask whether she is okay. She talks directly to us constantly, making the audience her private accomplice while everyone around her receives a more edited version. And then the Priest (Andrew Scott) notices.

That tiny moment still gives me chills because Waller-Bridge, who also created and wrote the series, spends so long establishing the camera as Fleabag’s hiding place. She can escape into us whenever an interaction becomes too intimate. When somebody finally catches her doing it, the entire storytelling device becomes emotional rather than clever. That is why the second season hits so hard. Fleabag is funny because she is protecting herself with comedy, and the show gradually asks what happens when someone sees through the protection without demanding that she stop being herself. The final goodbye is devastating for exactly the same reason. She walks away, looks back at us, and gently tells us not to follow. Six episodes earlier, losing access to her thoughts would have seemed impossible. Now it feels like proof she might finally be able to live without needing us there.

#3475. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3474. NCIS’s 18-Year Original Character Recast Returns For A Better Spinoff Role

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Ana has also covered a wide-spread of topics in the past — from franchises like, the MCU and Star Wars, to classic TV favorites, such as Frasier and MASH.

Ana brings clarity and enthusiasm to every story she tackles—whether reporting on new releases or offering deep dives into fan-favorite franchises. Her coverage translates complex entertainment developments into engaging, audience-focused content.

NCIS has officially brought back the first major recast for a brand new character. Leading to the premiere of CBS's fall 2026 slate, there was so much discussion about Scott Caan's return to the franchise, as he was set to portray a new player. For context, the actor originally depicted Danny Williams in Hawaii Five-0 — a show that was firmly established to exist in the same universe as NCIS. Joining LL Cool J's Sam Hanna, however, Caan is now playing Nick Schaeffer in NCIS: New York.

The matter was a massive topic of discussion among fans for a couple of reasons. Firstly, prominent recasts are not normal in the NCIS franchise. Granted that supporting characters return for new roles from time to time, but nothing had been as big as Caan. Secondly, there remains an argument that Caan could have simply reprised his role as Williams in the new offshoot. Regardless, so far, so good for NCIS: New York, but he isn't the only returning NCIS actor who's playing a different role in this cycle.

After six years, Sean Harmon is officially back in the NCIS franchise. However, instead of playing Young Leroy Jethro Gibbs, he debuts an entirely new role in NCIS: Origins season 3. For context, Mark Harmon's son was the original actor to portray the young version of the legendary TV character, who was properly introduced in 2008's "Heartland" episode. The outing tackled the beginning of his love affair with Shannon and offered context regarding his difficult relationship with his father.

Sean played the role a couple of more times as the NCIS flagship continued to explore the younger years of Gibbs. These episodes were done long before the idea of NCIS: Origins was born. His final outing in the role was in 2020's "Everything Starts Somewhere," which revealed the origins of Gibbs and Donald "Ducky" Mallard's friendship. In 2024, Young Gibbs was officially recast with Austin Stowell, and now, Sean returns to the NCIS franchise as FBI agent Casey Bloom. So far, he's had a couple of appearances in the prequel, and it's safe to say that it will continue to do that as season 3 moves forward.

Regardless of anyone's favorite character, the undisputed truth is that Gibbs is the poster character for NCIS. Even after Harmon left the series in 2021, his character's legacy has lived on. The debut of Stowell's version in NCIS: Origins and Old Gibbs recent return have all reinforced that idea. That said, Sean is better off playing Bloom rather than reprising his original role in the franchise. For starters, the FBI agent allows the actor to flex his acting muscles in an entirely different way. Bloom is a peculiar player; he's quirky, cocky, and even funny. He's a tad incompetent, but in a charming way. It has been fun seeing Sean bring him to play.

The NCIS franchise has been on a great run since the network TV cycle started, but CBS is disrupting its impressive season with an announcement.

Now, he can exist in the NCIS franchise with no canonical burden. As great as it is to play Gibbs, it comes with pressure, considering how well known he is. Stowell is doing well with the character, especially in NCIS: Origins season 3, as he becomes fully comfortable in the role. The recast also allows Sean to fully fulfill his duties behind the scenes as an executive producer for the franchise. Overall, it's a win-win situation for everyone.

#3473. Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

The fall festivals have come and gone, leaving specialty sugarplums dancing in Oscar pundits’ heads, from Netflix’s Spanish favorite “La Bola Negra” to Searchlight’s hilarious “Wild Horse Nine,” which just boasted a raucous Academy screening reception.

But don’t forget the big guns, movies of scale and scope that wowed audiences earlier in the year. Some will fill the craft categories (see “Spider-Man: Brand New Day”) or dominate Best Animated Feature (see Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” which might land Taylor Swift an Oscar for Best Song). Others will wow not only cinephiles but the mainstream voters in the Academy. Their campaigners must push them back into voters’ consciousness, remind them of what they liked so much, all those months ago. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

On November 11, “Disclosure Day” Best Actress contender Emily Blunt will launch her award season push for an “Oppenheimer” follow-up Oscar nomination with a SAG Q&A in New York, followed by November 13 in LA. On November 15, she’s conducting press conferences for the Critics Choice Awards and the Golden Globes. She’ll also do rounds of press interviews. And on December 10, she’ll accept the Kirk Douglas Award for Excellence in Film from the Santa Barbara International Film Festival.

In other words, Blunt is in it to win it.

Best Shots: Truth is, Universal is pragmatically putting Blunt front and center for “Disclosure Day” for her remarkable turn as a foreign-language-spouting weatherwoman inhabited by aliens, as opposed to filmmaker Steven Spielberg or costar Josh O’Connor. Craft contenders will include five-time Oscar-winning composer John Williams, possibly up for his 55th and last Oscar nomination, two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, Editing, Sound, and VFX.

The well-reviewed March blockbuster has come roaring back, with filmmakers Phil Lord and Chris Miller doing most of the promo duties so far. The heart-tugging sci-fi epic produced by Amy Pascal is competing at the Golden Globes for comedy as “The Martian” did before it. The DVD released in May. “PHM” will re-release in IMAX and IMAX 70 theaters starting December 11.

Best Shots: Ryan Gosling is a Best Actor contender as scientist Ryland Grace — not a trained astronaut — who is in way over his head on a space mission to save the Earth but uses science to figure out the many problems that come his way. Gosling carries the movie but also interacts beautifully with not only his commanding mission director Sandra Hüller (who is competing with herself in Supporting Actress for “PHM” and “Fatherland”) but James Ortiz, who was on set as puppeteer and voice for another solo space traveler, a crablike alien named Rocky. He’s contending for Supporting Actor. (Whether the actors branch will accept him is a big question.)

Lord & Miller are in the mix for Best Director, and “The Martian” Oscar nominee Drew Goddard could be in the running again for Adapted Screenplay. The movie could land several craft categories as well, including VFX, Sound, Cinematography, Editing and Daniel Pemberton‘s Original Score, which supports the different tones of the movie, through action, comedy, and pathos.

Universal just released their robust screening and panel schedule for “The Odyssey,” with Christopher Nolan and his cast and key crew to be grilled by the likes of Guillermo del Toro and Robert Downey, Jr. as they step in front of Guild and Academy voters. Not coincidentally, the movie hits DVD, Blu-ray, and 4K Ultra HD on November 17.

Best Shots: “The Odyssey” is in front-runner position for Best Actor. Matt Damon has wisely leaned into the degree of difficulty required to play the peripatetic wily warrior Odysseus in harsh locations that helped Leonardo DiCaprio win for “The Revenant.” Damon is a wily and charming campaigner who is well-liked not only in Hollywood — he has worked with everyone — but around the world. (Check out his Criterion Closet Picks.) He won a Screenplay Oscar with Ben Affleck (“Good Will Hunting”) but has never won an Acting Oscar.

The ubiquitous Anne Hathaway (who won for “Les Mis”) is leading the Supporting Actress field for her performance as the patient Penelope. Constantly promoting a slew of movies this year as she became more and more pregnant did not hurt her cause. She’s competing with two-time nominee Samantha Morton, a Brit, as the witch Circe. Veteran American John Leguizamo, never nominated, leads the British “Odyssey” Supporting Actor contenders Rob Pattinson and Tom Holland.

Of this group, “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” will dominate the Oscar nominations, likely scoring from 10-15 each. “Sinners,” a period movie with original music, holds the record with 16.

#3472. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.
