#3471. CBS' 'Boston Blue' Is Breaking the 'Blue Bloods' Formula for Season 2

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for Boston Blue Season 2.Danny Reagan (Donnie Wahlberg) is experiencing a major change in Boston Blue that never took place during his entire career with the New York Police Department in Blue Bloods. Boston Blue Season 2, Episode 1, "The Crash," revealed that Danny Reagan was up for a detective sergeant promotion with the Boston Police Department. Despite Danny's hesitance to accept the role, his partner, Lena Silver (Sonequa Martin-Green), encouraged him to take it, and Danny eventually accepted the job. This marks a bold new era for Danny's character arc as his career progresses in an exciting new way.

Throughout his NYPD career, as depicted in Blue Bloods, Danny always stayed in his detective role, without moving up the ladder. Danny preferred fieldwork, and he likely felt it was the best fit for him in the shadow of his father, Francis Reagan (Tom Selleck), and his grandfather Henry Reagan (Len Cariou), who became NYPD commissioners. However, in Boston Blue, Danny finds himself in a new city, giving him a fresh start, and now he finally feels determined to advance his career.

However, Danny was initially hesitant to accept the promotion, fearing it would upset the balance of his partnership with Lena, who was gunning for the same position back in the series premiere. It demonstrates how far Lena and Danny's partnership has come because he values her career and judgment over his own. Later, in the best scene in "The Crash," Lena reveals she didn't put in for the sergeant’s promotion, realizing she's happy with her current role, and she gives Danny her blessing to accept the promotion.

Another great scene between Danny and his son Sean Reagan (Mika Amonsen) in the Season 2 premiere reveals that Danny promised Sean that he intends to advance in the BPD, just like Francis and Henry did in New York. This is a major moment for Danny as it reinforces that he plans to fulfill the Reagan family legacy in the BPD and is taking steps that he previously avoided. It's a new era and path for Danny Reagan in Boston Blue.

Season 2, Episode 3, "Fire in the Hole," shows Danny adjusting to his new role as sergeant detective in the BPD's major case unit. Danny's new role essentially makes him the lead detective and the division's boss. Early in the episode, Danny gets incredibly strict with one of the unit’s detectives, Bruce Sullivan (Tyrone Savage), for taking his shoes off and putting his feet on the desk while scrolling on his phone. Danny quickly recognizes that he might have lost his temper with Sullivan, but he doesn't want the unit to be lax with decorum and their duties while on shift.

This is a major change for Danny, who has mentored other detectives and given orders to patrol officers before, but he's never actually been "the boss." It's a refreshing angle for the character and interesting to see because the Sullivan scene portrays a bit of Danny’s old-school hotheadedness emerging in his new role. Danny generally portrays a much nicer and softer image in Boston Blue, so it was amusing to see a bit of the old Danny come out with Sullivan. Later, Sullivan steps up his game, as Danny's teachable moment definitely got through to him. The episode also includes Danny and Lena managing an incredibly difficult and intense case, where an off-duty officer shoots an undercover detective, creating a powder-keg situation for the entire BPD. Danny exhibits incredible grace under pressure and keeps a cool head throughout the emotionally charged investigation.

Boston Blue has had its share of issues, but Danny finally progressing in his law enforcement career is one of the most exciting aspects of Season 2. Blue Bloods kept Danny quite stagnant at times in his role as a detective, never moving up the ladder or chain of command. Now, Danny is genuinely motivated to progress his career, and his new role as detective sergeant gives the character a whole new energy.

Future seasons of Boston Blue could explore Danny transitioning to higher offices. He began the series as a consulting NYPD detective, eventually becoming an official BPD detective, and now he's graduated to a detective sergeant. It might be too early to say he could become a future chief of police, but why not? Sean said his dad's goal is to move up the ladder like Danny's dad and grandfather, who both became NYPD commissioners. That means becoming commissioner is Danny's ultimate goal, and it will be interesting to see if it ever comes to fruition during Boston Blue's run.

#3470. 10 John Wayne Movies Better Than Their Rotten Tomatoes Scores, Including Brannigan

John Wayne has a truly sprawling filmography for viewers to watch through, with plenty being arguably underrated in their own respective ways, and being better than their Rotten Tomatoes review scores may at first suggest. The strength of John Wayne's most well-received movies, including the likes of Stagecoach, The Shootist, and Red River, does put some of his weaker entries in a harsher light, and mean viewers are more likely to judge the latter as even worse than they truly are.

Indeed, John Wayne being known for having plenty of Western B movies to supplement the wider run of his career and provide some lighter capers of sorts naturally places any films that fall under this category into a complicated position, wherein they may appear inherently lesser based on their nature.

However, this doesn't mean these movies are devoid of value. Ultimately, even films that aren't perhaps Wayne's best deserve some credit both as individual releases and as stepping stones for John Wayne's wider career and success. For many viewers, the matter of whether some of these movies are worth watching will likely end up at the same conclusion that famous film critic Roger Ebert once did in his two-star review of Brannigan: "besides, it’s got John Wayne in it."

The Man From Utah is by no means John Wayne's best movie. However, it is a fascinating look at the early ways in which the Western genre and Wayne's career began to establish themselves, which arguably means the movie is more valuable and insightful in this alone than its lack of critic review score and 34% audience Popcornmeter score suggest.

The Man From Utah's premise has John Wayne's hero find himself engaging in a rodeo competition in order to uncover how the corrupt crew are rigging the games to ensure they win. This is effectively set up for the purpose of having half the movie be extensive scenes of rodeo stunts, which definitely is a feature viewers are likely to either love or hate.

With that said, the stunts in the movie certainly can't be overlooked, and the scale and spectacle of this leg of the journey alone are particularly notable for the 1930s, meaning The Man From Utah is far more worth a watch for those curious than its Rotten Tomatoes review scores might suggest.

Riders of Destiny's bad rap - with it having no critic score and a 31% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes - is one that seems to be earned in part by the questionable dubbing over the opening scene of John Wayne's Singin' Sandy Saunders serenading the open plains before the story begins proper, which perhaps starts the film out on a complicated foot.

While Riders of Destiny isn't ground-breaking, its narrative does seem to deserve at least better than an absent critic score. Wayne's hero manages to feel both like a hardened Western hero and a cunning protagonist capable of pulling the wool over everyone's eyes thanks to the final act of the story, wherein Saunders convinces the movie's antagonist he's going to work for him, despite this obviously not being the case.

Riders of Destiny also features a solid showing from co-protagonist, Fay Denton - who opens the story seeming to be robbing a stagecoach for her own letter, setting her up as an enjoyably independent heroine in many senses - and some characteristic action and gunslinging scenes. As such, the film isn't without its own sense of intrigue, making it once again of more value than its Rotten Tomatoes reviews may suggest.

There's a fair amount West of the Divide gets right throughout the course of its runtime, which contrasts somewhat with its Rotten Tomatoes scores, that once again consist of an absent critic score, alongside a 38% audience score.

Though West of the Divide still clearly reflects the filmmaking limitations many movies from the 1930s experience, it's not without its fair share of heart, which is balanced out alongside its action.

The story of John Wayne's hero taking on the identity of criminal Cat Ganns to try and solve who murdered his father is a genuinely interesting premise, for example, even if it doesn't shy away from clichés. Moreover, the story ends up with a roster of characters you can't help but root for, with the bond between John Wayne's Ted Hayden and Billy O'Brien's "Spuds" being genuinely endearing, and perhaps the standout star of the whole film being the genuinely adorable Peewee, who is Spuds' pint-sized horse.

The premise of Sagebrush Trail is one that's been repeated throughout time, demonstrating the lasting appeal of its story. John Wayne's John Brant begins the story fleeing from prison after being wrongly convicted of murder, with Brant joining a band of criminals after going undercover to catch the real killer.

It's a premise that only gets more interesting as Brant continues to befriend one of the team, Joseph Conlon, with the dynamic between the two carrying most of the film, and leading to some scenes that still hold up well, such as Brant and Conlon breaking the eggs the other is carrying home for their gang with comedic timing.

All in all, Sagebrush Trail is again another 30s Western movie that still has some clear flaws looking back now - with its script and pacing having some issues that are evident with a revisit - but its qualities do mean it's better than its absent critic review score and 38% audience score would denote.

Between its story of panning for gold, and its protagonists trying to protect their ranch from the villains who seek to obtain it, The Lucky Texan couldn't be more of a classic Western if it tried.

This works to the film's benefit and detriment, as its story is immersed well and truly in the genre it's so clearly entrenched within, but also contains its own fair share of clichés played straight.

That said, it is also balanced with its fair share of twists, including Grandy Benson disguising himself as an old lady in order to enter a court scene unidentified. When looking at the bigger picture of things, this means the movie does have more substance to it than its lack of critic score and 32% audience Popcornmeter score would imply, even if it isn't a film that's aged universally well.

The movie also benefits from an early feature by Yakima Canutt, who has been referred to as the King of stuntmen, whose stunt and acting talents are on prime display in the film. Though easy to miss, this also makes it worth watching for those curious to look at the growth of cinema over the decades, and those who played their roles in this process.

While Texas Cyclone doesn't have John Wayne in its central role, that doesn't detract from its story, which sees Tim McCoy's "Texas" Grant ride into a town where he discovers he's being mistaken for lawman Jim Rawlins, who was killed some time prior.

Wayne's role is a more understated one, with the actor playing Steve Pickett. Pickett ends up being one of the other law-abiding citizens in town, who aids Grant in his efforts to help out Jim's widow, Helen Rawlings, with the ranch she's been left, and to thwart the corrupt members of the town who have been sabotaging her.

John Wayne serves well as the debonair but more withdrawn secondary protagonist of sorts, and the story is one that you want to see to the end the minute Grant is first mistaken for Jim, making Texas Cyclone more interesting than its lack of critic score and 20% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes indicate on a first glance.

With a considerable cast and plenty of action befitting a classic Western, Lawless Range has immediate appeal even without looking at the movie's actual story more directly.

Though Lawless Range's horse riding and action in some ways hold up better than its plot, even said plot has its own appeal, as the tale of John Wayne's John Middleton donning a criminal disguise in order to help a town's sheriff deal with bandits isn't exactly boring material.

Lawless Range also has the benefit of its finale, which comes with a pretty dramatic extended shootout scene, even if the fight scene that comes after this isn't exactly award-winning. Altogether, Lawless Range has more spectacle and story than its 20% Popcornmeter score and lack of Tomatometer critic score might denote, even if it's also unlikely to be in the front spot for most lists of all-time best Westerns.

Island in the Sky is a particularly interesting addition to John Wayne's wider film roster, given the movie is not a Western, but rather an adventure drama centered in a very different setting to the dusty plains of cowboy movies.

Island in the Sky sees John Wayne play Captain Dooley, a pilot who finds himself and his crew crash landing in the unchartered and icy wilderness. With the extreme winter threatening the lives of Dooley and his men as they seek to survive the harsh conditions, the story is split between this story, and the story of those searching for the lost crew, making it a tense overall plot to say the least.

While Island in the Sky has higher review scores than many of Wayne's other works, it does have a lower audience score than this might suggest, with its 86% critic Tomatometer score being far higher than its 62% audience Popcornmeter score. This does seem to be at least in part because it's a departure from the usual John Wayne Western, though Island in the Sky does deserve its flowers for seeing Wayne going out of his comfort zone of sorts and trying something a bit different overall.

The Night Riders is, for all intents and purpose, a sort of modern reimagining of Robin Hood, so to speak. The film's trio of titular heroes come together to rob the tax collectors who are carrying out an illegal scheme wherein the villains of the story falsely claim they own a huge parcel of land, placing sky-high prices on buying or renting these areas across the territory.

This unfolds into a story with substantially more narrative complexity than many of John Wayne's other Western movie stories, which involves US President Garfield, a range of fights, and plenty of plot twists involving false or hidden identities.

Given The Night Riders has no audience or critic scores, it's easy to miss for those looking at John Wayne's works on Rotten Tomatoes, but it is definitely a notable part of his filmography all the same, even if some aspects of its story seem far more outdated now.

The prospect of a John Wayne caper that delves into the movie world of British crime dramas is of course a naturally exciting one.

However, the full potential of Brannigan arguably wasn't realized, as was noted both by critics when the film first released back in 1975, and still today. This is reflected by its current Rotten Tomatoes scores, which are that of a 46% critic Tomatometer score, and an even lower 39% audience Popcornmeter score.

While there are clear flaws with the awkward way the movie tries to combine Wayne's American gunslinger sensibilities and a British crime mystery, there are still evident strengths in the film all the same.

John Wayne's performance as a hardened Chicago lieutenant lands, and works well alongside co-star Judith Amanda Geeson's Detective-Sergeant Jennifer Thatcher, which plays on the contrast between them and their respective law enforcement groups. This by itself makes the film worth watching, though the exaggerated stunts and fights in the film certainly don't hurt either.

#3469. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3468. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

What does an audience need from its movie theater on election night?

A provocation? A distraction? Something… else? Across our semi-united, Letterboxd-loving nation, new microcinemas are opening up, old movies are selling out, and local programmers are giving film fans tons of exciting reasons to hit the box office.

Also breaking, I guess: the U.S. midterms. (Go vote!)

This election cycle, the future of Hollywood remains an open question, as does the strength of our democracy. With control of Congress at stake, voters are debating what they want their country to become — and, in many cases, what they’re afraid it already is — to spectacular and exhausting effect. Related Stories ‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama Billy Evans Hosts AMA on (His Own) X Account: ‘You Can See Everything’ Subject on Not Being a Cocaine Fan, Going Full Frontal, and What His Cousin’s Thing Was

Boarding yourself up in a movie palace like one of Joe Dante’s gremlins seems sort of reasonable under the circumstances. Thick walls, emergency snacks, and no checking your phone makes buying a movie ticket on November 3 an intriguing proposition in the U.S.

IndieWire spoke with 14 theater operators, programmers, filmmakers, educators, and authors across 12 states, including California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, and Wisconsin. Their answers offer a weirdly hopeful view of communities looking for comfort, perspective, and somewhere to be when the results come in.

At Las Vegas’ Beverly Theater at least, the connection is intentional: Reese Witherspoon and Matthew Broderick’s “Election” shares the day’s lineup with “The Devils” and “The History of Concrete.”

“We program The Beverly as a reflection of what’s happening outside our doors,” founding creative director and CXO Kip Kelly wrote. “Politics has become such an absurd spectacle that a dark comedy about a high school student council election might actually be one of the more sophisticated conversations you’ll have that day.”

Meanwhile, at Nashville’s Belcourt, a popcorn bag oversees the transfer of programming power. The theater’s monthly Staff Picks series typically falls on the first Tuesday, with a name drawn from a bag determining the employee who chooses the film. This time, someone picked “Under the Silver Lake”: the L.A. conspiracy thriller that’s paranoid enough to make anyone start connecting the deep-state dots.

“It’s totally a coincidence,” programming director Toby Leonard told IndieWire, laughing on the phone. “We realized what we had done after the fact.”

AFS Cinema programmer Lars Nilsen was similarly blunt about his Austin theater’s approach.

“We just programmed it as a regular week.” Nilsen resisted recruiting “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly” into any kind of election commentary, instead describing its Italian vision of the Old West as “the kind of dream America that Italians thought they understood about America itself.”

That said, tonight’s gathering still matters to Nilsen — even when the movie AFS is showing has nothing to do with the election itself. He pointed to the Texas organization’s addition of a third screen as a vote of confidence in people continuing to show up for one another through repertory culture.

“I think very intricately and carefully programmed cinemas are one of the places where community is being reborn,” Nilsen said. “Thank goodness.”

For Harlem’s Maysles Documentary Center, building community and considering who gets to tell that community’s story is the program’s point. Executive director Kazembe Balagun deliberately selected “BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions” for an evening that’s ordinarily devoted to watching the news.

He said he wanted to ask: “How do we imagine ourselves, represent our communities and think about power beyond the ballot box?” Plus, “I just think it’s a dope film.”

The “BLKNWS” screening is followed by a neighborly gathering echoing the center’s other events, from World Cup sidewalk screenings to group viewing for the Knicks playoff games. “I think that it’s not just what we put on the screen, but also the rooms that we create,” Balagun said. “The party afterwards is intentional because right now we live in a time where our communities are so fragmented.”

At Pennsylvania’s Gap Theatre, Spectral Cinema programmers Adrianna Gober and Dan Santelli are confronting power as an ambitious intellectual team. Their 35mm selection, Bresson’s “The Devil, Probably,” follows a young man overwhelmed by disillusionment with the institutions around him.

“The film speaks so much to the feelings of alienation and powerlessness that a lot of people are grappling with right now,” Gober wrote. She described the struggle to find meaning and control as “a tug of war between hope and despair.”

Santelli sharply cautioned against allowing that despair to become another reason to give up. “In the current political climate, it’s all too easy to fall into a feedback loop of despair and resignation, whereby the recognition of one’s apparent powerlessness becomes a justification for further inaction,” he wrote, adding he’s “less interested in offering audiences an opportunity for catharsis than one for reflection.”

That distinction runs through other programmers’ choices, too. Just look at “The Devils.”

At Minneapolis’ Trylon, John Moret chose Ken Russell’s film to cap the witchy “Evil Incantations” series after its restoration was announced at this spring’s national Programmers’ Jam in L.A., which he co-organized. The Warner Bros. Clockwork news sent a room full of repertory devotees into a frenzy months before “The Devils” mania got properly started — and Moret saw the opportunity to send his audience at Trylon from the voting booth straight into Russell’s religious nightmare back then.

Every screening has sold out since, Moret said. And personally, he often spends election night at the movies: “I think that there’s going to be plenty of people who are looking for distraction.”

Art can offer distance while leaving a lot to recognize on a deeper level, but even outrageously visual, avoidance and arthouse rarely mix. Moret praised the magical appeal of Russell and “The Devils” specifically, and said great film “should reverberate truth in a way that connects with you, but also allows you to be at a different time and place and truly put it into perspective.”

At Brookline’s Coolidge Corner Theatre, the 1971 film is sticking around for the same reason: The worshippers just keep coming. Now in its third week, “The Devils” shares the November 3 calendar with “Voting Counts: Elections in Film,” an adult film class that proved popular enough to require a second section. The program was conceived for election season, but “Network” also got its turn on Election Eve.

“We want this to be everybody’s movie house. We want our audiences to feel at home here,” Coolidge Corner artistic director Mark Anastasio told IndieWire. “There has to be a variety of programming appealing to the diverse appetites of the Boston area.”

In Milwaukee, author Matthew J. Prigge is about to discover what his favorite movie feels like in a theater.

His book event at the Oriental Theatre includes a screening of “Dog Day Afternoon,” which Prigge spent years researching for his nonfiction “Dog’s Day.” But somehow has never actually seen on the big screen. The election timing was mostly coincidental, though Prigge recognizes the relevance of Sidney Lumet’s film — about a man robbing a bank to fund his lover’s gender-affirming surgery — in 2026.

The actual robbery, the writer cautioned, has a more complicated history than its Hollywood adaptation. Still, Prigge said, “I think that the movie works just because it’s such a human story and it gets to the actual people that are involved and it makes it relatable, it makes it very raw.”

He also noted that for one evening watching the 1975 title wouldn’t be work for him: “That’s a big deal for me to see it as a communal experience. It’s been a while since I’ve been able to just sit back and enjoy it.”

For Hyperreal Film Club’s Blake Williams in Texas, finding an audience to join helped make a new city feel like home — but things are “definitely tense” in Austin, he said. After moving south from Indiana, Williams discovered the organization through its eclectic programming and eventually joined their team.

Now, he says his closest LGBTQ friends in the local film scene are considering leaving the state because they feel unsafe. His election-night offering to a community he wants to keep together? “Hardball.” After a month of Halloween horror, Williams wanted the kind of crying that comes with a good ol’ sports movie, and Keanu Reeves coaching a group of kids offers a true tale of common ground through weepy comfort.

“You kind of want to see a change in these things happen and you hope that it’ll happen, but at least film can kind of make people forget about these things,” he said. “I think it’s cool that we’re able to offer our comforts to the community to put them at ease, even if it’s just for a few hours.”

Relief means different things to different moviegoers, and at North Kansas City’s Screenland Armour, co-owner Adam Roberts is offering the new “Wild at Heart” restoration, alongside animation studio Laika’s first-run “Wildwood.” The former’s booking followed the remaster’s pre-planned release schedule, but Roberts nevertheless sees David Lynch’s dark vision of American life as an prime excuse for escapism.

“We are highly engaged in our local community and routinely show political films,” he wrote to IndieWire. “I think for patrons looking for a distraction on Election Night, there is no better place than the cinema.”

Charlotte’s Independent Picture House discussed special election programming before deciding its existing lineup already had the assignment covered, too. Creative director Jay Morong, also a senior lecturer at UNC Charlotte, pointed to “Wild at Heart,” “The Devils,” and specifically “Digger.”

“These are all movies that are addressing very specific things that are in the consciousness of the voter at this moment in time,” he said. “Let’s just roll with what we got because this is what independent and art house theaters do.” IPH’s monthly filmmaker meetup also happened to fall on election night, giving North Carolina’s indie community somewhere to discuss results that could affect their livelihoods.

“We are constantly battling against the state government and the incentives and them cutting back on budgets here,” Morong said, lamenting a decline in area film and TV productions. “So the film community is very actively involved in who is winning these state and federal elections and how they’re [using their voice] or cheerleading for the film industry in North Carolina.”

In Los Angeles, moviegoers can leave the voting booth for something that looks suspiciously like… another one? At WHAMMY, Julie Orlick’s One Person Cinema fits a chair, a television, and a viewer wearing headphones inside a five-by-three-by-six-foot room. The resemblance wasn’t intentional, but when someone pointed it out, an election-night opening felt fitting.

“We all just thought it’d be a good fun thing to do after a serious day of activities,” she said.

The premiere offering features her erotic short “DÉSIR,” and unlike an actual voting booth, this one has a peephole through which someone outside can watch the person watching.

“The only people who get to experience it are the people that go inside the room,” Orlick said. “And I think that also brings a secrecy to the film.” The experimental artist said she built the installation as a final project at UCLA, conceiving a private encounter with intimate images she wanted to keep off the internet. With WHAMMY and TAPE, she developed a residency featuring other filmmakers’ work, too.

An accompanying screening of “Les fantômes du hard” in WHAMMY’s larger microcinema rounds out an evening with considerably more erotic material than the average polling place — and you can find Orlick’s One Person Cinema inside the Echo Park microcinema all month.

Alternatively, over in Illinois, audiences at Chicago’s Gene Siskel Film Center can travel the globe without leaving their seats. Jia Zhangke’s “The World” — set among workers at a Beijing theme park filled with miniature global landmarks — screens as part of “Contact Zones,” a public series and lecture class taught by School of the Art Institute of Chicago professor Daniel Quiles.

“We’re given a sort of official line that we’re a polarized country or that we have arch enemies around the world,” Quiles said. “How can art give us a different way of framing these things?”

The professor’s interest in globalization’s recent past grew from questions about what retreating from it might cost. The screening film’s he’s chosen bring students, museum curators, and other moviegoers together to consider their stakes seriously: “I think by watching a film like ‘The World, ‘we might see parallels to the underclass in our own country rather than seeing China as some big bad guy.”

Finally, among respondents to IndieWire’s latest Reddit inquiry, several welcomed a few hours away from the election. Being “expressly forbidden from looking at my phone” was a selling point for one; but another, invested in a tight race, couldn’t contemplate the disconnect.

Meanwhile, others had already discharged their civic duties to make room for a different national emergency: Godzilla. “I voted early specifically so I can see Godzilla Minus Zero on Godzilla Day without having to worry about making it back to vote on time,” one kaiju fan wrote.

In Washington, D.C., another moviegoer plans to see A24’s “The Drama” at Suns Cinema.

“I didn’t realize it was election night when I bought the tickets, but I love supporting Suns any day of the year,” they wrote in an email to IndieWire. With its would-be wedding mired in finger-pointing, the popular flick from earlier this year feels well-suited to the socially charged D.C. setting — even if this moviegoer’s turnout concerns are more personal than political.

“I will hopefully be going with my crush (fingers crossed) if they respond to my texts,” they said.

#3467. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3466. 8 Classic Books That Are Still Perfect From Start to Finish

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

A lot of the books on this list were probably assigned to you at some point, which is a good reason to avoid them. School has a way of making a great story feel like homework, and I’ll admit I rolled my eyes at a couple of these before I actually sat down and read them. Then I got to the end and wished I’d done it sooner.

What they share is that none of them lose steam. Some are short, some are enormous, and a couple are more than two hundred years old, but you never reach a chapter where you start counting the pages left. Here are some of the most iconic books I’d pick up on a quiet weekend which I think everybody should read at least once.

Mary Shelley was only eighteen when she came up with the idea for Frankenstein during a rainy summer in 1816 at a villa near Lake Geneva. She was stuck inside with her future husband, Percy Shelley, and Lord Byron, and the group decided to see who could write the scariest ghost story. The weather was so bad that year, after a volcano erupted in Indonesia, that nobody could go out, which gave her plenty of time to think. She finished the novel at twenty and published it anonymously in 1818.

Victor Frankenstein, the young scientist who builds a living creature out of dead body parts, is arguably the real villain of the story, even though most people call the monster Frankenstein. The creature never gets a name, and he teaches himself to speak by secretly listening to a family through a hole in a cottage wall. Shelley tells it through letters from a sea captain in the Arctic, which makes everything feel like a confession. It’s much sadder than you’d expect, and the creature is hard not to feel sorry for.

Scott Fitzgerald first wanted to call The Great Gatsby “Trimalchio in West Egg,” which is a mouthful, and he only gave it up close to publication. Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to Long Island in the summer of 1922, tells the story of his mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, a millionaire who throws huge parties every weekend hoping that Daisy Buchanan, the woman he loves, will walk through the gates. The book is short, around 180 pages, and every sentence is carefully chosen.

It barely sold when it came out in 1925, and Fitzgerald died in 1940 thinking it had been a failure. What changed things was World War II, when roughly 150,000 copies were handed out to American soldiers overseas, and a whole new generation of readers fell for it. The green light at the end of Daisy’s dock and the giant eyes on a faded billboard are probably the most analyzed images in American fiction. It ends quietly, and it hurts.

Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, because she worried that critics wouldn’t take a woman writer seriously. Jane is an orphan who gets sent to a harsh boarding school, grows up determined to be treated as an equal, and takes a job as a governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls for the moody owner, Mr. Rochester. The school, Lowood, is based on a real place, Cowan Bridge, where two of Brontë’s older sisters caught illnesses and died.

Jane tells her own story, and she often speaks straight to the reader, which makes you feel like she’s confiding in you. Strange laughter in the night and a locked room on the third floor hint at a secret that takes a long time to come out, and when it does, the story takes a turn nobody saw coming. Jane’s refusal to give up her self-respect for love is why the book is contemporary. Jean Rhys later wrote Wide Sargasso Sea to tell the story of the woman in the attic.

Jane Austen wrote the first version of Pride and Prejudice in her early twenties under the title First Impressions, and her father tried to sell it to a London publisher in 1797, who turned it down without even reading it. Years later she rewrote it, and it came out in 1813 with “by the author of Sense and Sensibility” on the cover instead of her name. Elizabeth Bennet, the clever second daughter of a family with five girls and no son to inherit the estate, meets the proud Mr. Darcy at a dance and decides she can’t stand him.

Austen sold the rights for just £110, a small sum even then, and the publisher made a good profit from it. She called Elizabeth “as delightful a creature as ever appeared in print,” and it’s hard to disagree. Mr. Collins’s marriage proposal is one of the funniest scenes in English fiction, and the slow shift in how Elizabeth sees Darcy is what keeps you reading. Everybody jokes about it being a romance, but it’s really a sharp comedy about money, class, and first impressions.

J.R.R. Tolkien was a professor grading exam papers when he found a blank page and scribbled a single sentence about a hobbit living in a hole in the ground. He didn’t know what a hobbit was yet, but he kept going, telling the story to his kids at bedtime, and The Hobbit came out in 1937. Bilbo Baggins, a comfortable homebody, gets talked into joining thirteen dwarves and the wizard Gandalf on a trek to take back a mountain from the dragon Smaug.

Tolkien’s publisher let his ten-year-old son, Rayner Unwin, read the manuscript and give his opinion, and the boy’s short report helped get it printed. The chapter where Bilbo plays a game of riddles with Gollum in a dark cave is one of the best pieces of writing in fantasy, and Tolkien later rewrote it so the magic ring would feel more dangerous in The Lord of the Rings. He drew the maps and illustrations himself. It’s funny, warm, and quick, and it never feels like it’s trying too hard.

Gabriel García Márquez spent about eighteen months in Mexico City writing One Hundred Years of Solitude, while his wife, Mercedes, kept the family afloat and reportedly pawned their appliances to pay for the postage to send the manuscript to a publisher. The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the made-up town of Macondo, which is based on Aracataca, the Colombian village where he grew up. The first print run of 8,000 copies sold out in a week.

Strange things happen in the book as if they were completely normal. A girl floats into the sky while folding sheets, yellow butterflies follow a man everywhere he goes, and it rains for almost five years straight. García Márquez said the style came from his grandmother, who told impossible stories in a flat, matter-of-fact voice. He won the Nobel Prize in 1982, and the book has sold tens of millions of copies. It’s dizzying, funny, and sad in equal amounts.

George Orwell wrote 1984 on a remote Scottish island, Jura, while he was seriously ill with tuberculosis, and it came out in June 1949, only about seven months before he died. Winston Smith, a quiet clerk at the Ministry of Truth, spends his days rewriting old newspaper articles so they match whatever the government wants people to believe. When he starts a secret relationship with a colleague named Julia, he knows that even thinking against the Party is a crime.

Room 101, where prisoners face their worst fear, was reportedly named after a boring BBC conference room where Orwell sat through meetings during the war. The Ministry of Truth was modeled partly on the Senate House in London, where the wartime Ministry of Information worked. Words like Big Brother, doublethink, and Newspeak have become part of everyday language. It’s one of the few books where the ending leaves you cold, and you finish it feeling like you’ve seen how easily the truth can disappear.

Harper Lee published To Kill a Mockingbird in 1960, and for fifty-five years it was the only novel she let anyone read. Scout Finch, a six-year-old tomboy in Maycomb, Alabama, tells the story of the summer when her father, Atticus, a lawyer, defends a Black man named Tom Robinson, who is falsely accused of assaulting a white woman. Scout and her brother Jem spend the same summer trying to figure out their reclusive neighbor, Boo Radley.

Dill, the imaginative boy who visits every summer, is based on Lee’s childhood friend Truman Capote. Friends gave her a year’s pay one Christmas so she could quit her job as an airline clerk and write, and her editor had her rewrite the book several times. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1961. Atticus’s quiet courage in the courtroom has made him one of the most loved fathers in literature, and the book’s mix of humor, childhood, and injustice is why it keeps topping lists of the greatest American novels.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

#3465. A Studio Ghibli Veteran's New Movie Is Only 3 Months Away, And It's Beyond Gorgeous

A spiritual Studio Ghibli installment comes next year from the mind of a Hayao Miyazaki pupil. Studio Ghibli developed a clear visual and narrative style that's instantly recognizable across different genres and historical periods due to its movies' extraordinary hand-drawn animation and expressive character designs, as well as its mature themes and its willingness to let stories unfold at their own pace. Ghibli movies find beauty in seemingly insignificant moments, and their fantasy elements tend to coexist with relatable human experiences.

Studio Ghibli's reputation is largely associated with a handful of exceptionally successful productions, particularly Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, Howl's Moving Castle, and Kiki's Delivery Service. All of these movies introduced millions of viewers to the studio's unmistakable art style. Spirited Away famously became an international phenomenon and won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, and Totoro's adorable forest spirit became the studio's official mascot. However, the studio's catalog contains several exceptional films that receive considerably less attention, including the teenage drama Ocean Waves, the environmental commentary Pom Poko, and the nostalgic romance From Up on Poppy Hill.

While Hayao Miyazaki is widely known as the mind behind Studio Ghibli, the studio has served as a cradle of talented artists with their own impressive animation careers.

Cocoon – One Summer of Girlhood brings together some remarkable talent from the Japanese animation industry. Director Yukimitsu Ina is one of the creative minds behind Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken!, and SASAYURI is the animation studio founded by former Studio Ghibli animator Hitomi Tateno, whose credits include My Neighbor Totoro and Howl's Moving Castle. Adapted from Machiko Kyo's 2009 manga of the same name, Cocoon – One Summer of Girlhood follows two schoolgirls, San and Mayu, whose peaceful summer on a secluded island comes to an abrupt end when war reaches their community.

Although Cocoon – One Summer of Girlhood is set during the war, its point of view is that of two young women who find their innocence and sense of security gradually stripped away.

Yukimitsu Ina is accompanied by recruited veteran animators Akihiko Yamashita, known for his work on Spirited Away and The Boy and the Heron; as well as Shinji Otsuka, known for Kiki's Delivery Service and Princess Mononoke. The involvement of so many artists associated with Studio Ghibli makes Cocoon – One Summer of Girlhood a must-watch, with Hitomi Tateno bringing decades of experience to a project that approaches its historical subject with as much sensibility as all Studio Ghibli productions. Originally premiered in Japan on March 30, 2025, Cocoon – One Summer of Girlhood received a U.S. theatrical release through GKIDS on September 4, 2026, and its Blu-ray release is scheduled for January 19, 2027.

Numerous animation studios and filmmakers honor Studio Ghibli's hand-drawn artistry. Founded in 2015 by former Ghibli producer Yoshiaki Nishimura and populated by several former Ghibli artists, Studio Ponoc carries Ghibli's legacy in its debut feature, Mary and the Witch's Flower, which has been followed by touching animated movies such as the anthology Modest Heroes and the fantasy film The Imaginary. Other Japanese filmmakers have continued similar storytelling traditions through their own studios. Mamoru Hosoda's Wolf Children and Mirai explore the extraordinary experiences hidden within everyday life, Makoto Shinkai has found massive success with Your Name, and Studio Colorido has produced several particularly Ghibli-adjacent coming-of-age adventures, including Penguin Highway and A Whisker Away.

Looking for that trademark Studio Ghibli atmosphere in a book? These cozy, wholesome, and sometimes a little dark books feel like a warm Ghibli hug.

Other productions favor supernatural storytelling. Directed by former Ghibli artist Masashi Ando, The Deer King builds an elaborate fantasy world around a father struggling to protect an adopted child. Studio 4°C has also delivered visually ambitious alternatives in Children of the Sea and Fortune Favors Lady Nikuko, the former exploring humanity's relationship with the ocean and the latter finding warmth in an unconventional mother-daughter relationship. Outside Japan, Ireland's Cartoon Saloon has established one of the strongest independent counterparts to Ghibli, with folklore-inspired productions like The Secret of Kells, Song of the Sea, and Wolfwalkers, alongside the more grounded historical drama The Breadwinner and the fantasy adventure My Father's Dragon.

#3464. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3463. Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Clipfarming, influencer screenings, and meme-bait popcorn buckets: promoting a movie in the internet age is often a full-court offensive to get noticed. In that spirit, why not just get down to business and resort to modern civilization’s oldest method for seeking attention: dangling some money in people’s faces?

That’s what the marketing teams behind “How to Rob a Bank,” from Amazon MGM Studios, and “Ebenezer,” from Skydance’s Paramount Pictures, have tried in the weeks leading up to their shared November 13 release to North American theaters.

For the former ensemble heist thriller, a branded ATM was moved between multiplexes throughout the Los Angeles area over the course of four days. Those who learned of the campaign on the film‘s social media channels could gain clues about the machine’s location and a specified PIN number, which would spark payouts of a single one-hundred-dollar bill to those who bothered to seek out (or stumble upon) it. Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

“Ebenezer” took a more cheeky, trifling approach, promoting an official Venmo account for Johnny Depp’s Christmas crab apple that users could request funds from. Those who scrolled through the account’s transactions would see it shares the character’s penny-pinching spirit: the only completed transactions were those giving away one single cent. The Venmo account was only active for a few hours, though a Paramount Instagram post from last week teases followers to “check back” as “Ebenezer might be feeling generous on @venmo again.”

Several film news aggregation accounts like Culture Crave and DiscussingFilm reported that the account “crashed” due an overwhelming amount of requests, though Paramount declined to comment on if such a description was accurate. Venmo did not respond to a request asking if the company partnered with the studio on the sponsorship.

Much like that line, there is also a tackiness du jour to both money-mindset stunts, especially in a world where awards shows, professional sports and geopolitical events can hardly be watched without outlets asking you to bet — erh, predict — on them. A video posted to Paramount’s socials opens with a Venmo request for $500, asking Scrooge to help pay off a user’s student loans.

Not to mention the real inadvertent quirk: the account has been able to receive payments from users. Considering the scant number of one-cent payouts from the account and the number of influxes, it is almost certain that Paramount could have made money on the stunt, though an individual with knowledge of the account shared that all received funds were sent back to users via private transactions.

Krystyna Ursta, a 27-year-old actress, video editor, and Depp fan in Los Angeles, shared that she gave about $30 to the account and received a full refund a few days later — plus an extra penny and an invitation to a special screening of the film in New York on Monday. She will be attending a local press screening instead. Ursta also posted a video of herself reacting to the account, one of many fan responses that flooded in on social media.

“I kind of figured that they will probably return it,” Ursta wrote over text after being reached through her Instagram handle, which she included in her Venmo transactions. “I’m such a big fan. I was happy to support the film.”

The rather gimmick-less gimmick of waving around money also helps capture the attention of people that aren’t necessarily interested in seeing the movie, but are going through the average modern experience of thinking about one’s financial situation. Aggregation accounts were quick to post graphics reporting on both stunts, with captions like “HOW TO ROB A BANK ATM’S ARE BEING SET UP AROUND LOS ANGELES AND GIVING PEOPLE FREE MONEY AND IT COULDN’T HAPPEN AT A BETTER TIME” and “EBENEZER SCROOGE WILL SEND YOU REAL MONEY ON VENMO BUT THERE’S A CATCH SWIPE FOR MORE.”

There’s also people like Scott, a 35-year-old based out of Atlanta that couldn’t help but engage with the “Ebenezer” Venmo account after seeing it on X. He sent a penny, then received one in return. (A disclaimer: six Venmo users were reached for interview about their Ebenezer experience by sending them $0.01 with this reporter’s contact information in the caption; Scott was the only response that timed out before publication.)

“Seeing Ebenezer is now on Venmo was too funny and stupid to not engage with,” he wrote over text. “There’s something very boring dystopia about it: the idea of a fictional character from a 200-year-old Christmas story being commercialized on Venmo just shows how dumb Hollywood can. … It’s like McDonald’s Monopoly: take our slop and we might give your money.”

Also helpful for the studios is how little dangling the potential of money actually costs. Sans staffing fees, producing the “Ebenezer” Venmo account and its activity used a sum less than the coins between the couch cushions on the Paramount lot. Per the “How to Rob a Bank” promo’s website, each location’s prize pool gave away ten one-hundred-dollar bills and twenty twenty-dollar-bills ($1,400 total), plus some theater-supplied prizes like gift cards. An employee at the Regal Sherman Oaks that worked on the day of the on-site promotion said the ATM seemed to deal out the rewards in a random order, as opposed to $100 dollar bills for the first finders. Amazon MGM declined to comment, while Stellar Agency Inc., which sponsored and administered the promotion, did not respond to a request.

Both had much smaller overheads than a “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” promotion than ran in April 2025. To launch the magician threequel’s first trailer, Lionsgate reportedly gave away roughly $250,000 to those that texted a mysterious phone number displaying in Times Square in the hours up to the drop. Like “Ebenezer” and “How to Rob a Bank,” it was a promotion that sparked a viral moment with plenty of user-generated content, each sharing the widely desired fantasy of receiving free money.

Neon handed out basic resources for an “I Love Boosters” promotion in May, where stars KeKe Palmer and LaKeith Stanfield took over a Shell gas station in West Pico to give out complimentary refills to the first 70 cars that arrived. The stunt played on then-peaking fuel prices, which had skyrocketed in the wake of the U.S.’ initial bombing of Iran in February and the subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In the months since, President Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retains control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump announced the idea, his approval rating was at a dismal 35 percent, per a CNN aggregate of various polls. Though the offer is unprecedented and dubious on its face, it has been covered extensively — and it cost nothing to float it.

#3462. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.
