#3461. 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound

In 2024, archivist Michael Chaiken was approached by the Criterion Collection about what was being described as a “big Kubrick project.” It would start with remastering the director’s last film, “Eyes Wide Shut,” but for months the scope of the ambitious project remained an open question: Was a complete Stanley Kubrick box set even possible?

Kubrick was a precise director, and his control over every aspect of his filmmaking process extended to its home video presentation. But home video technology has developed in ways (widescreen TVs, high dynamic range, 4K resolution, Dolby Atmos) that Kubrick could never have imagined before he died in 1999. As a result — from the image to sound to design of the box itself — there was the underlying question driving Chaiken and the team’s work: “What would Stanley do?” Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night?

“I had to research the history of Stanley Kubrick on home video, and that’s a very specific thing,” said Chaiken. “It’s almost like for a biographer that would be [an important] footnote.”

In an interview with IndieWire, Chaiken broke down the challenges and key work behind “The Complete Kubrick,” which hit stores and mailboxes last week.

Home video fanatics are often completists. And if you are going to invest the time in a $599.95 box set (on sale for 30 percent off at most retailers), the motivation to make it comprehensive and definitive is obvious, but with a career spanning five decades, that isn’t always possible.

“You have to kick around the idea, ‘What does ‘complete’ mean? And how would we make that so?,” said Chaiken.

The heart of Kubrick’s feature film career has been well preserved. His final five films were made with Warner Bros., and the studio’s archive team has kept the original elements well preserved. Meanwhile, Criterion, back in its laser disc era, in the 1980s and ’90s, had a good working relationship with Kubrick himself (more about that later) and was already familiar with what was available (and already in-house) when it came to having to remaster his key films into the HDR/4K standards of today.

“It’s the early stuff that was tricky because he wasn’t working for a studio; he was an independent,” said Chaiken. “[A complete box set] almost didn’t happen; it was really at the 11th hour that it came together.”

In the case of “The Seafarers,” a 1953 30-minute documentary Kubrick was commissioned to make for the Seafarers International Union, the issue became untangling the project’s rights. “We thought we knew [who owned the rights], and then somebody said, ‘Hey, by the way, I’m actually the rights holder of that,’” Chaiken chuckled, retelling the story and imagining Kubrick himself groaning at the idea that Criterion had dug it up and restored it. “ I laugh because it’s a work for hire, but at the same time, it’s a very beautiful film, and it’s his first color film, and there’s elements in it that are so Kubrickian.”

The final missing piece was the original 12-minute version of the 1951 documentary “Day of the Fight,” which Kubrick shot and edited independently for Look magazine in 1949.

“There’s a version that [Kubrick] financed and made himself, and then there’s the version that exists,” said Chaiken. “He sold the film to RKO Pictures, and they re-edited the film; they added footage that he didn’t shoot, and they changed the narration and the soundtrack that Kubrick had commissioned Gerald Fried to make.”

Kubrick’s original version had never been presented in 4K, and locating the original elements was the final piece, in Chaiken’s mind, to the set being “complete.”

“Why do you need two cuts of Day of the Fight?” Chaiken rhetorically asked before answering the question: “They are different, and to reinforce that completeness, especially with [this being] Stanley’s very first film.  His cut is actually [four minutes] shorter than the one that RKO made [and] the very first film edited and produced and directed by him.”

Chaiken’s need to present both versions of a film also applied to “The Shining,” which, after it was released domestically in May 1980 — where it bombed with critics — Kubrick spent three months re-editing, making it 25 minutes shorter, for the international release in September 1980.

What’s fascinating is that both versions have been widely available for decades; they just didn’t cross the ocean. The shorter international version is Kubrick’s final cut, and what he considered his director’s cut, never made its way to the U.S.

“[Kubrick] never pulled the U.S. theatrical version, so that version is what has existed here on video. And if you’re doing complete Kubrick, the final edit of ‘The Shining’ has to be on there. It  just has to be,” said Chaiken, noting the significant differences. “The international version is a different experience. The tone of it does shift. It does leave open the possibility that none of this is happening, and it’s all happening in Jack’s head. You really don’t understand [Jack’s] relationship with Danny in the same way in the international version.”

As IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill fully explored, the significant differences between the versions are disorienting for those who grew up loving the longer U.S. version. Chaiken anticipated what “a headscratcher” the international version would be, which is why he commissioned a new commentary track. In the new box set, the U.S. version preserves steadicam operator and founder Garrett Brown’s original Criterion commentary track, but the international version features a newly recorded track by the great Pixar animation director Lee Unkrich, who co-authored a decades-in-the-making, 1,396-page, two-volume “Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining” book, which drew from rare documents, script notes, and storyboards in the Kubrick Archive, and is based on extensive interviews with the surviving cast and crew, to tell the definitive story of the legendary and misunderstood production.

“I imagine American audiences, who love the movie, saying, ‘Why would I want to watch a shorter version of ‘The Shining’? But I think having Lee Unkrich there walking you through it and talking about some of these decisions, and talking about the production of the movie, makes it a rewarding experience,” said Chaiken. “If you’re a skeptic, it’s at least worth watching once with Lee’s commentary because it is like a master-class in ‘The Shining.’”

Twenty years after Francis Ford Coppola and Walter Murch’s groundbreaking “Apocalypse Now” sound design and roadshow ushered in surround sound, and George Lucas used the box office power of his “Star Wars” franchise to leverage theaters into adapting the new technology he was pioneering at Skywalker, Kubrick was still avoiding even doing stereo mixes of his final films.

“He stuck with mono until the end,” said Chaiken. “He was obsessed with presentation, and he truly felt, ‘I would rather have good mono than bad stereo,’ and he didn’t trust that these theaters were set up in such a way that the stereo mix.”

For the box set, Criterion does offer 5.1 mixes of Kubrick’s films, but the default audio is Kubrick’s preferred mono mix. Chaiken and Criterion audio supervisor Ryan Hullings felt it important to go back to original mono mixes, which hadn’t been touched for home video in 30 years, to do new masters for the box set. In most cases, locating the original mono mix assets was not a problem, but there were exceptions, most notably “Full Metal Jacket.”

While Warner Archives had preserved all the original assets, identifying which was the final mono mix proved difficult, explained Chaiken, “ ‘Full Metal Jacket’ was a tricky one because they were trying to convince Stanley to do it in stereo. So there was the beginning of a stereo mix.” In going through what Hullings thought were the final mono mixes, they didn’t conform with the 35mm print he was using as a comparison. As they did throughout the process of making the box set, the Criterion team turned to Kubrick’s surviving collaborators, in this case “Full Metal Jacket” editor Martin Hunter and Nigel Galt, who would go on to edit “Eyes Wide Shut,” but had done Foley and sound work on “Full Metal Jacket.”

According to Chaiken, it was Galt who helped them solve the puzzle, telling Hullings, “You’ll know you have the right mono mix of ‘Full Metal Jacket’ because during the end credits, in the original mono theatrical mix, we screwed up.” The final song over credits is The Rolling Stones’ “Paint It Black,” but according to Galt, ‘When it went out originally theatrically, we had it at 25 frames per second, so it’s actually sped up. So if you have the mix that has ‘Paint It Black’ at 25 frames per second, that’s it.’”

And yes, on the new Criterion, the “Full Metal Jacket” mono mix preserved “Paint It Black” playing approximately four percent faster than The Rolling Stones recorded it.

“Stanley passed away in 1999, and that was the beginning of when the DVD revolution was starting to happen,” said Chaiken. “So, the idea of Blu-ray and then 4K, you’re in a realm that Kubrick could never have imagined.”

Chaiken confronted this head-on, starting the project with “Eyes Wide Shut”—which he described as one of Kubrick’s hardest films to bridge the gap between the filmmaker’s original intention and the latest in modern home video technology. In working with “Eyes Wide Shut” cinematographer Larry Smith, Chaiken came to understand how much of a “dreamy quality” is a product of the unique way Smith and Kubrick exposed and developed the celluloid.

“It’s never going to be a one-to-one correlation between film and video; you can get close, but video is getting sharper and sharper and sharper,” said Chaiken. “I saw it with ‘Eyes Wide Shut,’ that you could go very hardcore into the 4K, and you could see details in the shadows and things that Kubrick would never have wanted you to see.”

Chaiken and Criterion worked closely with the Warner Archives, Smith, and other collaborators, going back and forth with different passes to figure out how best to find a happy medium, which, with most films, meant sometimes dialing down the HDR and leaning into “more filmic, warmer curve” with the color grade.

The more Chaiken researched, the more he learned just how obsessive Kubrick was about the presentation of his films, and admitted he would get obsessive wondering if they had gotten the colors of a particular transfer right. He sought out advice from Maria Palazzola, long-time restoration supervisor, colorist, and former transfer expert at The Criterion Collection during 1980s and ‘90s, having overseen “director approved” versions of Kubrick’s Criterion laser discs.

“I had assumed that there was an intermediary, or Leon Vitali, Stanley’s longtime assistant, helping Maria,” said Chaiken.”But when I talked to her, she said, ‘No, no, Stanley was calling me directly.’”

Chaiken said he flooded Palazzola with questions trying to find out just how obsessive Kubrick was about his home video transfers and what, in particular, he obsessed about. Chaiken had heard the stories that Kubrick had made Palazzola re-transfer films countless times.

Chaiken explained his assumptions were wrong, “She said that was absolutely not the case. That  [Kubrick] understood the limitations of the technology at that time, and he wanted them to look as good as they could possibly look on home video.”

For example, according Palazzola told Chaiken with “2001: A Space Odyssey,” Kubrick only pressed hard on two key sections.

“He wanted to be sure that the Dawn of Man sequence — that was front projected: The backgrounds were projected when they were filming it — and so he wanted to make sure that you couldn’t see any reflection in the eyes of the apes from that front projection,” said Chaiken. “And she said the one reel that he made her re-transfer a few times was the last reel, in the French boudoir, because [Kubrick] didn’t want it to be too bright.”

Chaiken said the anecdotes of Kubrick’s collaboration with Palazzola changed his perspective on his own work: “Hearing that he was relatively easy to work with was a bit of a relief because he cared about this stuff immensely, but he understood that film is not video. It’s a completely different medium.”

Chaiken gives full credit to visual artist Drusilla Adeline (aka Sister Hyde) for the design of the Kubrick box set, and in this video, you can hear them discuss how the fonts, color, layout, and the box itself were built around the theme of “Kubrick at work,” and how, in going through his archive, you get a sense of him leaving his fingerprints (literally and figuratively) on the making of his films.

One of the things that is striking about the box set, loaded with 16 different films, extras, and supporting materials, is how — compared to most box sets — it is laid out in a way that it is very easy to find what you are looking for, but also clear explanations for each film (each separated by a tab and film poster) of what versions, audio, and extras are available. Chaiken said that in going through Kubrick’s work, it was clear what an organized and clear archivist the filmmaker was himself.

“In my mind, I was thinking about the Library of America —  what would a Library of America compendium of Stanley Kubrick look like? That  was definitely a touchstone,” said Chaiken. “Library of America editions, where they’ll [be] a single compendium of a great American author and you have the major works, but then you also have these interesting tangential pieces, and they’re laid out so beautifully, they’re just so uniform. They have the little tab that marks a page.”

#3460. Bestselling Fantasy Author Returns With Dark, Action-Packed Romantasy That Will Cure Your ACOTAR 6 Hangover

For romantasy readers who devoured A Court of Splintered Harmony the moment it released, the wait for ACOTAR book 7 feels far too long. Thankfully, the next few months are treating us to an impressive number of romantasy sequels and first books in brand-new series alike. That includes some promising new debuts alongside exciting new books from more established names like Danielle L. Jensen.

Known for balancing slow-burn romance and high-stakes political machinations, Jensen is the bestselling author of the Bridge Kingdom series and, more recently, the New York Times bestseller A Fate Inked in Blood. Now, a little over a year after the epic conclusion to the Saga of the Unfated duology, Jensen is back with the first book in her next high-stakes fantasy series. Defy the Dusk, which released on November 3rd, kicks off the new Sundering Duet series. Steeped in harsh, post-apocalyptic vibes and magic, it sounds like the perfect new romantasy read for fans of Fourth Wing and ACOTAR.

Available in a limited-edition sprayed-edge, foiled-stamp hardcover for its first print run, Defy the Dusk is practically begging for a spot on romantasy readers' bookshelves. Its stunning cover artwork shows off the kind of dark, gritty vibes that the book's synopsis promises. For those who prefer to read digitally, Defy the Dusk is also available as an eBook or audiobook, with dual narration from Jay Myers and Emily Shaffer.

Defy the Dusk centers on Lirien, a woman whose magic once fractured the world and opened it up to the creatures of darkness. The most powerful of the survivors escaped aboard Dawnrider, while the rest remained to deal with a world plagued by dangerous and deadly monsters. Aboard the Dawnrider, Lirien has spent 20 years honing her magic and plotting to overthrow the ship's tyrant king. But her plans are thwarted when an unexpected foe kidnaps her and forces her to join his fight against the very darkness Lirien herself unleashed. Soon, her loyalties and her very purpose are brought into question... as are her feelings for her captor.

Described by publisher Del Rey as a, "gritty post-apocalyptic fantasy," this story is packed with magic and danger thanks to Lirien's powers and the creatures of night she unwittingly let loose. From the sound of it, Defy the Dusk will also deliver on the kind of intense, slow-burn enemies-to-lovers vibes her readers have come to expect. Readers will be treated to scheming, seduction, and moral questions as Lirien debates her place in the war against the night.

Defy the Dusk is just the beginning of the two-part Sundering Duet series. But there's plenty for readers to sink their teeth into, as book one clocks in at just under 700 pages. We don't yet have an official title or release window for the second book, but if this new series is anything like Jensen's prior works, readers will be ready and waiting to see what happens next. And unlike long-running series with multiple books still to come, a duology comes with the promise that we'll be able to see the story's epic conclusion when the next book arrives.

#3459. 'Jimmy' Gets To the Heart of James Stewart, but Fails To Explore His Depths | Review

In Frank Capra’s classic It’s a Wonderful Life, a defeated George Bailey sits alone at the local Bedford Falls bar and prays for God to show him the way. It’s one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the 1946 classic, made all the more powerful by James Stewart’s trembling voice and anguished expression. But for a scene hailed as one of the best in movie history, what if some of George’s pain actually came from Stewart himself? That’s the heart of Jimmy, director Aaron Burns’ new biographical drama starring KJ Apa as the beloved actor. Following Stewart’s experiences during World War II and his difficult return to acting, Jimmy offers a moving portrait of the man behind the iconic character, even if it doesn’t always dig deep enough into who Stewart really was.

Written by Justin Strawhand, Jimmy explores the period between the height of Stewart’s Hollywood success and his decision to join the military, where he eventually works his way up the ranks to become a decorated combat pilot. While there’s a great deal of sincerity in Apa’s portrayal, particularly through Stewart’s compassion and patriotism, Jimmy rarely explores the experiences that shaped him. The result is an affectionate, occasionally moving biopic that feels more like a polished dramatization of familiar history than an intimate portrait of an extraordinary man.

Fresh off his Oscar win for The Philadelphia Story in 1941, Jimmy finds the 32-year-old Jimmy Stewart (Apa) evolving into one of Hollywood’s most prominent rising stars under the MGM banner. With Louis B. Mayer (Jason Alexander) guiding him through a career so many actors envied, Jimmy shortly after admits he has other plans. With the influence of his father, Alexander (Neal McDonough), and a rich family history of military service behind him, Jimmy wants to enlist despite doubts about whether an actor could handle the realities of war. It’s a compelling starting point for a film about a man willing to leave behind everything he has worked so hard for, even if Jimmy only briefly explores these primary relationships and experiences that shaped his determination.

Under Lieutenant Colonel Terrill (Rob Riggle)’s command, Jimmy eventually earns the responsibility of leading his own squadron, while quickly needing to prove he can bring his men home safely and isn’t just some Hollywood leading man. The film also introduces Lady Julia (Kara Killmer), a British aristocrat who helps him escape from the realities of war. As we see them interact, their growing affection brings out a boyish, vulnerable side of Jimmy as we learn he longs for ordinary conversations and companionship. Yet those moments of joy outside the war become increasingly difficult to keep as the losses mount around him, particularly after he forms meaningful bonds with his men.

Burns, whose prior work has been in faith-based independent films, handles this progression with sensitivity, allowing the consequences of war to build rather than rush from one tragedy to another. Through this, we see Jimmy’s own devastation slowly grow between having to write condolence letters to grieving families and his struggle to reassure others while privately questioning his own confidence. There’s also a sincere appreciation for Stewart’s patriotism and faith that never feels overtly preachy and becomes the emotional foundation of a story about a man whose experiences would eventually reshape who he is and the profession he once loved.

It should be known that an excellent portrayal of a beloved actor doesn’t automatically make it an excellent biopic, but Apa no doubt gives Jimmy its strongest reason to exist. For as long as I can remember, Stewart has been one of Hollywood’s most recognizable, but also frequently imitated actors, often exaggerated to the point of caricature. Somewhere along the way, between Dana Carvey’s impressions on SNL and a massively popular indie podcast from the 2010s lampooning him as a relationship advice guru, those mockeries have almost made it too easy to forget the sincerity that made Stewart so beloved in the first place.

Thankfully, Apa understands that distinction. He nails Stewart’s unmistakable voice, right down to its familiar cadence and hesitant delivery, without ever letting it become a parody. The former Riverdale star also captures the smaller shifts in his expressions, gentle manner, and the quiet vulnerability beneath his Hollywood persona. Sure, there’s an uncanny resemblance from certain angles, but more importantly, Apa makes Stewart feel like a real person again, rather than the impression of one.

That humanity becomes even more effective as the wartime experiences begin to change Jimmy. In one particularly affecting moment, he reassures his squadron about their plans, only for the camera to linger on his face afterward, revealing a quiet anguish beneath his encouraging words. Apa also shares some rather tender moments with Killmer, who brings a gentle counterbalance as Julia, the fictionalized romantic interest whose presence brings out his desires for an ordinary life.

Elsewhere, Max Casella brings warmth to director Frank Capra, who was a longtime friend and collaborator with Stewart, having worked together on 1938’s You Can’t Take It With You, and 1939’s Mr. Smith Goes to Washington before It’s a Wonderful Life. Alexander lends Louis B. Mayer an appropriately imposing presence, while Riggle is convincing as Terrill, but his role is largely functional and doesn’t give us much to go by. But this is unquestionably Apa’s film, as he carries much of the screenplay’s emotional weight even when the writing never quite gets to his level.

For all its sincerity and heart, Jimmy is more interested in what Stewart endured rather than exploring the man he was before these experiences changed him. And that’s a big difference when telling the story of one of America’s greatest actors and war heroes. Burns wisely avoids squeezing an entire lifetime into one film, but the screenplay still overlooks relationships that could have given its central character more depth. For starters, the dynamic between his father and his connection to his Pennsylvania hometown is under-explored — yet, in reality, the love was so mutual that there’s a museum and statue dedicated to him in its historic downtown.

Even Ginger Rogers (Jemma Donovan) is introduced without much development, despite the two having briefly dated. More frustrating is the attention given to Julia, a fictional composite of Stewart’s romantic relationships. While their scenes reveal his vulnerability and bring out another layer of Apa’s performance in the middle of war, she remains thinly written. It’s not that the film needed to include every important person in Stewart’s life, but the relationships it chooses to explore don’t always tell us enough about the man himself.

It’s only when Jimmy turns his attention to Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life that the biopic finds something genuinely moving. After serving for four-and-a-half years, Jimmy’s wartime trauma gives weight to George Bailey’s despair, particularly while filming the famous bar scene at Martini’s. It’s here that we see Apa beautifully convey the pain of a man struggling to find his way back to himself. The film earns that emotional and heartfelt payoff, even if a vision of Stewart’s fallen comrades beforehand feels unnecessarily heavy-handed. Unfortunately, his introduction to Gloria (Jen Lilley), the woman he eventually falls in love with and marries, arrives almost like a bright resolution, never exploring how he rebuilt his life after the war and PTSD.

The film ends on archival footage of the real Stewart, surrounded by family and reflecting on his extraordinary life in his own words, which is undeniably touching. As a longtime fan, it’s this part that made me sob like a baby. But it also highlights how much of the man remains unexplored. Jimmy understands the compassion and decency that made Stewart so beloved, and its depiction of wartime sacrifice carries genuine emotional weight. But seeing what the war took from him isn’t quite the same as understanding everything that made him who he was. Apa gives us a wonderfully human portrait of an American icon, but the film and its writing stop short of becoming the richer biopic that Stewart deserves.

Jimmy opens nationwide in theaters on November 6.

#3458. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3457. The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App

You shouldn’t ever take a photo of your midterm election ballot — it’s illegal in some states — but, thanks to Rian Johnson and his longtime DP Steve Yedlin, there is now a very cinematic way to take iPhone photos of everything else.

Yedlin has spent more than 20 years as a cinematographer, collaborating closely with Johnson on everything from “Brick” and “The Brothers Bloom” to “The Last Jedi” and the “Knives Out” films. But Yedlin has also spent 20 years delving into the science of color and how filmmakers can better craft imagery through the technical tools available. And now he and his friends are in the business of making new ones. Related Stories 5 Big Challenges in Creating Criterion’s ‘The Complete Kubrick’: From Navigating HDR/4K to Preserving Stanley Kubrick’s Love of Mono Sound Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

Yedlin, Johnson, and color science coder Eric Cameron have been in the process of creating new software for light controls to replace traditional dimmer boards, pixel mapping, and on-screen playback (ie., when actors are looking at phone or computer screens on camera) with something that embraces the world of color-tunable lights and LEDs. But as a side project, they’ve also just launched Chromagraph, an iPhone app that uses Yedlin’s deep, mathematical understanding of color to bypass the iPhone’s default photo processing settings for a more filmic look.

The app project started because Johnson wanted something on his phone that could capture photos the way that Yedlin captures film — using RAW images (ie., everything the sensor captures, not just what’s rendered on a screen) and bypassing the standard iPhone image processing protocols.

Surprisingly, it only took ten weeks to build, test, and refine the app Johnson wanted to a place the team was happy with it — although Yedlin admittedly told IndieWire the process to create Chromagraph was still pretty intense. The cinematographer had done the math to build an image processing look that works for cinema cameras like the Arri ALEXA, but even the newer, pro-level iPhone cameras have sensors so small they’re smol, and they also spread image information out in a different way from how film cameras work.

“ The code values themselves, like the actual numbers in the pixels, alone don’t tell you how bright something’s supposed to be. It’s the code values in the pixels plus this [metadata] evaluation,” Yedlin said of iPhone cameras, before worrying he was being way too technical for a 900-word article. “It’s not like we’re putting different parameters into existing processing math. It’s totally different math for the most part.”

To make a complicated story shorter, then, Yedlin and Cameron couldn’t reprogram the iPhone camera, but they could get it to behave differently in order to bring RAW images (everything the camera sensor captures) into Chromagraph and then do a bunch of different and complicated math to achieve the image processing for the cinematic look that Rian Johnson wanted to be able to pull up at the swipe of a screen.

The main thing that was important to the team to get right and reflect real color science, as opposed to “bullshit cinema color science,” according to Yedlin, was to work from the truth that images that look aesthetically pleasing are not clinical or technical reproductions. They are not photometrically or colorimetrically “correct.”

“What makes a good image is something that looks enough like what it’s representing to be recognizable and then to be beautiful,” Yedlin said. “Even when you have a very clinical-looking, like a broadcast look as opposed to a cinema look, it’s also not photometrically or colorimetrically correct. They’re just not correct in a different way, you know? It’s always a matter of taste.”

A lot of the very complicated math that went into how Chromagraph does image processing is based on Yedlin and Johnson’s taste for how to make an image look artful, but then the app has contrast and saturation tools for individual photographers to take the look of their work even further. The tools inside of Chromagraph are, in fact, meant to be exactly like the math of white balance in ISO on a film camera.

“It sort of gets repeated as giving photos the ‘Knives Out’ look, and that’s fine if people want to say that, but I don’t think of it that way. I think of it as generally artful rendering. Every single movie made with traditional film stocks was made with one of like three negatives and one of two print stocks, and they all have completely different looks based on the craftsmanship and the photography and what’s being photographed and lighting and everything,” Yedlin said. “This is just the image processing, so it’s one look for that part, but the image processing part isn’t the only thing that makes a photo.”

Where Chromagraph can really help photographers make their own photos, though, is in capturing color in a way that the iPhone default method can’t quite reach. “Vibrant colors is a place where I think Chromagraph really shows off. A lot of times, with garish colors, you can have that saturation clamped look where one of the three channels is slammed so the entire area kinda looks like it’s been just colored in like a coloring book,” Yedlin said. “So some people are posting photos [from the app] where the colors really stand out, but then somebody else is posting photos with the most subtle, nuanced colors. It’s only one look, but it’s for that last little bit of finesse for whatever kind of photo you take.”

For that reason, Yedlin, Johnson, and Cameron don’t necessarily want to support multiple looks inside of Chromagraph. They’re also not planning on building an Android version anytime soon, and while they’d like to support video, that’s still a long way from being worked out. But for photographers with an iPhone in their pocket, the app is a fun, easy shortcut past importing photos into professional post tools.

“It’s satisfying that every snapshot looks the way that we like it,” Yedlin said.

Chromagraph is now available in the Apple App Store.

#3456. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3455. The MCU's X-Men Is Immediately Correcting Fox's Biggest Missed Opportunity

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is taking advantage of Fox's missed opportunity with X-Men from the very beginning. While Marvel Studios has brought mutants into the MCU over the years through many means, it won't be until 2028 that the franchise introduces its first proper X-Men team.

After making Jean Grey (Sadie Sink) the villain of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she'll return as a central figure in the new film. Amid speculation about Sink's role, questions swirled about what other mutants would join her. Answers continue to come as Marvel Studios fills out X-Men's cast with actors playing known heroes and villains from this corner of the universe.

The assembled talent for the MCU's X-Men have brought plenty of insights into Marvel's approach, especially regarding how it compares to Fox's handling of the IP for decades. The MCU's X-Men skews younger than the originals, but older than Fox's prequels. Adam Driver's Mister Sinister will be the villain, rather than Magneto. The X-Men team he'll fight is notable, too.

While Fox delivered multiple iterations of X-Men teams throughout its various timelines, they missed out on uniting the original comic team. That mistake in the eyes of Marvel Comics readers is immediately being fixed for the MCU, as that's the team X-Men is starting with based on how casting has shaped up.

The X-Men were introduced in 1963's The X-Men #1 by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby with a roster constructed of Angel, Beast, Cyclops, Iceman, and Jean Grey, with Professor X teaching them. While the team has grown and changed in many ways throughout the years since then, those characters are the core of X-Men storytelling.

Marvel Studios is ensuring that is the same for the MCU by having all of them appear from the very first X-Men movie, as all of these characters have been cast. Jean was cast first for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, while Professor X (Christopher Abbott) and Cyclops (Kit Connor) were announced at D23 2026.

Since then, trade reports have come announcing the casting of Angel (Asa Germann) and Iceman (Ben Wang). There is also a report that Game of Thrones' Peter Claffey will play Beast, but that has yet to be confirmed. But given previous rumors that Charles Melton was in consideration for that role, all signs point to Beast being in the movie.

This makes the six founding X-Men members part of the team from its inception in the MCU. Jean, Cyclops, Angel, Beast, and Iceman should all be active team members, while Professor X remains their teacher. There may be more mutants on the team or teaching the students, but this will be the first time these six X-Men will be together in a movie.

Fox's X-Men movie franchise repeatedly missed the chance to bring the founding mutants together. Beast and Angel were missing from the first team in X-Men and X2. All but Professor X and Beast were absent from X-Men: First Class' initial roster, and that carried over into X-Men: Days of Future Past. The new-look team introduced in X-Men: Apocalypse brought Cyclops and Jean into the mix, and Angel eventually, but Iceman remained missing.

The closest Fox ever came to assembling X-Men's founding members was in X-Men: The Last Stand. The trilogy ender included all six characters in some capacity, but they did not all interact. Jean killed Cyclops early on and Professor X later before abandoning the X-Men to join Magneto's Brotherhood of Mutants. Angel and Beast joined Iceman as official X-Men members, but the rest of the team was different: Wolverine, Storm, Kitty Pryde, and Colossus.

It's a stunning oversight for Fox (one that likely left Kevin Feige scratching his head as he worked on those films early in his career). The franchise had seven core X-Men movies to bring these six characters together but failed to do so at every turn. Now, that missed opportunity has become the linchpin to the MCU's take.

Starting the X-Men franchise with the original team is the latest example of the MCU going back to fundamental comic elements when redoing previously adapted characters and stories. For instance, Tom Holland's Spider-Man spent an entire trilogy in high school, rather than speeding him to adulthood. Something similar is happening with the X-Men, as Marvel has clearly made the founding members a priority for the MCU.

This immediately sets the reboot apart from past adaptations and brings it closer to the comics fans know and love. X-Men may target younger audiences, but it will have the nostalgic lineup that lifelong comic readers know. It will feel incredibly familiar and new at the same time.

However, the MCU isn't just blindly following the comics either. Storm (Maya Boyd) and Rogue (Inde Navarrette) are confirmed to appear, and both should be part of the X-Men team. Emma Frost (Samara Weaving) also remains a wildcard regarding what side she will fall on. Some of these characters could have larger roles than some of the founding members, but the important thing is they all get to be together at last.

Other mutants are sure to appear in X-Men, with Gambit and Nightcrawler two popular suggestions. Wolverine's potential presence looms over the whole project, as the MCU needs to figure out if the iconic hero will be recast, replaced by X-23, or continue to be played by Hugh Jackman (until he's 90). But that decision can be delayed thanks to X-Men's focus.

With the founding members taking precedence for the MCU, Wolverine sitting out the movie becomes easier to explain away. He is not part of the original lineup, as his comics debut didn't come until 12 years later. Wolverine's popularity quickly led to him taking a prominent role in X-Men titles, and that will happen for the MCU once he is properly introduced.

Rather than have Wolverine overshadow the rest of the X-Men from the start, he can sit out the first movie and allow the founding members more time to shine. This will be a better approach for the health of the MCU's future, as audiences need to care about more than just the adamantium-strengthened mutant.

X-Men could still wind up referencing Wolverine, but it's easier for comic readers and general audiences to understand why he isn't in the 2028 movie if Marvel sells the founding members' focus. Those mutants could then encounter him in a follow-up project after being more established as the core of the team concept in the MCU.

#3453. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3452. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3451. Sherlock & Elementary Are Getting An Unexpected Replacement With A Twist

The BBC's Sherlock and CBS’ Elementary are some of the best detective TV shows of all time, as well as notable modern adaptations of a literary classic, and years after their endings, they are getting an unexpected replacement with a twist. The crime drama genre is one of the most popular ones on TV, delivering some of the best TV shows of all time. Among them are different adaptations of Sherlock Holmes, most notably Sherlock and Elementary.

Both shows were based on Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s stories about Sherlock Holmes but with a modern twist, with Sherlock being set in modern-day London and Elementary in modern-day New York City. While they have different strengths and weaknesses, Sherlock and Elementary are some of the best modern adaptations of Sherlock Holmes, and while they have had worthy replacements, there's one coming up that, although not a Holmes adaptation, could easily take their place.

In October 2026, it was announced that a TV adaptation of The Great Gatsby is in development, but with a couple of twists. Like Sherlock and Elementary, this will be a modern version, which already makes the project quite exciting, but it has two major twists: a gender-swapped main character and a different genre that could potentially change the novel’s well-known story.

Written by F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby was published in 1925 and was inspired by a romance Fitzgerald had with a socialite and the parties he attended in 1922. The Great Gatsby is narrated in first-person by Nick Carraway, and it tells his story as he moves to Long Island and meets Jay Gatsby, his mysterious neighbor who throws extravagant parties every weekend. Gatsby has a purpose with all those parties: to win back the socialite (and Nick’s cousin) Daisy Buchanan, who is married to the wealthy Tom Buchanan.

Although Nick roots for Gatsby and Daisy, Gatsby hides many secrets, which come to light and further complicate their relationship and more. The Great Gatsby has been famously adapted to film, and on TV, it has been adapted as TV movies and episodes of other shows, so this is the first time the novel has been adapted to TV – however, it won’t be a faithful adaptation, as in addition to being set in the present, it will also be a procedural drama.

The show, currently titled Gatsby, is being developed by NBC and will star a gender-swapped version of Nick, named Nicole Carraway, a detective at the NYPD who dreams of being a writer. Also starring is Detective Jay Gatsby, described as a charming investigator with “a con-man’s gift for reading human behavior.” At the time of writing, no more details have been revealed about Gatsby, and as intriguing as the project is, it’s also quite risky.

A procedural drama approach to The Great Gatsby is unexpected and intriguing, but it also raises many questions, as it’s a risky twist to the story of Jay Gatsby. Nicole and Gatsby working together as detectives will make way for an interesting dynamic, potentially deeper and more developed than in the book, but it makes one wonder where and how the rest of the characters, especially Daisy, will fit into the story.

It can’t be a Great Gatsby adaptation without Daisy, so it’s to be seen what her story with Detective Gatsby will be, how he will try to get her back, and if Tom Buchanan is also included. The biggest risk, however, is how the show as a procedural drama will translate the message of the book. The Great Gatsby is a critique of the American Dream, and explores the hollowness of wealth and the hard truth beneath that shiny surface, plagued by loneliness, tragedy, corruption, and more.

Gatsby has the potential to be a surprising success and the next hit in modern adaptations of literary classics, and one can only hope that, despite the changes to the novel, it can stay true to the main traits of the characters and the message of the book.

#3450. Henry Cavill's Prime Video Sci-Fi Series Officially Gets First Major Update in 4 Months

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

For Henry Cavill, getting to bring Warhammer 40,000 to the screen means taking on a universe where even explaining the basics can become an evening’s commitment. Games Workshop’s tabletop franchise has expanded into an enormous collection of novels, video games, and stories about a future nobody should want to live in. Picking which corner deserves the first adaptation is a formidable assignment before anyone starts calculating the cost of a Space Marine.

Cavill’s enthusiasm makes him an appealing person to help guide that decision. Fans of The Witcher know how much he values the material behind his characters, and his interest in Warhammer predates his involvement in bringing it to Prime Video. The question is how to translate that passion into a series that longtime players recognize and newcomers can follow without homework.

Mike Flanagan has revealed that the team has found a “very cool and unexpected on-ramp” into Cavill’s Warhammer 40,000 adaptation. Speaking in a new interview, the writer discussed the challenge of introducing audiences to such an extensive fictional world while keeping the actual story under wraps. “Henry Cavill would be furious if I divulged anything about what we’re working on,” Flanagan said. He pointed to the setting’s roughly 700 novels, alongside its games and wider mythology, as evidence of the scale involved. Despite that challenge, he expressed enthusiasm for the work:

"[We found] a very cool and unexpected on-ramp into it, which I think is very exciting. I’m sworn to secrecy on all of it, but I’m having the time of my life working on it.”

Flanagan’s involvement became public in July, when Games Workshop’s financial reporting stated that initial outlines had been completed and script work was expected to follow. Cavill subsequently reaffirmed his involvement as a performer as well as a producer in August, while keeping his role secret. The latest comments offer another indication of the project’s creative direction, although its entry point remains undisclosed. Finding that starting point matters because Warhammer offers far more than armored warriors fighting spectacular battles. Its oppressive institutions, religious fanaticism, and supernatural horrors provide material for a wide range of stories. A series needs characters worth following through that nightmare, particularly when the setting itself offers so little reassurance that anyone will survive it.

That is where Flanagan’s experience becomes interesting. The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass build their horror around people whose grief, loyalties, and convictions shape the danger around them. Those instincts could serve this universe well, where believing absolutely in a cause can be as frightening as anything waiting on a battlefield. For now, the mystery is which story Cavill and Flanagan have chosen to tell. An unexpected starting point gives fans something to debate, but the next substantial reveal will be learning whose perspective brings us into this very unpleasant future.

Warhammer 40,000 is in development for Prime Video. A release date has not been announced.

#3449. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3448. Greg Biffle's Estate Accused of Selling Property, Giving Away His Memorabilia

Greg Biffle's estate is allegedly being picked apart ... and the family of one of the victims killed alongside the NASCAR star wants a judge to put a stop to it.

According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, a woman named Elena Smith claims those overseeing Biffle's estate have been selling off millions in assets and even giving away his personal memorabilia while wrongful death claims are still pending against the estate.

Smith is the administrator of the estate of Craig Wadsworth, Biffle's longtime right-hand man who also died in the December 2025 plane crash.

Smith claims Biffle's niece, Jordyn Biffle Carpenter, who is administering his estate, took control of his real estate company, NC Property LLC, and has sold multiple parcels of land for a combined $1.6 million since June ... without disclosing where the money went.

And there's more ... Smith alleges Biffle's yacht, "Checkered Past," is listed for sale in Florida for more than $4 million, despite allegedly being left off the estate's inventory.

The filing also claims Carpenter hosted a party at Biffle's mountain ranch in August ... where she allegedly handed out the late driver's personal memorabilia to guests as party favors.

All of this is unfolding as Biffle's estate faces at least $50 million in wrongful death claims stemming from the fatal plane crash ... including a claim of more than $10 million filed on Wadsworth's behalf.

As TMZ Sports previously reported ... the estates of Dennis Dutton, who was piloting the plane, and his son Jack sued Biffle's estate for a combined $30 million in April, alleging the NASCAR star was responsible for the crash due in part to inadequate aircraft maintenance.

Smith is now asking the court to halt further sales and distributions, order a full accounting of the estate's assets, and remove Carpenter as administrator ... and she also wants a neutral party appointed to take over.

The petition also claims Carpenter concealed a will Biffle signed months before his death, which allegedly named other people to oversee his estate.

Biffle, Wadsworth, and five others died on December 18, 2025, when a private jet crashed shortly after taking off from Statesville Regional Airport in North Carolina.

Biffle was a NASCAR legend who racked up 19 Cup Series wins during his career and made history as the first driver to win championships in both the Truck and Xfinity Series.

A hearing on Smith's petition to freeze Biffle's estate assets is scheduled for next week.

#3445. HBO Max's Lanterns Replacement Is Officially The Start Of A New DC Universe

HBO Max has found its Lanterns replacement in the perfect series, and it will mark the start of an exciting new DC Universe. Lanterns is one of the first projects in James Gunn's DCU, which has released six movies and TV shows thus far, with more confirmed to be on the way, such as 2027's Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow.

Lanterns was not the first DCU project to feature a Green Lantern, with David Corenswet's Superman movie marking the DCU debut of Nathan Fillion's Guy Gardner, who also showed up in the HBO sci-fi series. However, Lanterns served as the debut project for Kyle Chandler's Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre's John Stewart, the two most popular Green Lanterns from DC Comics.

After the old DCEU barely used any Green Lanterns, with no human versions ever making it to the big screen, it was exciting to watch Lanterns weave in three of the space cops into a mysterious storyline filled with twists. It remains to be seen whether HBO and DC will renew Lanterns for season 2, but with high viewership, positive reviews, and a writers' room already open, it is looking likely.

While Lanterns' fate remains undecided, DC Studios is already working on another Green Lantern TV show. However, this one is completely unrelated to Lanterns and Gunn's DCU, being one of the franchise's Elseworlds projects, which are either standalone or exist in separate universes outside DCU canon. That sci-fi series is My Adventures with Green Lantern.

After HBO's Lanterns came as a continuation of Gunn's DCU, My Adventures with Green Lantern will serve as the project that consolidates a new animated shared universe for DC Studios. In the past, DC has had multiple animated universes, including the Harley Quinn series and its spin-off Kite Man: Hell Yeah!, the Tomorrowverse movie continuity, the DC Animated Universe, and more. My Adventures with Green Lantern adds to that as a spin-off set in the same universe as My Adventures with Superman, which has three seasons currently streaming on HBO Max. The show is going for a different take on Green Lantern lore.

Rather than focusing on Hal Jordan, John Stewart, or Guy Gardner, My Adventures with Green Lantern stars a female hero, Jessica Cruz, who is a teenager in the story, having to deal with the result of an ancient space war as Green Lantern heroes and villains make their way to Earth, with Jessica being chosen by a power ring to serve as the new beacon of hope for an updated Green Lantern Corps. Jessica Cruz will be voiced by Moana star Auliʻi Cravalho, who made her debut in the role as a cameo in My Adventures with Superman season 3.
